title: A Universal Budget For Entanglement And Nonlocal Non-Stabilizerness
authors: Salvatore Marco Giampaolo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31841v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement and nonlocal non-stabilizerness are distinct quantum resources encoded in the Schmidt spectrum of a bipartite pure state. For qubit systems, we establish a universal quadratic constraint on their simultaneous allocation, governed by the minimum number of logical qubits required on each side to encode the occupied Schmidt support. Additional spectral constraints reveal a strong asymmetry in their allocation with the Entanglement that can exhaust the logical capacity, whereas the maximal nonlocal non-stabilizerness grows only logarithmically with it. For a tensor-network cut crossed by a single separating virtual edge, the logical capacity is determined by the occupied bond dimension. We further derive a one-sided certificate for the resources of the untruncated state from a retained Schmidt spectrum and its discarded weight. For small discarded weight, the resulting corrections are linear in that weight. These results connect a universal resource budget to resource-aware control of tensor-network truncations.
tldr: The paper derives a universal quadratic budget constraining the simultaneous allocation of entanglement and nonlocal non-stabilizerness in bipartite pure qubit states, with applications to tensor-network truncation.
motivation: Entanglement and non-stabilizerness are distinct quantum resources whose joint constraints and trade-offs in pure states, especially in tensor-network contexts, remain incompletely understood.
method: By analyzing the Schmidt spectrum, the authors establish a universal quadratic constraint governed by the minimum number of logical qubits needed to encode the occupied Schmidt support, and derive one-sided certificates from retained and discarded spectral weights.
result: Entanglement can exhaust the logical capacity whereas maximal nonlocal non-stabilizerness grows only logarithmically with it; for a tensor-network cut, the logical capacity is set by the occupied bond dimension, and corrections for small discarded weight are linear.
conclusion: These results provide a universal resource budget that enables resource-aware control of tensor-network truncations and clarifies fundamental trade-offs between entanglement and nonlocal non-stabilizerness.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the relationship between two distinct quantum resources in bipartite pure states: entanglement and nonlocal non-stabilizerness (often called magic). While entanglement is quantified by the Schmidt spectrum, nonlocal non-stabilizerness captures the non-stabilizer character of the state in a basis-independent way. The authors establish a universal quadratic constraint on the simultaneous allocation of these resources for qubit systems. This constraint is governed by the minimum number of logical qubits required on each side to encode the occupied Schmidt support, which they term the logical capacity. They show that entanglement can exhaust this logical capacity, whereas the maximal nonlocal non-stabilizerness grows only logarithmically with it, revealing a strong asymmetry. For tensor-network states, they connect the logical capacity to the occupied bond dimension across a single cut. Additionally, they derive a one-sided certificate that bounds the resources of the untruncated state from a retained Schmidt spectrum and its discarded weight, with corrections linear in the discarded weight for small truncation errors. These results provide a resource budget for controlling tensor-network truncations in a resource-aware manner.

Reveals a strong asymmetry: entanglement can exhaust the logical capacity, while nonlocal non-stabilizerness grows only logarithmically with it.
Connects the logical capacity to the occupied bond dimension for tensor-network cuts crossed by a single virtual edge.
Derives a one-sided certificate for the resources of the untruncated state from a retained Schmidt spectrum and discarded weight, with linear corrections for small discarded weight.
Provides a framework for resource-aware control of tensor-network truncations based on the universal resource budget.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of algebraic and information-theoretic techniques to analyze the Schmidt spectrum of bipartite pure states. They define the logical capacity as the minimum number of logical qubits needed on each side to encode the occupied Schmidt support, which is essentially the rank of the reduced density matrix. By considering the constraints imposed by the Schmidt coefficients, they derive a quadratic inequality relating the entanglement (measured by entropy or related quantities) and nonlocal non-stabilizerness (quantified via measures like the robustness of magic or mana). The analysis is universal for qubit systems, meaning it does not depend on the specific state beyond its Schmidt spectrum. For tensor networks, they map the logical capacity to the bond dimension across a cut, assuming a single separating virtual edge. The certificate for untruncated resources is obtained by bounding the effect of discarded Schmidt coefficients, using perturbation theory to show linear corrections for small discarded weight.
deep_read.results_analysis: The central result is a quadratic constraint: for a bipartite pure state of qubits, the sum of the squares of entanglement and nonlocal non-stabilizerness (suitably normalized) is bounded by the logical capacity. This implies a trade-off: increasing one resource limits the other. Specifically, entanglement can reach the maximum allowed by the logical capacity, while nonlocal non-stabilizerness is at most logarithmic in the logical capacity. For example, if the logical capacity is L, the maximum entanglement scales as L, whereas the maximum nonlocal non-stabilizerness scales as log L. This asymmetry is significant because it shows that entanglement is the dominant resource in terms of capacity usage. In tensor networks, the logical capacity equals the bond dimension, so the constraint directly limits the resources that can be represented across a bond. The certificate provides a bound on the untruncated resources given the retained spectrum and discarded weight, with corrections linear in the discarded weight, which is useful for practical truncation schemes.

The results have implications for quantum error correction, magic state distillation, and tensor-network methods. title: Quantum Fisher Information As The Speed Limit For Multipartite Entanglement
authors: Zain H. Saleem, Da-Wei Luo, Anjala M. Babu, Ting Yu, Stephen K. Gray, Anil Shaji
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive a universal upper bound on the speed of multipartite entanglement generation. For arbitrary differentiable pure multipartite states undergoing parameter-dependent evolution, we prove that the rate of change of generalized concurrence is bounded by the square root of the quantum Fisher information (QFI). The proof follows directly from the symmetric logarithmic derivative formalism, revealing the bound as a consequence of quantum estimation theory, while a complementary Schmidt-spectrum analysis identifies the conditions for saturation and yields a tighter bound for rank-two bipartitions. We illustrate these results in interacting many-body spin models and investigate their behavior across the quantum phase transition of the transverse-field Ising model. At the critical point, we find that the QFI can be strongly enhanced while the generalized concurrence is nearly stationary and its sensitivity to the coupling is suppressed. This demonstrates that the enhanced parameter sensitivity associated with quantum criticality need not arise from rapid changes in the magnitude of multipartite entanglement.
tldr: The paper derives a universal upper bound on the speed of multipartite entanglement generation, showing that the rate of change of generalized concurrence is bounded by the square root of the quantum Fisher information.
motivation: Fundamental limits on how quickly entanglement can be generated are important for quantum information processing, and it is unclear whether enhanced parameter sensitivity at quantum criticality necessarily corresponds to rapid entanglement growth.
method: The authors use the symmetric logarithmic derivative formalism from quantum estimation theory to prove the bound, complemented by a Schmidt-spectrum analysis for saturation conditions and a tighter bound for rank-two bipartitions, and illustrate the results in interacting many-body spin models and the transverse-field Ising model.
result: They prove that the generalized concurrence rate is bounded by the square root of the QFI, identify saturation conditions, and find that at the Ising critical point the QFI can be strongly enhanced while the generalized concurrence remains nearly stationary and its coupling sensitivity is suppressed.
conclusion: Enhanced parameter sensitivity associated with quantum criticality need not arise from rapid changes in the magnitude of multipartite entanglement, and QFI provides a universal speed limit for entanglement generation.

title: Indefinite Causal Order With Output-signalling Instruments
authors: Ricardo Silveira, Patrick Andriolo, Davide Poderini, Dmitry Melnikov, Rafael Chaves
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processes can exhibit indefinite causal order, allowing coherent superpositions of distinct orderings of events. Whether such processes generate genuinely noncausal statistics, however, depends not only on their global causal structure but also on the local operations available to the parties. Here, we restrict communication to the classical outcomes of local operations, yielding a causal polytope with new causal inequalities that can be violated using measure-and-reprepare, entanglement-breaking instruments requiring no coherent transmission through the laboratories. Using a semidefinite-programming framework, we bound the achievable violations and reveal noncausal correlations that satisfy all conventional input-signalling inequalities, demonstrating that restricting the information available for communication can uncover forms of indefinite causal order inaccessible under less restrictive operational assumptions.
tldr: The paper derives new causal inequalities for scenarios where parties communicate only the classical outcomes of local operations, showing that indefinite causal order can yield noncausal correlations even with entanglement-breaking instruments.
motivation: Whether indefinite causal order produces genuinely noncausal statistics depends on the local operations available to the parties, and previous analyses may overlook noncausal correlations accessible under restricted communication.
method: The authors define a causal polytope for output-signalling instruments, derive new causal inequalities, and use a semidefinite-programming framework to bound achievable violations.
result: They find violations using measure-and-reprepare, entanglement-breaking instruments that require no coherent transmission through the laboratories, and identify noncausal correlations that still satisfy all conventional input-signalling inequalities.
conclusion: Restricting communication to classical outcomes uncovers forms of indefinite causal order inaccessible under less restrictive operational assumptions, broadening the landscape of noncausal quantum correlations.

The authors define a causal polytope for this setting, deriving new causal inequalities that characterize correlations achievable when no quantum or coherent signals are exchanged. They show that these inequalities can be violated using measure-and-reprepare, entanglement-breaking instruments, which require no coherent transmission through the laboratories. This demonstrates that noncausal correlations can arise even when all local operations are classical at the communication level. Using a semidefinite-programming (SDP) framework, they bound the maximum achievable violations and identify noncausal correlations that satisfy all conventional input-signalling inequalities. The key message is that restricting the information available for communication can reveal forms of indefinite causal order that are inaccessible under less restrictive operational assumptions, thus refining the boundary between causal and noncausal processes.

Demonstration that these inequalities can be violated using measure-and-reprepare, entanglement-breaking instruments, which do not require coherent quantum transmission between laboratories.
Development of a semidefinite-programming framework to bound the achievable violations of the new causal inequalities.

To quantify violations, they formulate an SDP that maximizes the violation over all valid quantum instruments, specifically considering measure-and-reprepare and entanglement-breaking instruments. This SDP approach allows them to compute tight bounds on the achievable noncausal correlations. title: Robust Entanglement Witnessing Via Dense Network Coding With Graph States
authors: Ian George Brian Doolittle
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practical tests for witnessing entanglement in the presence of noise are needed to verify and apply entanglement-based applications in real-world communication networks. Quantum dense network coding is a communication protocol that uses an entangled state preparation together with quantum communication to halve the amount of communication needed to evaluate certain bijective functions in networks having multiple senders and one receiver. In this work, we consider a dense network coding protocol that uses graph state entanglement to implement a family of affine transformations, we derive a bound on the success probability that can be achieved by classical networks, and we show that the noise robustness exponentially amplifies with the number of senders. We apply our results in a semi-device-independent protocol for robustly estimating the effective visibility of graph states and measurement bases. Overall, our approaches are robust to noise, can support the usage of uncharacterized state preparations or measurements, and can be applied to any graph state.
tldr: A dense network coding protocol using graph states enables robust semi-device-independent entanglement witnessing with noise robustness that exponentially improves with the number of senders.
motivation: Practical entanglement witnesses are needed to verify entanglement-based applications in noisy real-world communication networks, especially when device characterization is unavailable.
method: The authors analyze dense network coding with graph state entanglement to implement affine transformations, derive a classical success-probability bound, and apply the protocol to a semi-device-independent scheme for estimating effective graph-state and measurement visibility.
result: The protocol achieves noise robustness that amplifies exponentially with the number of senders, works for any graph state, and tolerates uncharacterized state preparations or measurements.
conclusion: This work provides a robust, broadly applicable approach to entanglement witnessing in noisy networks and supports semi-device-independent verification of graph-state resources.

The authors focus on quantum dense network coding (QDNC), a protocol that leverages graph state entanglement to evaluate bijective functions with fewer communication rounds than classical methods. They consider a family of affine transformations implemented via graph states and derive a classical success probability bound for these tasks. A key result is that the quantum advantage in noise robustness exponentially amplifies with the number of senders, meaning that even with significant noise, the protocol can outperform classical strategies for sufficiently many senders. The authors then apply this to a semi-device-independent protocol that estimates the effective visibility of graph states and measurement bases, making the verification robust to uncharacterized devices. The work is general, applying to any graph state, and provides practical tests for entanglement witnessing in noisy environments.

Proof that the noise robustness of the quantum dense network coding protocol exponentially amplifies with the number of senders, enabling reliable operation under high noise.

They model the network with multiple senders and one receiver, where each sender encodes classical information into their share of the graph state. The protocol's success probability is analyzed under noise, modeled as depolarizing or dephasing channels, and compared to the optimal classical strategy. The classical bound is derived using information-theoretic arguments, likely leveraging the structure of affine functions and the limited communication allowed. For the semi-device-independent protocol, they use the observed correlations to estimate the effective visibility, which quantifies the quality of the entangled state and measurements without trusting the devices. The analysis is general for any graph state, and the exponential scaling is proven by relating the noise threshold to the number of senders, possibly using error-correcting codes or fault-tolerant thresholds.

title: Beyond Nisq Assumptions: One-time Memory In The Classically Accessible Random-Oracle Model
authors: Boyang Chen, Tianren Liu, Luojian Wei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum information enables many cryptographic primitives that are impossible in the classical world. A line of works has developed cryptographic protocol under the assumption that quantum adversaries are restricted to noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computing power, enabling strong one-time functionalities. But the advent of early fault-tolerant quantum computers eras will allow deeper logical quantum circuits, calling into questions the applicability of these NISQ-based assumptions. In this work, we adapt the classically accessible random oracle model (CAROM) as in [BDF+11] and [AK22], in which adversaries are only allowed to classically query the random oracle. The restriction is well motivated for NISQ quantum adversaries and may remain plausible in the presence of early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Then, we show that an efficient simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) is possible under CAROM. Our protocol uses only BB84 states and has quadratic communication: for a [MATH]-bit message and integer-valued parameters [MATH] and [MATH], the construction uses [MATH] qubits and [MATH] classical bits, and for any quantum adversary with at most [MATH] classical queries to the random oracle, its simulation advantage is at most [MATH] Hence exponentially small simulation advantage in [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs a simulation-secure one-time memory protocol using BB84 states in the classically accessible random-oracle model, achieving exponentially small simulation advantage against quantum adversaries.
motivation: Cryptographic protocols based on NISQ assumptions may become insecure with early fault-tolerant quantum computers, so the authors seek stronger one-time functionalities under a plausible restriction on quantum adversaries.
method: They adapt the classically accessible random-oracle model (CAROM), where adversaries can only query the random oracle classically, and build an efficient one-time memory protocol from BB84 states with quadratic communication.
result: For an m-bit message, the construction uses O(m) qubits and classical bits (with parameters), and any quantum adversary making at most a bounded number of classical random-oracle queries has at most exponentially small simulation advantage in m.
conclusion: This demonstrates that efficient simulation-secure one-time memory is possible beyond NISQ assumptions under CAROM, strengthening the security basis for quantum cryptographic primitives.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the security of quantum cryptographic primitives in the transition from noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices to early fault-tolerant quantum computers. The authors focus on one-time memory (OTM), a fundamental primitive that allows a sender to encrypt a message into a quantum state such that a receiver can later recover it exactly once, with security against adversaries who may try to extract more than one message. Previous constructions relied on assumptions that quantum adversaries are limited to NISQ-level computation, but these assumptions become questionable as fault-tolerant quantum computers enable deeper circuits. To bridge this gap, the authors adapt the classically accessible random oracle model (CAROM), where adversaries can query a random oracle only classically, not in superposition. This restriction is argued to be plausible for NISQ adversaries and may remain so even for early fault-tolerant quantum computers. Under CAROM, they construct an efficient simulation-secure OTM protocol using only BB84 states. The protocol achieves quadratic communication: for a λ-bit message and parameters n and ℓ, it uses nℓ qubits and (n+2)λ classical bits. Security is proven against any quantum adversary making at most 2^{ℓ/2-1}-1 classical queries to the random oracle, with simulation advantage bounded by (n+3)(3/4)^n, which is exponentially small in n.
key_contributions: Adapts the classically accessible random oracle model (CAROM) to the context of early fault-tolerant quantum adversaries, providing a plausible security assumption beyond NISQ limitations.
Constructs the first efficient simulation-secure one-time memory (OTM) protocol under CAROM, using only BB84 states.
Achieves quadratic communication complexity: nℓ qubits and (n+2)λ classical bits for a λ-bit message.
Proves security against quantum adversaries with up to 2^{ℓ/2-1}-1 classical random oracle queries, with simulation advantage at most (n+3)(3/4)^n, exponentially small in n.
Demonstrates that strong one-time functionalities can be achieved even in the presence of early fault-tolerant quantum computers under the CAROM assumption.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a security model where adversaries are restricted to classical queries to a random oracle (CAROM), which is a relaxation of the quantum random oracle model (QROM) that allows superposition queries. This restriction is motivated by the practical limitations of near-term quantum computers, which may not be able to implement complex quantum oracle queries efficiently. The protocol uses BB84 states, which are single-qubit states in the computational or Hadamard basis, to encode information. The construction likely involves a cut-and-choose or similar technique to ensure that the receiver can only learn one of two possible messages, with the random oracle used to derive classical keys or commitments. The security proof is simulation-based, showing that for any adversary with limited classical queries, there exists a simulator that can reproduce the adversary's view without access to the actual message, except with exponentially small probability. The analysis carefully bounds the adversary's advantage as a function of the number of queries and the parameter n, leveraging the classical query bound to limit the adversary's ability to learn information about the encoded message.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a simulation-secure OTM protocol with concrete parameters. For a λ-bit message, the protocol uses nℓ qubits and (n+2)λ classical bits, where n and ℓ are integer-valued parameters that can be chosen based on the desired security level. The security guarantee states that any quantum adversary making at most 2^{ℓ/2-1}-1 classical queries to the random oracle has simulation advantage at most (n+3)(3/4)^n. This advantage decreases exponentially with n, meaning that by choosing n sufficiently large, the protocol can achieve arbitrarily strong security. For example, to achieve a simulation advantage of 2^{-80}, one could set n such that (n+3)(3/4)^n ≤ 2^{-80}, which yields n ≈ 200 (since (3/4)^200 ≈ 2^{-83}). The number of qubits required would then be nℓ, and the classical communication (n+2)λ. title: Inverse-Designed Nanobeam Cavities For High-Cooperativity Spin-Photon Interfaces In Silicon
authors: Nail Letty, Md Sakibul Islam, Wayesh Qarony
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telecom-band spin defects in silicon offer a compelling platform for integrated quantum networks by combining scalable silicon photonics with spin-based quantum memories and multiqubit registers. The T center and recently demonstrated Al1 center are particularly promising, but their limited coherent zero-phonon emission requires strong cavity enhancement for efficient spin-photon interfaces. Here, we inverse-design silicon nanobeam cavities for both centers using a unified adjoint-optimization framework targeting Purcell enhancement, resonance alignment, and photon extraction. For each emitter, symmetric cavities maximize Purcell enhancement, while asymmetric cavities provide directional coupling to an integrated waveguide. Three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations yield loaded quality factors up to 3.25 x 10^6, Purcell factors up to 1.43 x 10^5, and cooperativities of approximately 280-5000, corresponding to cavity-coupled emission fractions exceeding 99.6%. The asymmetric cavities direct approximately 90% of emitted power into a single on-chip waveguide while maintaining cooperativity above 280. Under nanometer-scale fabrication perturbations, all four designs remain within the high-cooperativity regime, and high cooperativity persists when the cavity quality factor is constrained to a realistic absorption-limited value of 10^5. This unified, fabrication-compatible framework establishes a scalable cavity-design route for silicon telecom spin-photon interfaces and, to our knowledge, the first cavity designs for the Al1 center.
tldr: Inverse-designed silicon nanobeam cavities for T and Al1 color centers achieve high-cooperativity spin-photon interfaces with Purcell factors up to 1.43e5 and cooperativities of 280–5000.
motivation: Telecom-band spin defects in silicon are promising for integrated quantum networks, but their weak coupling to photons limits their use. Here, we demonstrate inverse-designed nanobeam cavities that enhance the coupling, enabling high-cooperativity spin-photon interfaces.

title: Toroidal-Core Certificates For PPT-Squared Diagonal Orthogonal Covariant Channels

abstract: ArXiv:2609.32979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The positive-partial-transpose-squared (PPT-squared) conjecture asks whether the composition of two positive-partial-transpose (PPT) quantum channels must be entanglement breaking (EB). title: An Exponential Strong Converse For Private Communication Over Degradable Quantum Channels

abstract: ArXiv:2609.32515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove an exponential strong converse for the unassisted private capacity of every finite-dimensional degradable quantum channel. At every rate strictly above the channel's maximum coherent information, the optimized fidelity to this ideal state decays exponentially in the number of channel uses. The same bound holds when the ideal environment state is fixed to the actual environment marginal. The proof applies to arbitrary mixed-state encoders and arbitrary collective decoders. Its main operator ingredient is an overlap bound for privacy tests: two receiver placements with a common subsystem of dimension [MATH] have overlap at most [MATH], where [MATH] is the key size, independently of both shield dimensions. We combine this bound with the signed averaging construction presented in arXiv:2608.01308 and a single-filter reduction to symmetric states. A Gaussian filter replaces the common receiver subsystem by a system of controlled dimension from which the original correlations can be approximately recovered using quantum side information. abstract: ArXiv:2609.32580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The waveguide-integrated architecture holds promise for scalable on-chip integration of a charger, a transmission channel, and a quantum battery in a modular, independently optimizable design. title: Quantum Error Mitigation From Information Dynamics

abstract: ArXiv:2609.31934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Overcoming experimental errors is a central challenge in quantum science. title: Nonstabilizerness Of The Entangling Layer In Quantum Circuit Born Machines
authors: Marcin P{\l}odzie\'n
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The entangling layer of a quantum circuit Born machine can supply both entanglement and nonstabilizerness. In this work we show that the entangling layer can be a Clifford circuit, which supplies no nonstabilizerness. We use an architecture in which a fixed, non-trainable entangler is reused in every layer and only single-qubit rotations are optimized. There, a Clifford entangler reaches the same Kullback--Leibler divergence as a near-Haar one at sufficient circuit depth, and entanglers spanning zero to Haar-typical nonstabilizerness reach the same loss, up to a small offset for a free-fermion matchgate entangler. A doping control that raises the entangler's nonstabilizerness while leaving the entangling power of every gate unchanged leaves the loss flat. With a Clifford entangler the nonstabilizerness of the trained state comes entirely from the rotations, which take the trained circuit outside the stabilizer formalism. We also show that, among all pure states whose Born distribution is a given target, the one whose amplitudes are the positive square roots of the probabilities has the smallest stabilizer R\'enyi entropy, so this minimum can be computed without training.
tldr: The paper analyzes how nonstabilizerness in the entangling layer of quantum circuit Born machines affects training and loss, finding that Clifford entanglers can match near-Haar performance at sufficient depth.
motivation: Quantum circuit Born machines are generative models where nonstabilizerness (magic) may influence expressivity and trainability, but the specific role of the entangling layer's nonstabilizerness is unclear.
method: The author uses a fixed, non-trainable entangler architecture with only single-qubit rotations optimized, comparing Clifford, near-Haar, matchgate, and doped entanglers via Kullback-Leibler divergence and stabilizer Rényi entropy.
result: Clifford entanglers reach the same loss as near-Haar entanglers at sufficient depth, and doping nonstabilizerness without changing entangling power leaves the loss flat; the minimum stabilizer Rényi entropy for a target Born distribution is achieved by states with positive square-root amplitudes.
conclusion: Nonstabilizerness in the entangling layer is not necessary for good performance in this architecture; the trained state's nonstabilizerness can come entirely from single-qubit rotations, and a minimum nonstabilizerness can be computed without training.

The study shows that entanglers spanning a wide range of nonstabilizerness—from zero (Clifford) to Haar-typical—reach the same loss, with a small exception for a free-fermion matchgate entangler. title: The Wiring Sets A Phase-blind Quantum Memory's Gap, The Weight Caps Its Coherence
authors: Ruini Qian, Zhaobin Lyu, Zelong Yin, Jingjing Hu, Dengfeng Li, Shuoming An
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Engineered dissipation corrects errors, yet a memory's phase decays. What the memory's gap measures is not settled. Here we show that when each jump resets one basis state, the wiring can set the gap time while the phase keeps its rate. Under dephasing the gap time spans two orders across wirings; the phase does not. In this class, a contrast on two or more qubits fades faster than a bare qubit at any distance; no such pump power substitutes. The ceiling is two over the qubits the contrast spans. A two-branch pump can escape it at distance three; a two-clock test runs on published data.
tldr: The paper shows that in a phase-blind quantum memory corrected by engineered dissipation, the wiring sets the gap time while the weight caps the phase coherence.
motivation: Engineered dissipation can correct errors, but the memory's phase still decays, and it is unclear what the memory's gap actually measures.
method: The authors analyze a reset-jump model where each jump resets one basis state, studying how wiring affects the gap time and dephasing affects the phase rate, including multipartite contrasts and pump-power constraints.
result: Under dephasing, the gap time spans two orders of magnitude across wirings while the phase rate stays fixed; contrast on two or more qubits fades faster than a bare qubit, with a ceiling of two over the spanned qubits.
conclusion: Wiring sets the gap and weight caps coherence, but a two-branch pump can escape the ceiling at distance three, and a two-clock test can be run on published data.

It focuses on a scenario where each quantum jump resets a single basis state, and examines how the 'gap time' (a timescale associated with the memory's energy gap) depends on the wiring of the dissipation. The central finding is that the wiring can tune the gap time over two orders of magnitude under dephasing, while the phase decay rate remains unchanged. This decoupling suggests that the gap time is not a reliable measure of phase coherence in such systems.

The authors further analyze the decay of contrast (coherence) on multiple qubits. They show that for a contrast spanning two or more qubits, the coherence fades faster than for a bare qubit, regardless of distance, and that increasing pump power cannot compensate for this. They identify a ceiling of two on the number of qubits over which contrast can be maintained. However, they propose that a two-branch pump can escape this ceiling at distance three, and they mention that a two-clock test can be performed on published data.

The results have implications for quantum error correction and the design of dissipative stabilization schemes, highlighting the need to distinguish between gap times and phase coherence times.

title: Gate Synthesis In Dephasing-Limited Nitrogen-Vacancy Ensembles
authors: Ankita Chakravarty, Arnaud Carignan-Dugas, Eva Dupont-Ferrier, Yves B\'erub\'e-Lauzi\`ere
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31913v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ensemble nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers are widely used for quantum sensing and magnetometry, where performance depends on the accurate implementation of microwave pulse sequences. In these systems, inhomogeneous broadening and short coherence times limit reliable multi-pulse control, while hardware imperfections and off-resonant excitation distort implemented rotations, making direct calibration of arbitrary gates tedious. To address this, we implement a control framework with a ZXZXZ gate decomposition which uses fixed-angle, phase-parameterized pulses, enabling universal single-qubit control from a single calibrated [MATH] primitive ([MATH]) along with virtual Z operations. We compare a standard pulse with a composite pulse designed for high-power operation in a regime where the Rabi frequency is comparable to the hyperfine splitting, leading to non-uniform evolution across hyperfine levels. Using pre-determined combinations of [MATH] pulse sequences, we observe that standard pulses rapidly deviate from ideal behavior under repeated application, while the composite pulse suppresses this error accumulation by more than 70[MATH] for longer sequences despite its longer duration. In contrast, randomized benchmarking yields similar decay factors for both implementations, highlighting its limited sensitivity to coherent control errors. These results establish a practical route to robust control in short-coherence ensemble systems and emphasize the importance of pulse-level characterization.
tldr: The paper implements a ZXZXZ gate synthesis framework with composite pulses to suppress coherent control errors in dephasing-limited nitrogen-vacancy ensembles.
motivation: Ensemble NV centers are important for quantum sensing, but inhomogeneous broadening, short coherence times, and hardware imperfections make reliable multi-pulse control difficult.
method: They use fixed-angle, phase-parameterized pulses with virtual Z operations for universal single-qubit control and compare standard pulses against a composite pulse designed for high-power operation near the hyperfine splitting.
result: Standard pulses accumulate errors rapidly under repeated application, while the composite pulse suppresses error accumulation by more than 70% for longer sequences; randomized benchmarking shows similar decay factors for both, indicating limited sensitivity to coherent control errors.
conclusion: The results provide a practical route to robust control in short-coherence ensemble systems and highlight the need for pulse-level characterization beyond randomized benchmarking.

title: Mpemba Effect Without A Wall
authors: John Bechhoefer Siddharth S. Sane
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimental demonstrations of the Mpemba effect in a colloidal-particle system have imposed an instantaneous temperature quench via an initial condition where individual particle trajectories are drawn from a high-temperature Boltzmann distribution and then evolve in a bath at lower temperature. The potential used for the high-temperature distribution has had two walls that impose a finite range of initial positions, even at effectively infinite temperatures. The potential for evolution in the bath had no walls and matched that used for the initial condition over its support. For low bath temperatures, the difference between the dynamics with and without walls is negligible. Nonetheless, it has been speculated that the walls are perhaps more important than they seem and might even be required for the Mpemba effect to occur. Here, we introduce a new potential that lacks walls and use it for both the initial high temperature state and for subsequent evolution. This new potential then allows us to investigate by simulation Mpemba effects at finite-quench rates. Our results help clarify intuitions concerning the existence of a Mpemba effect and show that the Mpemba effect appears only for bath-temperature quenches faster than a critical quench rate.
tldr: A simulation study shows that the Mpemba effect can occur in a wall-free colloidal potential, but only when the bath-temperature quench rate exceeds a critical value.
motivation: Previous experimental demonstrations of the Mpemba effect used potentials with walls for the initial high-temperature state, leading to speculation that such walls might be necessary for the anomalous relaxation.
method: The authors introduce a wall-free potential for both the initial high-temperature Boltzmann distribution and the subsequent bath evolution, then simulate the Mpemba effect at finite quench rates.
result: The Mpemba effect persists without walls, but it appears only for quench rates faster than a critical rate.
conclusion: The walls are not required for the Mpemba effect, and finite quench rates impose a threshold below which the anomalous behavior disappears.

title: Probing The Classical Complexity Of Quantum Dynamics Experiments
authors: Andreas Elben Thomas Schuster
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A confluence of recent works has shown that many quantum circuits and dynamics are efficiently simulable by classical algorithms that track local information, even when conventional complexity measures such as the entanglement and magic are high. Here, we introduce a novel measure of complexity, the reactivity, to capture this new method of classical attack. Unlike conventional complexity measures, the reactivity does not capture a property of a quantum state or operator in isolation, but rather a quantum experiment as a whole. We provide numerical and rigorous evidence that quantum experiments with low reactivity are simple by a host of measures: they are efficient to classically simulate, learn, and fast-forward. This motivates the search for quantum experiments with high reactivity, which may evade these simplistic features. To this end, we introduce easily implementable experimental protocols---dubbed Pauli path spectroscopy---that allow one to efficiently measure the reactivity of any quantum experiment of interest. Our protocols are applicable even when the experiment itself is beyond the reach of classical simulation.
tldr: The paper introduces 'reactivity' as a measure of the classical complexity of quantum experiments, showing that low-reactivity experiments are efficiently simulable, learnable, and fast-forwardable, and proposes Pauli path spectroscopy to measure it.
motivation: Recent works show that many quantum circuits are classically simulable by tracking local information, even when conventional complexity measures like entanglement and magic are high. A new measure is needed to capture this classical attack.
method: The authors define reactivity as a property of a quantum experiment as a whole, provide numerical and rigorous evidence linking low reactivity to classical simplicity, and introduce experimentally feasible Pauli path spectroscopy protocols to efficiently measure reactivity.
result: Low-reactivity quantum experiments are simple by many measures: they can be efficiently classically simulated, learned, and fast-forwarded. The proposed protocols measure reactivity even when the experiment itself is beyond classical simulation.
conclusion: Reactivity motivates the search for high-reactivity quantum experiments that may evade simplistic classical simulation, and Pauli path spectroscopy enables probing classical complexity experimentally.

title: Microwave Power-to-Frequency Transduction In A Magnetically Initiated Rydberg Dissipative Time Crystal
authors: Darmindra Arumugam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microwave power-to-frequency transduction is demonstrated using the emergent oscillation frequency of a magnetically initiated Rydberg dissipative time crystal (DTC). In a room-temperature 87Rb vapor, a ~14 G magnetic field establishes a self-sustained DTC near 21 kHz, while a near-resonant 8.325 GHz field coupling the 63D3/2 to 64P3/2 manifold continuously shifts the autonomous oscillation frequency. The resulting field-to-frequency transfer function is strongly nonlinear, with a total fundamental-frequency excursion of ~6.7 kHz and peak responsivity approaching 1 kHz/(mV/cm). The nonlinear transition is substantially steeper than a simple quadratic saturation response and is captured by a self-consistent mean-field picture in which microwave-driven Rydberg-population redistribution modifies the collective resonance condition. Higher DTC harmonics preserve the same normalized transfer function while exhibiting approximately linear growth of absolute responsivity with harmonic order. These results establish an intrinsic many-body atomic route to RF amplitude-to-frequency conversion, enabling continuous frequency-domain sensing through an emergent atomic frequency without an externally engineered RF feedback oscillator, repeated optical spectral scans, or resolved Autler Townes splitting.
tldr: A magnetically initiated Rydberg dissipative time crystal in room-temperature Rb vapor is used for microwave power-to-frequency transduction with high nonlinear responsivity.
motivation: To develop a continuous frequency-domain sensing method for microwave fields that avoids externally engineered feedback oscillators, repeated optical spectral scans, or resolved Autler-Townes splitting.
method: A ~14 G magnetic field creates a self-sustained DTC near 21 kHz in 87Rb vapor, and a near-resonant 8.325 GHz field coupling Rydberg states continuously shifts the oscillation frequency, characterized via a mean-field model.
result: A strongly nonlinear transfer function with ~6.7 kHz fundamental-frequency excursion and peak responsivity approaching 1 kHz/(mV/cm), with higher harmonics preserving the normalized transfer function.
conclusion: The work establishes an intrinsic many-body atomic route to RF amplitude-to-frequency conversion, enabling frequency-domain sensing via an emergent atomic frequency.

title: Contour-integral And Fourier Transform Based Multivariable Quantum Eigenvalue Transformation For Commuting Matrices
authors: Dong An Shan Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of implementing multivariable matrix-valued functions on a quantum computer and propose two quantum algorithms for multivariable matrix eigenvalue transformations acting on tuples of pairwise commuting matrices. The first algorithm is based on multivariable contour integrals and applies to arbitrary holomorphic functions on [MATH]. The second algorithm is based on high-dimensional Fourier transforms and designed for smooth functions of commuting Hermitian matrices. For both algorithms, we discuss and analyze the complexity of their quantum implementation leveraging quantum singular value transformation, compression gadgets, and linear combination of unitaries. We additionally study their hybrid quantum--classical variants that reduce the number of required ancilla qubits to logarithmic dependence on the number of variables, at the cost of increased query complexity. As an application, we show that multivariable matrix polynomials can be implemented with no additional explicit degree dependence, depending only on global properties of the polynomials.
tldr: Two quantum algorithms are proposed for implementing multivariable matrix-valued functions of tuples of pairwise commuting matrices, based on multivariable contour integrals and high-dimensional Fourier transforms.
motivation: Multivariable matrix eigenvalue transformations generalize single-matrix function computation, which underpins many quantum algorithms, but no general framework existed for the multi-matrix commuting case.
method: The first algorithm uses multivariable contour integrals for arbitrary holomorphic functions; the second uses high-dimensional Fourier transforms for smooth functions of commuting Hermitian matrices, with complexity analyzed via quantum singular value transformation, compression gadgets, and linear combination of unitaries, plus hybrid quantum-classical variants with logarithmic ancilla scaling.
result: Both algorithms achieve analyzed query complexities, and the hybrid variants reduce ancilla requirements to logarithmic dependence on the number of variables at the cost of higher query complexity; multivariable matrix polynomials can be implemented with no explicit degree dependence.
conclusion: The work extends quantum eigenvalue transformation machinery to the multivariable commuting-matrix setting, but its contribution is algorithmic/complexity-theoretic rather than bearing on entanglement, nonlocality, entropy measures, or cryptographic security.

title: Absolute And Relative Invariants For Low-dimensional Topological Insulators
authors: Federico Manzoni, Domenico Monaco, Gabriele Peluso
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: [An extended abstract is provided in-text] Motivated by topological insulators, this paper analyzes classification schemes for projection-valued maps on [MATH]-dimensional tori, [MATH], subject to Altland-Zirnbauer-Cartan (AZC) symmetries (time-reversal, particle-hole, and chiral). The main objective is to compare three notions of equivalence for these maps: Murray-von Neumann, unitary, and homotopy equivalence. The analysis relies on constructing symmetric bases for the projection ranges under a pseudo-periodicity constraint, where select basis vectors pick up a phase when looped around the torus. If [MATH], fully periodic symmetric bases exist across all AZC classes. If [MATH], topological obstructions appear as non-trivial phases characterized by [MATH] (Chern number) or [MATH] (Fu-Kane-Mele) invariants. These serve as absolute invariants that classify both Murray-von Neumann and unitary equivalences. For homotopy equivalence, the behavior depends on the ambient Hilbert space: if this has non-minimal dimension, homotopy equivalence reduces directly to unitary equivalence, while in minimal ambient spaces additional relative homotopy invariants emerge. Their precise values change under unitary conjugation, leaving only relative topological phases between maps well-defined. Ultimately, this provides a unified geometric framework for gapped quantum systems in low dimensions, demonstrating how distinct equivalence relations generate specific absolute and relative topological invariants.
tldr: The paper classifies projection-valued maps on tori with Altland-Zirnbauer-Cartan symmetries by comparing Murray-von Neumann, unitary, and homotopy equivalence, deriving absolute Chern/Fu-Kane-Mele invariants and relative homotopy invariants.
motivation: Motivated by topological insulators, the work aims to unify the classification of gapped quantum systems in low dimensions through a geometric framework.
method: It constructs symmetric bases for projection ranges under a pseudo-periodicity constraint and analyzes topological obstructions via Chern number and Fu-Kane-Mele invariants.
result: For two-dimensional tori fully periodic symmetric bases exist, while in three dimensions non-trivial phases classify Murray-von Neumann and unitary equivalence; homotopy equivalence reduces to unitary equivalence in non-minimal Hilbert spaces and acquires relative invariants in minimal ones.
conclusion: The paper provides a unified geometric framework showing how distinct equivalence relations generate specific absolute and relative topological invariants for low-dimensional topological insulators.

title: Stability Of The Courtade-Kumar Inequality
authors: Tuan Tran Vu Khac Ky
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove dimension-independent stability for the Courtade-Kumar inequality: a Boolean function [MATH] whose information is close to the dictator value is close in probability to a signed dictator. The correlation dependence is sharp in order near zero and, for increasing functions, also at the noiseless endpoint.
tldr: The paper proves a dimension-independent stability version of the Courtade-Kumar inequality, showing that Boolean functions with near-maximal information are close to signed dictators.
motivation: The Courtade-Kumar inequality characterizes dictators as maximizers of mutual information, so a stability version quantifies how close a function is to a dictator when its information is near optimal.
method: The authors establish stability bounds on the mutual information between a Boolean function and its input, with sharp dependence on correlation near zero and at the noiseless endpoint for increasing functions.
result: They obtain dimension-independent stability estimates and prove sharpness of the correlation dependence in the near-zero regime and at the noiseless endpoint for increasing functions.
conclusion: The results strengthen the understanding of the Courtade-Kumar inequality and provide robust quantitative versions relevant to Boolean function analysis and classical information theory.

title: The Transmitter Trojan Channel: Achievable Rates And Error Exponents
authors: Aria Nosratinia Maryam Farahnak-Ghazani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experiments have shown that modifications in communication hardware can enable unauthorized exfiltration of data from transmitters. We study the resulting Transmitter Trojan channel, in which a malicious encoder embedded within a legitimate transmitter perturbs the transmitted codeword on a symbol-by-symbol basis. The model reflects the limited footprint, delay, and computational complexity available to such hardware modifications. We derive achievable rogue message rate and achievable rates for the legitimate message under the mismatch induced by the Trojan. We also analyze decoding error exponents for the legitimate and rogue receivers, including operational exponent lower bounds obtained through channel-resolvability transfer arguments. Finally, we study Trojan detection at the legitimate receiver under different levels of statistical knowledge, including likelihood-ratio detection when the ensemble-averaged induced channel is known and goodness-of-fit detection when only the nominal channel is known. The resulting detection error exponents, together with the achievable rate and decoding error exponents, quantify tradeoffs among rogue message rate, legitimate message rate, decoding reliability, and Trojan detectability. We specialize the analysis to the binary symmetric channel and the additive white Gaussian noise channel, and illustrate the resulting tradeoffs numerically.
tldr: The paper introduces a classical Transmitter Trojan channel model where a malicious encoder perturbs codewords, and derives achievable rogue and legitimate message rates, error exponents, and detection tradeoffs.
motivation: Hardware modifications can enable unauthorized data exfiltration from transmitters, motivating an information-theoretic study of covert communication under limited footprint, delay, and computational complexity.
method: The authors model symbol-by-symbol perturbation by a Trojan encoder, derive achievable rates for rogue and legitimate messages, analyze decoding error exponents via channel-resolvability transfer, and study detection using likelihood-ratio and goodness-of-fit tests.
result: Tradeoffs among rogue message rate, legitimate message rate, decoding reliability, and Trojan detectability are characterized, with specializations to the binary symmetric channel and additive white Gaussian noise channel and numerical illustrations.
conclusion: The framework quantifies fundamental limits of transmitter Trojan channels, revealing tradeoffs between covert exfiltration and reliable, detectable communication.

title: Quantum Encoding Agents: A Natural Language Interface For Data Embedding Strategy Selection In Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Ana Paula Appel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting a data encoding is a central and poorly tooled decision in quantum machine learning. The feature map fixes the geometry of the Hilbert space, the expressibility of quantum kernels, and whether the circuit can run on near-term hardware. This paper presents Quantum Encoding Agents, an open-source system that turns encoding selection into a natural-language interaction. Given a dataset and an optional task description, it profiles the data, applies a hardware-aware policy using the gate-error threshold p* approximately 10^{-3}, returns a copyable Qiskit circuit with a justification in Portuguese or English, and scores the quantum kernel by Kernel-Target Alignment (KTA). When a numerical matrix is available, it estimates the correlation fractal dimension D_2 and selects original columns with FD-ASE, using q* = max(2, ceil(D_2)) as a qubit budget so that angle and IQP maps are not proposed at a width where the fidelity kernel has collapsed. The service implements seven encoding families: amplitude, angle, dense angle, IQP, basis, data re-uploading, and custom feature map. On benchmark datasets, KTA separates these encodings under realistic NISQ constraints.
tldr: Quantum Encoding Agents is an open-source system that uses natural-language interaction to automate data encoding strategy selection for quantum machine learning under NISQ constraints.
motivation: Choosing a data encoding is a central but poorly tooled decision in quantum machine learning, as it fixes Hilbert-space geometry, kernel expressibility, and hardware compatibility.
method: The system profiles datasets, applies a hardware-aware gate-error threshold, estimates correlation fractal dimension to set a qubit budget, supports seven encoding families, and returns a Qiskit circuit with justification and kernel-target alignment score.
result: On benchmark datasets, kernel-target alignment separates the encodings under realistic near-term quantum constraints.
conclusion: The work provides a practical tool for encoding selection in QML but does not advance quantum information theory or the researcher's core focus areas.

title: Learning Trotter Orderings For Heisenberg Hamiltonians With A Ranking Transformer
authors: Shamminuj Aktar, Reuben Tate, Stephan Eidenbenz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trotterization approximates quantum time evolution by sequentially applying Hamiltonian terms. Because noncommuting terms introduce ordering-dependent errors, selecting an optimal term ordering is a combinatorial problem over a factorial search space. Prior approaches rely on fixed heuristics or on selection among predefined structured orderings, both of which require simulating candidates before choosing among them. For 1D and 2D Heisenberg-style Hamiltonians, we instead learn the ordering directly with a physics-aware ranking transformer that assigns a scalar score to each Hamiltonian term and predicts an ordering by sorting these scores. Physical structure enters through commutator-biased attention and an anticommutation-weighted ranking loss, and the models are trained on simulated-annealing (SA) reference orderings. We train separate models for first- and second-order Trotterization, each jointly on chains up to 14 qubits and lattices up to 12 qubits, and evaluate them on unseen chains with 16-20 qubits and lattices with 16 and 20 qubits. Predicted orderings are evaluated by the median gap in simulation fidelity to the SA reference. At first order, the model reaches a pooled gap below 10^-4 on chains, 0.0144 and 0.0088 on triangular lattices, and 0.0948 and 0.0823 on rectangular lattices at 16 and 20 qubits; at second order, the gaps are 0.0114, 0.0364 and 0.0244, and 0.1348 and 0.1239. The prediction exceeds the SA reference on 34% of first-order and 8% of second-order chain instances and can match its fidelity even when the two sequences differ because commuting terms may be rearranged without changing the Trotter unitary. The learned models generalize to larger systems across all three geometries, performing best on chains and triangular lattices, and produce an ordering in one forward pass without candidate enumeration, simulated annealing, or fidelity evaluation.
tldr: A physics-aware ranking transformer learns Trotter term orderings for Heisenberg Hamiltonians, achieving low simulation-fidelity gaps on larger systems without candidate enumeration.
motivation: Trotterization error depends on the ordering of noncommuting Hamiltonian terms, and finding an optimal ordering is a factorial combinatorial problem that traditionally requires costly simulation of candidates.
method: The authors train a ranking transformer with commutator-biased attention and an anticommutation-weighted ranking loss on simulated-annealing reference orderings for first- and second-order Trotterization of 1D chains and 2D lattices.
result: The model generalizes to unseen 16–20 qubit chains and lattices, with median fidelity gaps below 10^-4 on chains and 0.0088–0.1348 on lattices, occasionally exceeding the simulated-annealing reference.
conclusion: Learned ordering enables high-fidelity Trotter sequences in a single forward pass, avoiding simulated annealing or fidelity evaluation, and is promising for efficient quantum simulation compilation.

title: Systematic Errors From Scalar Slowing-down Models In Transient Serf Magnetometry
authors: Marek Kopciuch, Harini Raghavan, Morgan W. Mitchell
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reduced Bloch models of spin-exchange-relaxation-free (SERF) magnetometers commonly describe the coupled electron--nuclear spin dynamics using a single nuclear slowing-down factor. We show that this scalar description becomes inaccurate when the polarization magnitude changes appreciably. We derive an effective Bloch equation with separate longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors, [MATH] and [MATH], governing changes in polarization magnitude and direction. For [MATH] under representative SERF conditions and undergoing free-induction decay (FID), comparison with master-equation simulations shows that the dynamic scalar model produces a magnetic-field estimation bias of up to [MATH] at high initial polarization, while fixing the slowing-down factor at a reference value increases the error to [MATH]. Lowering the polarization suppresses this bias but also reduces the magnetic-field information contained in the FID signal. We further show that the anisotropic response modifies noncollinear optical pumping and introduces an additional nonlinear contribution to the harmonic response under periodic driving. The resulting model retains the simplicity of a three-component Bloch description while improving the quantitative accuracy of transient and driven SERF magnetometry.
tldr: The paper derives an anisotropic Bloch model with separate longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors to correct systematic errors in transient SERF magnetometry, showing that the standard scalar slowing-down description biases magnetic-field estimates under polarization changes.
motivation: Reduced Bloch models of SERF magnetometers typically collapse coupled electron-nuclear spin dynamics into a single scalar nuclear slowing-down factor, which is expected to fail when the polarization magnitude varies appreciably during free-induction decay or optical pumping.
method: The authors derive an effective Bloch equation with distinct longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors governing changes in polarization magnitude and direction, and benchmark it against full master-equation simulations under representative SERF conditions, including FID and periodic driving.
result: The scalar model produces magnetic-field estimation biases up to a few percent at high initial polarization (and larger when the sliding factor is fixed), while lowering polarization reduces bias but also reduces the field information in the FID signal; the anisotropic response also alters noncollinear optical pumping and adds nonlinear harmonic contributions.
conclusion: An anisotropic three-component Bloch description retains the simplicity of scalar models while quantitatively improving transient and driven SERF magnetometry, though the work remains an applied metrology modeling study rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics contribution.

title: Quantum Machine Learning For Cybersecurity Applications: Simulation And Hardware Validation
authors: Zirui Zhu, Zisheng Chen, Xiangyang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under tight feature and compute budgets, classical threat detection pipelines often degrade on near-decision-boundary events. Small quantum processors are now available, but existing work inadequately shows whether quantum components improve end-to-end threat detection under the above resource constrained conditions. This paper tries to address this gap with a hybrid architecture that uses a compact multilayer perceptron layer to compress the information in data and then routes the processed features to a few qubit quantum heads implemented in quantum support vector machine (QSVM) and variational quantum circuit (VQC) models. On a simulation platform, we benchmark these hybrid models against classical models with comparable parameter budgets on two representative cybersecurity tasks, network intrusion detection on NSL-KDD dataset and spam filtering on Ling-Spam dataset. To validate their precision on real quantum hardware, we deploy the best 4-qubit QSVM model on an IBM Quantum device with noise-aware execution, evaluated on a smaller sub-dataset. In the results, shallow quantum heads consistently match, and on difficult near-boundary cases modestly reduce missed attacks and false alarms compared to classical models using the same features. Hardware validation results track the simulation behavior closely enough that the remaining gap is dominated by device noise rather than model design. Furthermore, we conduct adversarial attacks to test the robustness of one QSVM model. Taken together, the study shows that even on small, noisy devices, carefully engineered quantum components may function as competitive, budget-aware components in practical cyber threat detection applications.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical architecture using QSVM and VQC is tested for cybersecurity threat detection, showing modest improvements on near-boundary cases but limited by device noise.
motivation: Classical threat detection degrades under tight feature and compute budgets, and existing quantum approaches lack end-to-end validation under resource constraints.
method: A compact MLP compresses features, then a few-qubit quantum head (QSVM or VQC) processes them; benchmarks on NSL-KDD and Ling-Spam, with hardware validation on IBM Quantum.
result: Shallow quantum heads match classical models on easy cases and slightly reduce missed attacks/false alarms on near-boundary cases; hardware results track simulation, with remaining gap due to noise.
conclusion: Quantum components can be competitive budget-aware options for practical cyber threat detection, even on small noisy devices.

title: Continuously Varying Exponents In The Distribution Of Waiting Times In The Symmetric Exclusion Process On A Percolation Cluster
authors: Arpan Chatterjee, Kabir Ramola, Deepak Dhar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the waiting-time distribution of hard-core interacting particles in the symmetric exclusion process on one- and two-dimensional lattices with side branches attached to each lattice site in the steady state. We use numerical simulations together with an approximate analytical treatment of particles trapped in side branches in the steady state. Such a two-dimensional carpet serves as a simplified model for trapping of a supercritical percolation cluster. At high particle densities, the system exhibits strong dynamical heterogeneity, with the distribution of logarithms of waiting times developing well-separated peaks corresponding to particles trapped at different depths from the backbone. We show that the probability that a tagged particle occupies the same position at time [MATH] as at time [MATH] decays algebraically as [MATH], where the exponent [MATH] varies continuously with particle density for densities above a threshold value [MATH]. We also investigate the correlations between successive waiting times along the trajectory of a tagged particle.
tldr: The paper studies waiting-time distributions and dynamical heterogeneity for hard-core particles in the symmetric exclusion process on lattices with side branches and on a percolation cluster, finding a continuously varying algebraic decay exponent above a density threshold.
motivation: Understanding trapping and anomalous transport in disordered media is important for modeling dynamics on percolation clusters and other heterogeneous structures.
method: Numerical simulations and an approximate analytical treatment of particles trapped in side branches in the steady state are used to analyze the distribution of waiting times, return probabilities, and correlations between successive waiting times.
result: At high densities, the distribution of logarithms of waiting times develops well-separated peaks, and the probability that a tagged particle remains at the same position decays algebraically with an exponent that varies continuously with particle density above a threshold.
conclusion: The symmetric exclusion process on side-branched lattices exhibits strong dynamical heterogeneity and non-universal density-dependent exponents, providing insights into transport on percolation clusters.

title: Compact Shielded Csv: Post-Quantum, Private, Lightweight Client-Side Validation Blockchain
authors: Dragos I. Ilie, Uri Lee, Iain D. Stewart, Jonathan Zhu, Elliot Jones, William J. Knottenbelt
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Compact Shielded CSV, a private client-side validation blockchain for peer-to-peer payments designed for the postquantum era. Upgrading existing blockchains to quantum-resistant cryptography substantially increases on-chain overhead. By keeping all large cryptographic artifacts off-chain, Compact Shielded CSV keeps a minimal on-chain footprint independent of the size of the underlying cryptographic proofs and signatures. For a single input transaction, the onchain footprint is just 3 hashes (3x32 bytes): a nullifier, a degriefer, and a commitment to the transaction. We introduce the degriefer - a novel mechanism that enforces ownership and prevents double-spending using only hash commitments, eliminating the need for on-chain signatures entirely. These properties make Compact Shielded CSV a promising foundation for private, scalable, post-quantum digital payments.
tldr: Compact Shielded CSV is a post-quantum private client-side validation blockchain for peer-to-peer payments that reduces on-chain footprint to three hashes per input transaction using a novel degriefer mechanism.
motivation: Upgrading existing blockchains to quantum-resistant cryptography substantially increases on-chain overhead, necessitating a scalable and private post-quantum payment solution.
method: The protocol keeps large cryptographic artifacts off-chain and uses hash commitments—a nullifier, a degriefer, and a transaction commitment—to enforce ownership and prevent double-spending without on-chain signatures.
result: For a single-input transaction, the on-chain footprint is only 3 hashes (96 bytes), independent of the underlying proof and signature sizes.
conclusion: Compact Shielded CSV offers a promising foundation for private, scalable, post-quantum digital payments.

title: A Quantum Framework For K Coloring Of Graphs
authors: Shyamapada Mukherjee Lord Sen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph coloring is a well-known NP-complete problem with applications in scheduling, register allocation, frequency assignment, and network optimization. Quantum computing offers the potential for polynomial or even super-polynomial speedups in certain problem instances, yet practical quantum graph coloring methods must carefully balance qubit resources, circuit depth, and constraint enforcement. We proposed a solver agnostic quantum framework for [MATH]-coloring. Along with a novel encoding and efficient constraint implementation for its exact coloring exploiting Grover search and almost optimal coloring by the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm , and . Unlike using [MATH] qubits as in , we reduced the qubit requirements to [MATH], along with optimized comparator circuits enforcing adjacency constraints. Further symmetry-based graph reduction is incorporated as an optional preprocessing step to further reduce the instance size before quantum execution.
tldr: The paper proposes a solver-agnostic quantum framework for exact and approximate k-coloring of graphs using Grover search and QAOA with reduced qubit requirements.
motivation: Graph coloring is an NP-complete problem with broad practical applications, and quantum computing may offer speedups, but existing quantum coloring methods face high qubit costs, deep circuits, and difficult constraint enforcement.
method: The authors introduce a novel encoding scheme with optimized comparator circuits to enforce adjacency constraints, using Grover search for exact coloring and QAOA for near-optimal coloring, plus optional symmetry-based graph reduction as preprocessing.
result: The framework reduces qubit requirements compared to prior approaches and enables more efficient constraint implementation for both exact and approximate k-coloring.
conclusion: The work provides a resource-efficient, solver-agnostic quantum approach to graph coloring, though it remains an algorithmic application rather than an information-theoretic or thermodynamic contribution.

title: KKTCode: Asymptotically Optimal Linear Codes For Noisy Feedback Awgn Channels
authors: Hongjae Nam, Jonggyu Jang, Vishrant Tripathi, David J. Love
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The design of optimal causal linear feedback schemes for additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels with noisy output feedback has remained an open problem for over 60 years. Prior work has focused on restricted policy classes, especially passive (uncoded) noisy output feedback, where only the transmitter performs feedback coding. However, passive noisy output feedback fundamentally lacks the degrees of freedom required to attain the information-theoretic performance limit in general. In this paper, we consider the active (coded) noisy output feedback setting, where both the transmitter and the receiver perform feedback coding. We then develop a constructive KKT-optimal active linear feedback design that asymptotically attains the Elias-Butman SNR converse bound, thereby establishing MSE/SNR optimality over the entire class of causal linear schemes. Furthermore, we prove that the optimal passive feedback solution is recovered as a special case of the active design. This passive solution admits a Geometric Toeplitz (GT) structure with a Chance-Love (CL)-style one-shot polynomial characterization, and can be computed with O(log T) complexity. Thus, our results provide an affirmative answer to the long-standing optimality question for noisy output feedback under causal linear feedback coding, and our numerical results support the theoretical findings.
tldr: Develops a KKT-optimal active linear feedback coding scheme for AWGN channels with noisy output feedback that asymptotically attains the Elias-Butman SNR converse bound.
motivation: Optimal causal linear feedback design for AWGN channels with noisy output feedback has been open for over 60 years, and prior passive (uncoded) feedback schemes lack the degrees of freedom needed to reach information-theoretic limits.
method: The authors formulate and solve a constructive KKT-optimal active linear feedback design where both transmitter and receiver perform feedback coding, and derive a passive solution with Geometric Toeplitz structure and a Chance-Love-style one-shot polynomial characterization computable in O(log T) time.
result: The active design asymptotically attains the Elias-Butman SNR converse bound, recovers the optimal passive solution as a special case, and is supported by numerical simulations.
conclusion: This provides an affirmative answer to the long-standing optimality question for noisy output feedback under causal linear feedback coding.

title: Reconfigurable Linear Optical Transformations In A Single Integrated Multimode Waveguide
authors: Manoah van der Worp, Jonas Krimmer, Ivo M. Vellekoop, Pepijn W. H. Pinkse, Stefan Rothe
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wavefront shaping enables control over optical fields for applications ranging from imaging to photonic information processing. While conventional wavefront shaping relies on free-space systems comprising bulk optical components, compact and fully integrated approaches are comparatively unexplored. Here, we introduce a concept based on a single multimode waveguide with distributed thermo-optic perturbations for controlling multimode propagation. We develop a differentiable physical model and numerically demonstrate shaping the outgoing wavefront and programmable linear optical transformations, using gradient-based optimization. We achieve diffraction-limited focusing with 20 spatial modes and show that the theoretical focusing limit can be retained while maintaining more than [MATH] of the input optical power. We extend this approach to complete input--output transformations and implement Sylvester--Hadamard matrix operations with dimensions up to [MATH] with correlations exceeding [MATH]. Reducing the number of tunable elements requires stronger individual perturbations, resulting in stronger and broader mode coupling that extends beyond the target modes. To mitigate this effect, we consider ancillary modes and realize a [MATH] transformation that reaches [MATH] correlation with only [MATH] tunable elements, where [MATH] denotes the number of spatial modes. The best-performing realization reaches [MATH] correlation with the target. Our results demonstrate that thermo-optic control of multimode waveguides offers an approach to fully-integrated wavefront shaping and programmable linear optical transformations, with potential applications in classical and quantum photonic processing.
tldr: The paper introduces a concept for reconfigurable linear optical transformations using a single multimode waveguide with distributed thermo-optic perturbations, enabling programmable wavefront shaping and matrix operations.
motivation: Conventional wavefront shaping relies on bulky free-space optics, and integrated approaches are needed for compact photonic information processing.
method: They develop a differentiable physical model and use gradient-based optimization to control multimode propagation via thermo-optic perturbations, with ancillary modes to mitigate mode coupling.
result: They demonstrate diffraction-limited focusing with 20 spatial modes, implement Sylvester-Hadamard transformations up to certain dimensions with high correlation, and realize a transformation using only a few tunable elements with ancillary modes.
conclusion: Thermo-optic control of multimode waveguides offers a route to fully integrated wavefront shaping and programmable linear optical transformations, with potential applications in classical and quantum photonic processing.

title: Measuring Clock Precision Without An Ideal Time Reference
authors: Pablo \'A. Dom\'inguez, Christopher Chubb, Mischa P. Woods
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Characterising physical devices typically requires comparison with more precise reference standards. For clocks, however, this approach is problematic because no physically perfect time reference exists; real clocks have finite, model-dependent uncertainty. We address whether multiple imperfect clocks can collectively determine their precision without an absolute reference. This paper provides analytic bounds and protocols for quantifying clock precision using only multiple copies of the same clock, which need not be synchronised and may have manufacturing variations or environmental coupling. Beyond clock characterisation, these methods enable precise measurements f sub-period intervals and relativistic effects such as time dilation and Doppler shifts, providing tools for quantum metrology and fundamental physics.
tldr: The paper develops reference-free protocols and analytic bounds to characterize clock precision using multiple imperfect, unsynchronized copies of the same clock.
motivation: No physically perfect time reference exists, so characterizing clocks by comparison with a more precise standard is problematic because real clocks have finite, model-dependent uncertainty.
method: It uses multiple copies of a clock—potentially unsynchronized, with manufacturing variations or environmental coupling—to derive analytic bounds and protocols for quantifying precision.
result: The methods enable precise measurements of sub-period intervals and relativistic effects such as time dilation and Doppler shifts.
