conclusion: The work provides tools for quantum metrology and fundamental physics without requiring an absolute time reference.

title: Scattering Amplitudes From Quantum Hardware A La RESOs
authors: Raul A Briceno, Ivan M Burbano, Anthony N Ciavarella, Ermal Rrapaj, Thomas R Richardson, Andre Walker-Loud
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the first quantum-hardware implementation of Real-time Estimators for Scattering Observables (RESOs). The physical model is a one-dimensional lattice theory of non-relativistic spin-1/2 fermions with a single contact interaction. The lattice sizes studied are up to [MATH] lattice sites and up to [MATH] time steps. Spacetime correlation functions were computed on IBM's quantum computers, using [MATH] qubits with [MATH] CZ gates applied, reaching a two-qubit gate depth of [MATH]. We demonstrate how to study bound states and extract scattering amplitudes from these correlation functions.
tldr: The first quantum-hardware implementation (on IBM devices) of Real-time Estimators for Scattering Observables (RESOs), applied to a 1D lattice model of non-relativistic spin-1/2 fermions with a contact interaction to extract scattering amplitudes and bound states.
motivation: Lattice field-theory calculations of real-time scattering observables are classically intractable, motivating a quantum-computing approach to compute spacetime correlation functions that encode scattering data.
method: Spacetime correlation functions are computed on IBM quantum hardware using up to ~100 qubits and several thousand CZ gates with substantial two-qubit gate depth, within a one-dimensional lattice model of spin-1/2 fermions with a single contact interaction.
result: The authors demonstrate that bound states and scattering amplitudes can be extracted from the measured correlation functions, establishing a proof-of-principle workflow for quantum simulations of scattering.
conclusion: The work shows hardware-level feasibility of RESOs for studying scattering in lattice theories, though it does not address quantum information-theoretic, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-platform questions.

title: Feedback-based Quantum Optimization With Low Depth And Measurement
authors: Zi-Wen Huang, Jia-Cheng Fan, Xiao-Hui Ni, Su-Juan Qin, Xiao-Kai Hou, Wei Huang, Bing-Jie Xu, Fei Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feedback-based ALgorithm for Quantum OptimizatioN (FALQON) is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, which circumvents classical parameter optimization but requires a deep quantum circuit. To reduce circuit depth, Arai et al. proposed second-order FALQON (SO-FALQON), achieving the best depth reduction among existing approaches. However, SO-FALQON brings a 2.3 times per-step measurement overhead, as it needs to calculate an additional second-order control coefficient. In this paper, inspired by the Backtracking Line Search (BLS) theory, we propose another method called BLS-FALQON, which not only reduces circuit depth to a comparable extent, but also achieves fewer measurements than SO-FALQON. Numerical simulations on max-cut problem with 8 to 20 vertices demonstrate that BLS-FALQON reduces the total measurement count by 37.7% compared to SO-FALQON, while maintaining a comparable circuit depth. Furthermore, we conduct real quantum hardware experiments on the Tianyan-176 quantum computer, which uses the zuchongzhi2 superconducting quantum processor, confirming that BLS-FALQON remains effective under real quantum hardware conditions.
tldr: BLS-FALQON reduces circuit depth and measurement count for feedback-based quantum optimization compared to second-order FALQON.
motivation: FALQON avoids classical parameter optimization but requires deep quantum circuits; SO-FALQON reduces depth yet incurs a 2.3x per-step measurement overhead.
method: Inspired by backtracking line search, the authors propose BLS-FALQON and test it via numerical simulations on max-cut problems with 8 to 20 vertices and on the Tianyan-176 superconducting quantum computer.
result: BLS-FALQON cuts total measurements by 37.7% relative to SO-FALQON while maintaining comparable circuit depth, and remains effective on real quantum hardware.
conclusion: BLS-FALQON offers a measurement-efficient, low-depth approach for feedback-based quantum combinatorial optimization.

title: Fewer Qubits, Better Choices: Coupling-Aware Sub-QUBO Selection For Quantum-Assisted Traffic Zone Partitioning
authors: Ruimin Ke Qianwen Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near-term quantum optimizers accommodate roughly a hundred binary variables, requiring large Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problems to be decomposed into hardware-sized subproblems while other variables remain fixed. Variables are typically selected by ranking the objective changes from individual flips. We show that this rule is uninformative once the incumbent is optimal under single-variable flips: every score represents a cost, while remaining improvements depend on overlooked pairwise interactions. A second-order expansion instead yields a prize-collecting densest-subgraph selection problem, solvable greedily in time linear in the number of variables, and two solver-free bounds bracketing the improvement achievable within a selected subset. On transportation networks from Chicago and Philadelphia, our rule with 16-variable subproblems outperforms random selection with 64, demonstrating that quadrupling device capacity cannot compensate for weaker selection. Replacing geometric adjacency with road-network connectivity widens the margin by a factor of 1.6-1.9. With the selection trace fixed, varying the fraction of subproblems solved on a 120-qubit device from zero to one leaves the final objective unchanged to six significant figures. At tested hardware-accessible sizes, gains therefore arise from selection rather than the backend. Hardware feasibility is limited by coupling terms: 120-variable problems fail to compile with 7,260 terms but succeed with 5,118. Compilation scales almost quadratically with term count and dominates execution cost, reaching 1,752 seconds versus 469 seconds of quantum processing.
tldr: The paper proposes a coupling-aware sub-QUBO selection method for quantum-assisted traffic zone partitioning, showing better selection can outweigh larger hardware capacity.
motivation: Near-term quantum optimizers are limited to about a hundred binary variables, so large QUBO problems must be decomposed into hardware-sized subproblems.
method: The authors analyze the standard flip-score variable selection rule, showing it is uninformative at a locally optimal incumbent, and instead derive a second-order expansion that yields a prize-collecting densest-subgraph selection problem solved greedily in linear time.
result: On Chicago and Philadelphia transportation networks, their selection rule with 16-variable subproblems outperforms random selection with 64-variable subproblems, and replacing geometric adjacency with road-network connectivity increases the margin by 1.6-1.9x; hardware performance on a 120-qubit device leaves the final objective unchanged.
conclusion: At tested hardware-accessible sizes, gains come primarily from variable selection rather than quantum backend execution, while hardware feasibility is limited by coupling terms and compilation cost.

title: Litter-Masked Block z-Channel: Designing Cover Distributions Against Public-Design Observers
authors: Bin Han, Wenwen Chen, Yao Zhu, Rafael F. Schaefer, Giuseppe Caire, Hans D. Schotten
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Networking defenses against traffic analysis fill idle slots with cover traffic, yet the physical layer carrying it still hands upper layers the erasure-only model of a silent-idle link, leaving the cover content unexploited. We shape that content: the idle-slot waveform is drawn from the codebook complement under a design distribution, the , chosen to defeat a public-design passive observer while the upper layer keeps its block z-channel model. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) receiver reduces to a single threshold on the log-likelihood ratio between the best codeword and the prior-weighted litter aggregate; its errors are silent corruptions the upper layer cannot detect and erasures that retransmission absorbs. Receiver design is thus one-dimensional, minimizing erasure under a cap on silent corruption, and the joint design a Stackelberg game against a Kullback-Leibler (KL) indistinguishability metric, solved by an alternating convex relaxation and corroborated by an independent reinforcement-learning policy. On a rate-[MATH] [MATH] parity-check (LDPC) code against an observer who knows her own channel but whose channel the transmitter knows only statistically, shaped litter cuts the observer's Stein detection exponent by [MATH] to [MATH] relative to uniform cover, flat over a [MATH]~dB span and in the activity rate. Below the point where the legitimate link turns reliable, no cover distribution admits an operating point; at that point shaping costs about one percent of throughput, and nothing measurable [MATH]~dB above it.
tldr: The paper designs cover distributions at the physical layer for a block z-channel to defeat a public-design passive observer while retaining an erasure-only upper-layer model.
motivation: Traffic-analysis defenses rely on cover traffic, but the physical layer usually treats idle slots as silent erasures, wasting the cover content's potential for covertness.
method: It shapes idle-slot waveforms from the codebook complement under a design distribution, reduces the MAP receiver to a log-likelihood ratio threshold, and solves the joint design as a Stackelberg game against a KL indistinguishability metric via alternating convex relaxation and reinforcement learning.
result: For an LDPC-coded link against an observer with known channel but only statistical transmitter knowledge, shaped litter reduces the observer's Stein detection exponent by orders of magnitude relative to uniform cover, flat over a dB span and activity rate, with about 1% throughput cost at the reliable-link threshold and no feasible operating point below it.
conclusion: Physical-layer cover shaping can significantly improve covertness against public-design observers while preserving the block z-channel abstraction for upper layers.

title: Particles, Localization And "Collapse"
authors: Anthony Rizzi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hegerfeldt's theorem shows that the localization of a particle (or field) is not possible under very general assumptions of quantum mechanics and special relativity. This theorem, and further developments and associated theorems force penetrating questions on the proper understanding of the theory and its use. In particular, the use of the collapse postulate is called into question. The existence of particles and even localized fields are called into question. And, this in turn challenges local measurements. It generally forces one to consider the profound problems and even wrong results that arise from the collapse postulate. We give a qualitatively new example of such a wrong result. Researchers and students alike are bothered by these fundamental issues. Students' ability to learn the material, and even their interest in physics, can be compromised by such disturbing conundra that seem to make physics, or at least QFT and its QM limit, seem incomprehensible and even inconsistent. This article resolves these issues in a way accessible to undergraduates, by applying the natural (minimal) interpretation of quantum mechanics (QM) (the ensemble interpretation) and explicating and clarifying the basic principles and premises used in QM and the Hegerfeldt theorem and its application to measurements.
tldr: The paper argues that Hegerfeldt's theorem and related results are best resolved by adopting the ensemble (minimal) interpretation of quantum mechanics, thereby defusing apparent paradoxes surrounding particle localization, the collapse postulate, and local measurements.
motivation: Hegerfeldt's theorem shows that localized particles or fields are incompatible with general quantum-mechanical and relativistic assumptions, which raises troubling questions about the collapse postulate, the existence of particles, and the validity of local measurements, confusing students and researchers alike.
method: The author applies the ensemble interpretation of quantum mechanics at an undergraduate-accessible level, clarifying the basic principles and premises underlying the Hegerfeldt theorem and its application to measurement, and constructs a qualitatively new example of an erroneous result derived from the collapse postulate.
result: A new example demonstrates that misuse of the collapse postulate produces incorrect conclusions, and the ensemble interpretation is shown to resolve the apparent inconsistencies arising from Hegerfeldt-type theorems without invoking collapse.
conclusion: The paper contends that foundational puzzles about localization and measurement dissolve once the collapse postulate is abandoned in favor of the ensemble interpretation, making quantum mechanics and its QFT limit conceptually coherent.

title: Conserved And Relaxing Modes Enable Polynomial-success Coherent Carleman Lattice Boltzmann Evolution
authors: Sauro Succi Hua-Dong Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Carleman linearization represents nonlinear lattice Boltzmann collision dynamics in a form amenable to quantum block encoding, but low postselection probabilities in existing population-space encodings make coherent multi-step evolution exponentially unlikely to succeed. We present a quantum Carleman lattice Boltzmann scheme based on the multi-relaxation-time collision operator in a weighted Hermite moment basis. In this basis, the lifted collision operator separates into small coupled blocks whose norm exceeds unity because of the coupling between conserved and relaxing modes. This block structure enables a norm-attaining block encoding with a single-step success probability close to unity. Crucially, scaling the pair sector for a prescribed evolution horizon makes the combined encoding and sector-selection overhead grow polynomially rather than exponentially with the number of steps. For a hundred-step evolution, the resulting complete-run success probability exceeds that of population-space encodings by orders of magnitude. Over horizons of several tens of steps, the truncated dynamics reproduces the nonlinearly generated modes of a benchmark flow to within a few percent. We verify the combined preparation, evolution and readout protocol as a single unitary circuit and give a complete gate-level resource estimate for extracting a nonlinear observable of the benchmark flow from a coherent Carleman evolution. The block structure of conserved and relaxing modes holds equally on three-dimensional lattices and provides a constructive route to norm-attaining encodings for lattice Boltzmann models with quadratic equilibria.
tldr: A quantum Carleman lattice Boltzmann scheme based on a multi-relaxation-time collision operator in a Hermite moment basis achieves near-unity single-step success probability and polynomial overhead via norm-attaining block encoding.
motivation: Existing population-space Carleman encodings suffer from exponentially low postselection probabilities, making coherent multi-step quantum evolution impractical.
method: The lifted collision operator is expressed in a weighted Hermite moment basis, where it separates into small coupled blocks; scaling the pair sector enables a norm-attaining block encoding with controlled overhead.
result: The scheme yields single-step success probability close to unity, polynomially growing encoding and sector-selection overhead, and complete-run success probability orders of magnitude higher than population-space encodings for a hundred-step evolution.
conclusion: The conserved-and-relaxing-mode block structure generalizes to 3D lattices and offers a constructive path to norm-attaining encodings for quadratic-equilibrium lattice Boltzmann models.

title: On $e$-doubly Stochastic Matrices Over Hyperbolic (polynomial) Systems
authors: Juyoung Jeong, M. Seetharama Gowda, Sudheer Shukla
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the setting of a hyperbolic (polynomial) system [MATH] of degree [MATH], an [MATH]-tuple [MATH] is said to be an [MATH]-doubly stochastic [MATH]-matrix if each [MATH] belongs to the hyperbolicity cone, has trace [MATH], and [MATH]. In this article, we characterize linear preservers of such [MATH]-matrices, describe some connections between [MATH]-doubly stochasticity and majorization, and study extreme points of the set of all [MATH]-doubly stochastic [MATH]-matrices. We show, for example, that [MATH] when [MATH], positive, unital, and trace-preserving transformations are (the only) linear transformations on [MATH] that preserve [MATH]-doubly stochasticity; [MATH] when [MATH] is [MATH]-doubly stochastic, the eigenvalue vector of the linear combination [MATH] is majorized by the coefficient vector [MATH]; and [MATH] when [MATH] is complete, [MATH]-doubly stochastic [MATH]-matrices induced by (generalized) Jordan frames are extreme points of the compact convex set of all [MATH]-doubly stochastic [MATH]-matrices.
tldr: The paper characterizes linear preservers, majorization connections, and extreme points of the set of e-doubly stochastic matrices over hyperbolic (polynomial) systems.
motivation: The authors aim to extend classical doubly stochastic matrix theory—linear preserver problems, majorization, and extremal structure—to the more general setting of hyperbolic cones arising from polynomial (hyperbolic) systems.
method: Pure convex analysis and linear algebra: hyperbolicity cones, trace-preserving unital maps, majorization order relations, and Jordan frames/algebras are used to characterize e-doubly stochastic matrix tuples.
result: They show that for certain degrees positive unital trace-preserving transformations are the only linear maps preserving e-doubly stochasticity, that eigenvalue vectors of linear combinations are majorized by coefficient vectors, and that Jordan-frame-induced matrices are extreme points of the compact convex set.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematically rigorous generalization of doubly stochastic matrix theory to hyperbolic polynomial systems, but contains no quantum-information, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-platform content.

title: Algebraic-Geometric Parvaresh--Vardy Subspace Designs And Rank Condensers
authors: Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Noam Goldgraber
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A subspace design is a collection of subspaces [MATH] of [MATH] with the property that no low-dimensional subspace [MATH] intersects the collection "too much". Subspace designs and related objects in linear-algebraic pseudorandomness have found a broad range of applications, ranging from list decoding, to derandomizing algorithms. We construct explicit strong subspace designs over every finite field. In the extremal case where the co-dimension [MATH] of each [MATH] is equal to the dimension of [MATH], for every constant field size our construction attains [MATH] and matches the probabilistic intersection bound up to a constant factor. All previous constructions required the field size to grow with [MATH] (or [MATH]). Our subspace designs also imply new construction of rank condensers over arbitrary finite fields. This result is the first to achieve an optimal dependence on [MATH] while maintaining both a constant output entropy rate and a constant field size. As an application, we construct lossless rank extractors for linear sources of rank [MATH], for all [MATH], with parameters matching those of Guo, Raj, Shangguan and Zhang (FOCS '26), thereby generalizing their result to prime fields and smaller field sizes. Our construction is based on an algebraic-geometric version of the Parvaresh-Vardy codes (Parvaresh-Vardy FOCS '05, Guruswami ECCC '05), extending the framework underlying the condensers of Guruswami, Umans and Vadhan (JACM '09). We view our construction as a linear-algebraic analysis - tailored to affine sources - of the GUV construction, generalized to functions over algebraic curves. More specifically, inspired by Ta-Shma and Umans (CCC 12') we develop a two-level evaluation scheme, where we first evaluate a function on a curve at extension-field points, and then evaluate a corresponding affine-linear polynomial to obtain outputs over the base field.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit strong subspace designs over every finite field via an algebraic-geometric generalization of Parvaresh-Vardy codes, yielding improved rank condensers and lossless rank extractors for linear sources.
motivation: Subspace designs and rank condensers are central objects in linear-algebraic pseudorandomness, with applications to list decoding and derandomization, but prior constructions required the field size to grow with the dimension, leaving open whether optimal designs exist over small or prime fields.
method: The authors develop a two-level evaluation scheme inspired by Ta-Shma and Umans, evaluating a function on an algebraic curve at extension-field points and then evaluating an affine-linear polynomial to obtain base-field outputs, extending the Guruswami-Umans-Vadhan framework to algebraic curves.
result: The construction yields explicit strong subspace designs over every finite field achieving optimal co-dimension-to-dimension ratio and matching the probabilistic intersection bound up to a constant factor for constant field sizes, implying rank condensers with optimal dependence and constant output entropy rate, plus lossless rank extractors generalizing Guo-Raj-Shangguan-Zhang to prime and smaller fields.
conclusion: This is a significant advance in classical algebraic pseudorandomness and coding theory, but it contains no quantum-information, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-platform content and lies outside the researcher's active directions.

title: Odd Stochastic Density Functional Theory
authors: Yael Avni, Michel Fruchart, David Martin, Tali Khain, Vincenzo Vitelli
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic density functional theory (SDFT) provides a powerful framework for studying the dynamics of many-body systems both in and out of equilibrium. In its standard form, it can be viewed as a density-based formulation of coupled Langevin equations with white noise. Here, we extend SDFT to a class of systems, ranging from magnetized electrolytes to chiral active matter, that possess a chiral overdamped limit in which a relaxation timescale and an oscillation period are simultaneously taken to zero. We derive this formulation, which we dub ``odd SDFT", by taking the overdamped limit of a fluctuating hydrodynamic description of underdamped particles subject to a Lorentz force. We establish the validity and utility of the resulting framework by calculating the collective mobility tensor of interacting particles using both direct linear response and a Green-Kubo relation. We then apply the theory to the Hall conductivity of electrolytes in magnetic fields. Going beyond mean-field theory and using two distinct Green-Kubo relations, we derive the full conductivity tensor, extending the relaxation part of the Debye-H\"uckel-Onsager theory to the case of finite magnetic fields.
tldr: The authors extend stochastic density functional theory to 'odd' systems with a chiral overdamped limit, deriving a fluctuating hydrodynamic framework for magnetized electrolytes and chiral active matter.
motivation: Standard stochastic density functional theory describes density-based Langevin dynamics but cannot capture systems possessing a chiral overdamped limit where a relaxation timescale and oscillation period vanish simultaneously, such as magnetized electrolytes and chiral active matter.
method: Starting from a fluctuating hydrodynamic description of underdamped particles subject to a Lorentz force, the authors take the overdamped limit to derive 'odd SDFT', then compute the collective mobility tensor via direct linear response and Green-Kubo relations.
result: The framework yields the full conductivity tensor for electrolytes in magnetic fields, extending the relaxation part of Debye-Hückel-Onsager theory to finite magnetic fields beyond mean-field theory.
conclusion: Odd SDFT provides a validated, versatile tool for nonequilibrium dynamics of chiral/magnetized classical many-body systems, with applications including Hall conductivity of electrolytes.

title: Accurate Density Of States Estimation: A Comparative Study
authors: Chao Yang Dong Min Roh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study density of states (DOS) estimation for large sparse real symmetric matrices by fitting the cumulative density of states (CDOS) and differentiating the fit. We use a stochastic Lanczos method to supply Ritz values and weights, which we average across Lanczos runs to construct CDOS midpoint data. Monotone piecewise-cubic interpolation of these data yields a smooth CDOS approximation that can be easily differentiated to yield a nonnegative, normalized, piecewise-quadratic DOS without requiring a Gaussian smoothing with a fixed bandwidth in its construction. We also consider approximating CDOS by using Gaussian-process regression (GPR) with single- and double-Gaussian covariance kernels, yielding an approximation with uncertainty information. DOS approximation is then obtained by analytic derivative of the GPR-based CDOS. Experiments on matrices from diverse scientific applications are performed to compare these estimators with Gaussian-broadened stochastic Lanczos and Jackson-damped kernel polynomial approximations. At a common Gaussian validation resolution, we use error measures that assess local discrepancies, integrated errors, and agreement in the overall spectral shape. The results demonstrate that the midpoint spline can produce accurate approximations to the DOS with relatively few matrix--vector products, supporting the use of cumulative interpolation as a practical DOS estimation.
tldr: Compares methods for estimating the density of states of large sparse symmetric matrices by fitting and differentiating the cumulative density of states.
motivation: Accurate density of states estimation is important for understanding spectral properties of large matrices, but existing Gaussian smoothing methods require a fixed bandwidth that can limit accuracy.
method: Uses stochastic Lanczos quadrature to obtain Ritz values and weights, constructs cumulative density of states midpoint data, then applies monotone piecewise-cubic interpolation and Gaussian-process regression with single- and double-Gaussian kernels.
result: The midpoint spline method produces accurate nonnegative normalized density of states with relatively few matrix-vector products, outperforming Gaussian-broadened stochastic Lanczos and Jackson-damped kernel polynomial approximations in local, integrated, and shape-based error measures.
conclusion: Cumulative interpolation is a practical and effective approach for density of states estimation, especially when matrix-vector products are expensive.

title: Randomized Lifting For One-Way Number-on-Forehead Communication
authors: Chenyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a lifting theorem from two-party public-coin one-way communication to multiparty public-coin one-way number-on-forehead (NOF) communication. For every fixed [MATH] and prime [MATH], there is a generalized inner product gadget [MATH] with [MATH] such that, for every partial Boolean function [MATH], where [MATH], \[ R_{1/3}^1(f)-O(1) \le R_{1/6}^{1,\NOF}\bigl(f\circ\GIP_{q,r}^k\bigr) \le R_{1/6}^1(f). \] Thus, composition with the gadget preserves one-way randomized communication complexity up to an additive constant and a change in the error parameter. The lower bound holds in the general one-way NOF model, where the last player sees the entire gadget input. This extends the deterministic one-way NOF lifting theorem of Yang and Zhang to randomized protocols, and extends the randomized lifting result of Wang and Wu from the conservative model to the general one-way NOF model. Our proof introduces a one-way cylinder partition bound that lower bounds public-coin one-way NOF communication complexity. We show that, for the lifted function, this bound is at least half the one-way partition bound of the outer function. The main technical step transfers a dual solution between the two bounds, using M\"obius inversion and a discrepancy estimate for generalized inner product to control the loss. Combining this transfer with the characterization of two-party one-way randomized communication complexity by the one-way partition bound yields the lifting theorem.
tldr: The paper proves a randomized lifting theorem from two-party public-coin one-way communication to the multiparty one-way number-on-forehead (NOF) model using a generalized inner product gadget.
motivation: Lifting theorems are central to communication complexity, transferring query/partition bounds to communication models; prior work covered deterministic NOF lifting and randomized lifting only in the conservative model.
method: Introduces a one-way cylinder partition bound for public-coin one-way NOF communication, and transfers a dual solution between bounds via Möbius inversion plus a discrepancy estimate for the generalized inner product gadget.
result: For every fixed q and prime r, composition with GIP_{q,r}^k preserves one-way randomized communication complexity up to an additive constant and a change in error parameter, with the lower bound valid in the general one-way NOF model.
conclusion: This extends deterministic NOF lifting to randomized protocols and generalizes earlier randomized lifting from the conservative to the general one-way NOF model.

title: Discrete Quality-factor Control In A Side-coupled Photonic Crystal Microcavity: Evanescent Bloch Tunnelling And The Finite-cell Correction
authors: Hasan Oguz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A point-defect microcavity side-coupled to a W1 waveguide in a two-dimensional photonic crystal of silicon rods immersed in an aqueous analyte is studied by plane-wave expansion and finite-difference time-domain computation. The resonance moves continuously through the transverse-magnetic band gap with the square of the radius of the defect rod, as first-order perturbation theory predicts for the dielectric area restored to the lattice site. The quality factor is set instead by the separation between cavity and waveguide, counted in lattice rows: each added row multiplies it by 7.10 at the reference defect radius, whereas moving the defect rod by up to a tenth of a lattice period changes it by less than 7 per cent. The per-row factor follows, at two defect radii and with no adjustable parameter, from the decay of the slowest evanescent Bloch channel of the crystal at the wavevector of the guided mode. Two checks are needed before such values can be trusted in a finite cell: convergence in cladding thickness and removal of the reflections from the waveguide ends. Without them the per-row factor comes out too low and the quality factor wrong by up to a factor of two. Scaled to 1550 nm the design gives a sensitivity of 634 nm per refractive index unit, which perturbation theory reproduces, and a Fano fit to an independently normalised transmission spectrum confirms the linewidth. The absorption of water at this wavelength lowers the quality factor of the reference geometry by a third and caps it near 9200, which limits the benefit of adding further rows.
tldr: A computational study of quality-factor control in a side-coupled photonic crystal microcavity, showing discrete per-row scaling via evanescent Bloch tunnelling and correcting finite-cell artefacts.
motivation: To understand and predict how the quality factor of a photonic crystal microcavity can be controlled deterministically by its separation from a waveguide, with implications for refractive-index sensing.
method: Plane-wave expansion and finite-difference time-domain simulations are used, together with perturbative and evanescent Bloch mode analysis, and validated by Fano fits and convergence checks on cladding thickness and waveguide-end reflections.
result: The quality factor multiplies by 7.10 per added lattice row at a reference defect radius and is largely insensitive to lateral defect displacement; water absorption at 1550 nm lowers the reference Q by one third and caps it near 9200, with a sensitivity of 634 nm/RIU.
conclusion: Discrete quality-factor control is achievable through lattice-row separation, but accurate predictions require removing finite-cell reflections and accounting for material absorption, which limits the benefit of adding further rows.

title: Inverse-Designed Time-Varying Multilayers For Programmable Frequency-Momentum Light Scattering
authors: Viktar Asadchy Mohammad M. Asgari
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Space-time-varying electromagnetic structures unlock wave-control mechanisms inaccessible to static media, including frequency conversion, harmonic generation, and joint control over frequency and momentum. Here, we introduce an inverse-design framework for multilayer space-time-periodic structures in which the spatial permittivity distribution and temporal modulation profile are optimized jointly. The proposed platform comprises multiple pixelated layers that are periodic along one or both transverse directions and harmonically modulated in time, enabling the direct synthesis of complex multichannel frequency-momentum scattering responses. We demonstrate two representative functionalities: independent control over the amplitudes and phases of three transmitted spatiotemporal channels and the generation of a frequency-momentum comb. Across these examples, we consider both continuous and binary permittivity distributions. To facilitate reproducibility and further development, we make the numerical implementation of the optimization framework freely available. These results demonstrate that inverse-designed time-varying multilayers provide a compact and versatile route toward programmable frequency-momentum multiplexing and the synthesis of space-time wave packets. The optimization code is made openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further development of the proposed inverse-design framework.
tldr: An inverse-design framework jointly optimizes spatial permittivity and temporal modulation of multilayer space-time-periodic structures to synthesize programmable frequency-momentum light scattering.
motivation: Space-time-varying electromagnetic media enable wave-control capabilities impossible in static media, such as frequency conversion and joint frequency-momentum manipulation, but designing such structures for complex multichannel responses remains difficult.
method: Pixelated multilayers periodic along one or two transverse directions and harmonically modulated in time are optimized by a joint inverse-design algorithm over both continuous and binary permittivity distributions, with open-source numerical implementation.
result: The framework achieves independent amplitude and phase control of three transmitted spatiotemporal channels and generates frequency-momentum combs, using compact multilayer geometries.
conclusion: Inverse-designed time-varying multilayers offer a versatile route to programmable frequency-momentum multiplexing and space-time wave packet synthesis.

title: Collinear Laser Spectroscopy Of The $1s2s\,^3\!S_1\rightarrow 1s2p\,^3\!P_{0,2}$ Transitions In Helium-like $^{11}$b$^{3+}$
authors: Axel Bu{\ss}, Konstantin Mohr, Volker Hannen, Zoran Andelkovic, Max Horst, Phillip Imgram, Kristian K\"onig, Bernhard Maass, W. N\"ortersh\"auser, Simon Rausch, Rodolfo S\'anchez, Christian Weinheimer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.33056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on hyperfine structure measurements of the [MATH] fine-structure transitions in the spectrum of [MATH]B[MATH] ions. The helium-like ions were created in an electron beam ion trap (EBIT) and ejected after a short production period of 15 ms. A challenge of the experiment was the treatment of the complex energy-time-profile of the created ion bunches and the sensitivity of the collinear laser spectroscopy to the starting potential inside the EBIT. Despite these complications and the low statistics of the experiment, we were able to confirm and improve the results of a previous measurement of these transitions. While we find moderate tension in the results for the hyperfine parameters of the [MATH] levels, their fine-structure level energies are in reasonable agreement between experiments and with theory.
tldr: Hyperfine structure measurements of helium-like 11B3+ via collinear laser spectroscopy, improving previous results but with moderate tension in hyperfine parameters.
motivation: Precision tests of atomic structure in helium-like ions can benchmark quantum electrodynamics and nuclear effects.
method: Helium-like boron ions were produced in an electron beam ion trap, ejected in short bunches, and probed using collinear laser spectroscopy of the 1s2s 3S1 → 1s2p 3P0,2 transitions.
result: The fine-structure level energies agree reasonably with theory and previous experiments, while hyperfine parameters show moderate tension.
conclusion: The experiment confirms and improves earlier measurements despite low statistics and complex ion-bunch energy-time profiles.

title: Certified Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design: From Expected Information Gain To Signal-to-Noise Ratio
authors: Mohamed Doumbouya, Arthur Vidard, Olivier Zahm
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal experimental design is often formulated as the maximization of the Expected Information Gain (EIG), which measures the expected reduction in uncertainty about a parameter of interest after observing the data. For nonlinear forward models and nonGaussian priors, computing the EIG typically requires costly nested Monte Carlo estimators or sophisticated density-approximation techniques. In this work, we derive new upper and lower bounds on the EIG using dimensional logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. The proposed bounds are expressed in terms of signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), preserving the simple matrix-based structure of the EIG in the linear-Gaussian setting and depending solely on covariance matrices and Fisher information matrices. We introduce two families of bounds: conservative bounds, designed to retain the entire information content, and incremental bounds, that prioritize early information acquisition for sequential experimental design. When model gradients are available, we further derive computable approximations of the Fisher-information terms that require only a small number of gradient evaluations, yielding substantial computational savings. The tightness of these bounds is controlled by the nonlinearity of the forward model, and in the linear-Gaussian setting, these bounds recover the exact value of the EIG. By eliminating the nested-sampling bottleneck, the proposed framework offers a tractable and theoretically grounded alternative to direct EIG estimation for large-scale Bayesian experimental design, while retaining the interpretability of the SNR-based bounds.
tldr: The paper derives new upper and lower bounds on Expected Information Gain using dimensional logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, expressing them in terms of signal-to-noise ratios and Fisher information for Bayesian optimal experimental design.
motivation: Expected Information Gain is central to optimal experimental design but is computationally expensive for nonlinear models and non-Gaussian priors, often requiring nested Monte Carlo estimation.
method: The authors use dimensional logarithmic Sobolev inequalities to bound Expected Information Gain by covariance matrices and Fisher information matrices, yielding conservative and incremental bounds, with gradient-based approximations of Fisher-information terms.
result: The bounds preserve the matrix structure of the linear-Gaussian case, recover exact Expected Information Gain in that setting, and avoid nested sampling, with tightness controlled by model nonlinearity.
conclusion: The framework provides a tractable and theoretically grounded alternative to direct Expected Information Gain estimation for large-scale Bayesian experimental design, especially when gradients are available.

title: One-Step Generative Modeling Via Unbalanced Optimal Transport
authors: Yirong Shen, Mengfei Xia, Junpeng Jing, Lu Gan, Cong Ling
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drifting models enable one-step generation by amortizing distribution transport into training, but this efficiency places greater demands on the transport field estimated at each update. In large-scale training, the field is computed from finite mini-batches of generated and real samples, which provide only imperfect approximations to the underlying distributions. Balanced optimal transport enforces exact mass matching within every mini-batch, making the estimated field sensitive to the particular composition of the real-data batch. We find that generated and real samples should be treated asymmetrically: letting the mass assigned to real samples adapt while keeping every generated sample fully transported improves generation across six feature-space metrics in controlled ablations, and is more robust to the relaxation strength than relaxing both marginals simultaneously, which falls below balanced transport under stronger relaxation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF), which keeps the generated-sample marginal fixed and relaxes only the real-data marginal. Under identical settings at DiT-B/2 on ImageNet-256, UOT-GF improves Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) from 1.53 to 1.46 over the balanced W-Flow baseline; scaling the same recipe yields 1.34 and 1.22 FID at L/2 and XL/2, the best FID among the one-step models we compare. We further derive the induced UOT transport force, establish a kinetic Vlasov--Fokker--Planck formulation whose overdamped zero-temperature limit recovers the drifting dynamics, and characterize non-target stationary states together with sufficient conditions for convergence.
tldr: The paper proposes Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF), a one-step generative modeling method that relaxes only the real-data marginal while keeping the generated-sample marginal fixed, improving FID on ImageNet-256.
motivation: Drifting models amortize distribution transport into training for one-step generation, but the transport field estimated from finite mini-batches is sensitive to batch composition under balanced optimal transport's exact mass-matching constraint.
method: The authors treat generated and real samples asymmetrically, keeping every generated sample fully transported while letting the mass assigned to real samples adapt, and derive the induced UOT transport force with a kinetic Vlasov-Fokker-Planck formulation.
result: UOT-GF improves FID from 1.53 to 1.46 over the balanced W-Flow baseline at DiT-B/2 on ImageNet-256, and scales to 1.34 and 1.22 FID at L/2 and XL/2, the best among the compared one-step models.
conclusion: Relaxing only the real-data marginal yields more robust and better generation than balanced transport or relaxing both marginals, with theoretical characterization of non-target stationary states and convergence conditions.

title: Almost Norming Vertices For Homogeneous Polynomials On The Cube
authors: Ignacio Zalduendo Dami\'an Pinasco
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be fixed. We consider the space [MATH] of real [MATH]-homogeneous polynomials on [MATH], endowed with the standard Gaussian measure [MATH] associated with the Bombieri norm. We study how well the norm of a typical polynomial on the unit ball of [MATH], namely the cube [MATH], can be recovered from its values at the vertices. For [MATH], set \[ M(P)=\max_{x\in[-1,1]^n}|P(x)|, \qquad V(P)=\max_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n}|P(\varepsilon)|. \] If [MATH] is chosen according to [MATH], we prove that the relative loss \[ 1-{M(P_n)} \] is of order at most [MATH] in probability. Consequently, for every [MATH], \[ \gamma_{m,n}\left\{ P\in_m(^n): V(P)\geq (1-n^{-\beta})M(P) \right\} \longrightarrow1 \] as [MATH]. Thus, with respect to the Bombieri Gaussian measure, the vertices of the cube are asymptotically norming for homogeneous polynomials of fixed degree.
tldr: The paper shows that, under the Bombieri Gaussian measure, the vertices of the cube are asymptotically norming for real m-homogeneous polynomials of fixed degree.
motivation: The authors aim to quantify how much of the supremum norm of a homogeneous polynomial on the cube can be recovered from its values at the 2^n vertices, a classical problem in multivariate polynomial analysis.
method: They equip the space of real m-homogeneous polynomials on R^n with the standard Gaussian (Bombieri) measure and use probabilistic estimates to bound the relative loss 1 - V(P)/M(P) in probability.
result: For fixed degree m, the relative loss is of order at most n^{-β} with high probability, so the set of polynomials for which V(P) ≥ (1-n^{-β})M(P) has Gaussian measure tending to 1.
conclusion: With respect to the Bombieri Gaussian measure, cube vertices are asymptotically norming for homogeneous polynomials of fixed degree, giving a quantitative probabilistic norming result.

title: Geometry-Controlled Polarization Photocurrents In Scalable PtSe2 Infrared Pixels
authors: Eunice Y. Paik, Owen A. Vail, Madaline R. Marland, William A. Beck, Antonio Llopis-Jepsen, Wendy L. Sarney, Jeffery H. Leach, Stefan Heiserer, Nikolas Dominik, Cormac \'O Coile\'ain, Paul B. Seifert, Georg S. Duesberg, Blair C. Connelly, George J. de Coster
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarization-sensitive photodetectors provide multi-dimensional optical information beyond the capabilities of traditional intensity-based detectors. The noble metal dichalcogenide PtSe2 presents unique opportunities for tunable polarization detection due to its strong spin-orbit coupling, material stability, customizable broadband polarization responses, and direct compatibility with a wide range of substrates for back-end-of-line silicon integration. In this work, we demonstrate room-temperature near-infrared to mid-wavelength infrared polarization photoresponses using scalable, as-grown, wide-area PtSe2 films, and we show that the measured polarization response is reshaped by device geometry. Finite-element current-flow simulations reproduce the observed spatial redistribution of the polarization-sensitive response and localize the transverse polarization response near the pixel center. This geometry-enabled separation allows wavelength-dependent laser spot scans to distinguish symmetry-allowed photocurrents from contact-proximate, dichroism-mediated photothermal contributions. At near-infrared wavelengths, we observe spatial response that is consistent with linear-dichroic photothermoelectric currents, whereas mid-wavelength infrared measurements reveal a helicity-dependent photothermal contribution under oblique illumination. These results identify pixel boundary engineering as both a design lever and a diagnostic tool for scalable PtSe2 polarization-sensitive infrared pixels.
tldr: This paper demonstrates room-temperature near-infrared to mid-wavelength infrared polarization-sensitive photodetectors based on scalable PtSe2 films and shows that device geometry reshapes the polarization photoresponse.
motivation: Polarization-sensitive photodetectors can provide multidimensional optical information beyond intensity-based detection, and PtSe2 is attractive due to strong spin-orbit coupling, stability, broadband response, and silicon integration compatibility.
method: The authors use as-grown wide-area PtSe2 films, fabricate devices with varied geometries, perform finite-element current-flow simulations, and use wavelength-dependent laser spot scans to separate photocurrent contributions.
result: The measured polarization response is spatially redistributed by pixel geometry, allowing symmetry-allowed photocurrents to be distinguished from contact-proximate dichroism-mediated photothermal effects; near-infrared response is consistent with linear-dichroic photothermoelectric currents, while mid-wavelength infrared shows helicity-dependent photothermal behavior under oblique illumination.
conclusion: Pixel boundary engineering is identified as both a design lever and a diagnostic tool for scalable PtSe2 polarization-sensitive infrared pixels.

title: Asymmetric Negative Refraction In Nonlocal Double-Wire Metamaterials
authors: Tiago A. Morgado, Sylvain Lanneb\`ere, Enrico M. Renzi, Andrea Al\`u, M\'ario G. Silveirinha
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate that heterogeneous double-wire metamaterials, comprising two dissimilar and nonconnected wire arrays, enable loss-asymmetric hyperbolic dispersion and strongly asymmetric negative refraction. We unveil that, owing to their strongly nonlocal response and distinctive microstructure, such geometry supports two independent hyperbolic propagation channels with unequal losses, which can be selectively excited by free-space propagating waves incident at opposite angles. This angular selectivity gives rise to asymmetric negative refraction at the air-metamaterial interfaces, characterized by strong angular asymmetry in transmission and absorption, while preserving reciprocity. This phenomenon is scalable and can be realized with metallic wire arrays over a broad frequency spectrum extending from microwave to infrared frequencies, showing that nonlocality can emulate shear-like dissipative asymmetry that, in local media, requires lower spatial symmetry. Our findings open new avenues for directional energy transport and angle-selective wave control in photonic platforms.
tldr: Heterogeneous double-wire metamaterials with strongly nonlocal response support two hyperbolic propagation channels with unequal losses, yielding loss-asymmetric negative refraction and angle-selective transmission while preserving reciprocity.
motivation: Conventional local media require broken spatial symmetry (e.g., shear-like dissipation asymmetry) to achieve asymmetric absorption and directional transport; the authors ask whether nonlocality in a reciprocal metamaterial can emulate the same effect.
method: Analytical and numerical electromagnetic modeling of two dissimilar, nonconnected metallic wire arrays, deriving the nonlocal effective-medium response and computing transmission, absorption, and refraction at air-metamaterial interfaces for opposite incidence angles.
result: The structure exhibits two independent hyperbolic channels with different loss rates, which can be selectively excited by free-space waves incident at opposite angles, producing strongly asymmetric negative refraction, transmission, and absorption without violating reciprocity.
conclusion: Nonlocality can emulate symmetry-breaking dissipative asymmetry in reciprocal media, offering a scalable route from microwave to infrared for directional energy transport and angle-selective wave control in photonic platforms.

title: Backward Kolmogorov Transport: Sampling Invariant Laws Of Reversible Diffusions From Trajectory Data
authors: Isao Ishikawa Yuanchao Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a reversible diffusion with unknown drift, observed through trajectories, and construct samplers of its invariant law. The trajectories contain samples of this law, but a sampler built from them by density or score estimation inherits the errors of these estimates, in particular on the barriers between metastable states. The trajectories also contain the dynamics, and for a reversible diffusion the ratio between the law of the process and its invariant law solves the backward Kolmogorov equation, so that the eigenpairs of the generator propagate it in closed form. Backward Kolmogorov transport (BKT) evaluates this ratio with eigenpairs estimated from the trajectories and coefficients computed once from the initial particles, and moves the particles along the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kullback-Leibler divergence. The particles do not interact, BKT defines a transport map, and no density, score or drift is estimated. With exact eigenpairs BKT transports the spectral projection of the initial law exactly when this projection is positive. For estimated eigenpairs we prove a transport identity in which truncation enters only through the initial law and estimation only through the residual of the eigenpairs, and a local stability bound in the 2-Wasserstein distance. With coefficients computed from the transported particles, the sampling error of the retained modes cancels, and a central limit theorem identifies the asymptotic variance. Experiments on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, multi-well potentials, separable products and alanine dipeptide, including comparisons with particle methods based on density estimates, agree with these results, and with an accurate spectrum the errors of BKT reach or fall below those of independent samples.
tldr: The paper introduces Backward Kolmogorov Transport (BKT), a method to sample the invariant law of reversible diffusions from trajectory data using generator eigenpairs and Wasserstein gradient flow.
motivation: Sampling invariant laws from trajectories is challenging because density or score estimators inherit errors, especially across metastable barriers.
method: BKT estimates generator eigenpairs from trajectories and uses them to evaluate the ratio between the process law and its invariant law, then transports particles along the Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kullback-Leibler divergence without density, score, or drift estimation.
result: The authors prove a transport identity and a local stability bound in 2-Wasserstein distance, with exact eigenpairs yielding exact transport of the spectral projection, and demonstrate accurate sampling on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, multi-well potentials, separable products, and alanine dipeptide.
conclusion: BKT provides a principled, estimation-error-resilient sampler for reversible diffusions, with theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

title: Typical Bohnenblust--Hille Ratios
authors: Eduardo V. Teixeira Daniel M. Pellegrino
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The polynomial Bohnenblust--Hille inequality controls the coefficient [MATH]-norm of an [MATH]-homogeneous polynomial by its supremum norm, with a constant independent of the dimension. We study the associated Bohnenblust--Hille ratio from a probabilistic point of view, by placing normalized surface measure on the Euclidean coefficient sphere. Our results reveal a sharp contrast between the extremal behavior governing the classical Bohnenblust--Hille constants and the typical scale seen in coefficient directions. For arbitrary prescribed monomial supports, the ratio is eventually at most [MATH] almost surely, and it tends to zero in spherical measure exactly when the number of monomials tends to infinity. On the full complex polynomial spaces we determine its typical asymptotic scale uniformly in the dimension; in the critical regime [MATH] this gives [MATH], in contrast with the nonvanishing extremal scale. For real polynomials, the corresponding ratio tends to zero in spherical measure exactly when the number of variables tends to infinity.
tldr: This paper studies the typical asymptotic behavior of the Bohnenblust--Hille ratio for homogeneous polynomials under spherical (probabilistic) coefficient measures, contrasting typical scales with extremal constants.
motivation: The classical Bohnenblust--Hille inequality bounds the coefficient norm of homogeneous polynomials by their supremum norm with dimension-independent constants, but little was known about how typical coefficient directions behave as opposed to extremal ones.
method: The authors place normalized surface measure on the Euclidean coefficient sphere and analyze the resulting ratio probabilistically, deriving almost-sure bounds for arbitrary monomial supports and determining typical asymptotic scales for full complex and real polynomial spaces.
result: For prescribed monomial supports the ratio is eventually bounded and vanishes in spherical measure exactly when the number of monomials diverges; on complex spaces the typical scale is determined uniformly in dimension, yielding a critical-regime value in contrast to the nonvanishing extremal scale, while for real polynomials it vanishes iff the number of variables diverges.
conclusion: The work reveals a sharp gap between extremal constants and typical behavior in Bohnenblust--Hille theory, characterizing probabilistically when the ratio degenerates.

title: The Erd\H{o}s--S\'os Conjecture: A Visual Exposition Of The Proof Discovered By Gpt-6 Astra
authors: Jay Cummings
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Erds--S\'os theorem states that every graph of average degree greater than [MATH] contains every tree on [MATH] vertices. A short counting proof was discovered by GPT-6 Astra in 2026. We give a visual, reader-centered exposition of that argument whose presentation differs substantially from the original. We recast the counting objects as in a reveal-and-stop procedure, organize the induction through explicit partitions and reversible swaps, and develop the proof through worked examples with consistent drawings. We also give direct and probabilistic conclusions, compare this formulation with other recent expositions, and record the classical consequence [MATH] for multicolor Ramsey numbers of trees.
tldr: A visual, reader-centered exposition of the counting proof of the Erdős–Sós conjecture for trees in graphs.
motivation: The Erdős–Sós theorem is a classical extremal graph theory result, and a recent short proof discovered by GPT-6 Astra motivated a clearer pedagogical presentation.
method: The authors recast the counting argument as a reveal-and-stop procedure, organize it via induction with explicit partitions and reversible swaps, and use worked examples and consistent drawings.
result: They provide a visual proof exposition, direct and probabilistic conclusions, comparisons with other recent expositions, and record the multicolor Ramsey number consequence for trees.
conclusion: This is a pedagogical graph theory exposition with no connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Positivity-preserving semi-Lagrangian Discontinuous Galerkin Methods For Multi-species Vlasov-Amp\`ere Models Of Plasma
authors: James A. Rossmanith Dauda Gambo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a high-order and positivity-preserving kinetic solver for the multi-species Vlasov-Amp\`ere system that is built within a semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin (SLDG) framework. The method is designed for efficiency and accuracy across a broad range of conditions, including stiff, multi-scale regimes with strong ion-electron scale separation. Phase space is discretized via high-order discontinuous Galerkin finite elements; time stepping is handled via high-order operator splitting and a series of one-dimensional, unconditionally stable, semi-Lagrangian updates. To improve both accuracy and efficiency, each plasma species is represented on a different phase-space mesh. On every element and for each species, local positivity-preserving limiters are applied to prevent spurious undershoots and rigorously ensure positivity of the cell averages at the next time step. The accuracy and robustness of the resulting method are verified on several standard single- and two-species test cases, including manufactured solutions, two-stream instability, weak and strong Landau damping, ion-acoustic wave propagation, ion-acoustic shock formation, and KEEN wave dynamics.
tldr: The paper develops a high-order, positivity-preserving semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin solver for the multi-species Vlasov-Ampère system of plasma physics.
motivation: Simulating kinetic plasma models across stiff, multi-scale regimes with strong ion-electron scale separation requires numerical methods that are both accurate and robust, particularly in preserving physical positivity of the distribution function.
method: Phase space is discretized with high-order discontinuous Galerkin finite elements, time stepping uses high-order operator splitting with unconditionally stable one-dimensional semi-Lagrangian updates, and each species is represented on its own mesh with local positivity-preserving limiters ensuring positive cell averages.
result: The scheme is verified on standard single- and two-species test cases including manufactured solutions, two-stream instability, weak and strong Landau damping, ion-acoustic wave propagation and shock formation, and KEEN wave dynamics.
conclusion: The proposed SLDG framework provides an efficient and accurate positivity-preserving kinetic solver suitable for challenging multi-species plasma simulation problems.

title: Isothermal Walls In The Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations: Affine Entropy, Ballistic Energy, And Entropy-stable Discrete Formulations
authors: Matteo Parsani, Rasha Aljahdali, Lisandro Dalcin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop entropy-stable isothermal-wall conditions for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations at continuous and semi-discrete levels. For a stationary, impermeable, no-slip wall at constant positive temperature, adding total-energy density divided by wall temperature to the canonical convex entropy cancels the wall contribution without suppressing heat transfer. This affine modification preserves the entropy Hessian, relative entropy, and volume entropy production. It is proportional to total ballistic-energy density and yields a conditional [MATH]-type bound based on the initial field under the stated assumptions. Two wall formulations use a common discontinuous Galerkin discretization with the summation-by-parts property and simultaneous approximation terms. Both give zero adapted wall contribution without a penalty and a nonpositive contribution with it. The complete-residual formulation penalizes the full wall-data residual and balances fluid energy through its complete numerical wall flux. The Fourier-energy-exact formulation combines an entropy-neutral skew correction with a momentum-projected penalty so that the complete numerical outward energy flux equals the one-sided numerical Fourier heat flux at every wall node and spatial resolution. Pointwise tests verify the local identities. Manufactured-solution studies with entropy-stable interior coupling demonstrate convergence rates consistent with order [MATH] in the discrete [MATH] norm, where [MATH] is the solution polynomial degree. Thermal-relaxation calculations verify the semi-discrete energy and adapted-entropy balances. Three-dimensional calculations demonstrate balance closure in a closed domain, convergence of curved-wall traces, and applicability to a complex supersonic separated flow.
tldr: The paper develops entropy-stable isothermal-wall formulations for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations using affine entropy modifications and discontinuous Galerkin discretizations.
motivation: Isothermal walls are common in compressible flow simulations, but enforcing them while preserving entropy stability and correct heat transfer is challenging.
method: The authors add total-energy density divided by wall temperature to the canonical convex entropy, yielding an affine entropy that cancels the wall contribution without suppressing heat transfer, and implement two wall formulations in a summation-by-parts discontinuous Galerkin framework.
result: Both formulations give zero adapted wall contribution without penalty and nonpositive contribution with penalty; the Fourier-energy-exact formulation matches the one-sided numerical Fourier heat flux at every wall node, with verification via manufactured solutions and thermal-relaxation tests.
conclusion: The affine entropy modification provides entropy-stable isothermal-wall conditions for compressible Navier-Stokes simulations and is demonstrated in three-dimensional complex supersonic separated flow.

title: Smooth Or Separable? Sparse Block Acceleration For Entropy-Regularized Linear Programs
authors: Irina Podlipnova, Maxim Mashtaler, Artem Agafonov, Yuriy Dorn, Alexander Gasnikov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study entropy-regularized linear programs with sparse affine constraints and compare two exact dual representations induced by whether a redundant normalization constraint is retained or eliminated. Eliminating it yields a partially separable sum-exp dual with sparse affine factors but unbounded curvature. Our main result is an accelerated randomized block method whose acceleration preserves sparse data-access cost. The key ingredient is a global entropy-specific Hessian--gap bound that remains valid for signed constraint matrices, admits computable block-overlap refinements, and provides deterministic curvature certificates before sampling. This geometry supports square-root importance sampling and an exact lazy implementation in which sparse arithmetic cost is weighted by local curvature rather than by a worst-block factor. We further introduce a gap-dependent curvature dimension that connects the generalized-smooth regime to the classical effective-rank intuition for coordinate methods. Retaining the normalization constraint yields a log-sum-exp dual with globally bounded higher derivatives, enabling gradient-regularized and cubic-regularized Newton methods. Experiments compare the resulting methods in terms of coordinate epochs, arithmetic operations, and wall-clock time, separating the effects of acceleration, touched-data sparsity, and problem-specific structure.
tldr: The paper develops an accelerated randomized block-coordinate method for entropy-regularized linear programs, comparing separable sum-exp and log-sum-exp dual formulations under sparse affine constraints.
motivation: Entropy-regularized linear programs admit multiple dual representations, and the choice of representation strongly affects curvature properties and hence which optimization algorithms can be applied efficiently.
method: The authors derive a global entropy-specific Hessian-gap bound valid for signed constraint matrices, construct a gap-dependent curvature dimension for square-root importance sampling, and design an exact lazy implementation preserving sparse data-access cost.
result: The acceleration preserves sparse data-access cost, with arithmetic cost weighted by local curvature rather than worst-block factors; experiments separate effects of acceleration, touched-data sparsity, and problem structure on coordinate epochs, operations, and wall-clock time.
conclusion: The proposed curvature certificates and gap-dependent dimension connect the generalized-smooth regime to effective-rank intuition, enabling efficient accelerated methods for both dual formulations.

title: Divergence Liftings And Regular Factorizations For Metric Cotype
authors: Yue Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study scalar linear factorizations of coordinate antipodal differences through sign increments on finite discrete tori and the corresponding adjoint divergence liftings. On tori of side length \(2m\) with \(m\) even, the optimal regular norms of both factorizations are \(m\). Quotient-space duality identifies the optimal nonlinear lifting constant with the corresponding Banach-valued difference constant. A sharp \(L_1\) metric-cotype inequality established jointly with Cheng and Xiang then yields \(\ell_\infty^N\)-valued nonlinear liftings with a uniform bound at the sharp metric-cotype scales, whereas the optimal regular norms of the normalized scalar linear liftings grow with the dimension of the torus.
tldr: The paper studies scalar linear factorizations of coordinate antipodal differences on discrete tori and the corresponding adjoint divergence liftings, establishing optimal regular norms and nonlinear lifting bounds via metric cotype.
motivation: The work aims to understand linear factorizations and divergence liftings in the setting of finite discrete tori, relating regular norms to Banach-valued difference constants and metric cotype inequalities.
method: It analyzes tori of side length 2m with m even, uses quotient-space duality to connect nonlinear lifting constants with Banach-valued difference constants, and employs a sharp L1 metric-cotype inequality established with Cheng and Xiang.
result: For tori with side length 2m and m even, the optimal regular norms of both factorizations are m; the optimal nonlinear lifting constant equals the Banach-valued difference constant, yielding ell_infty^N-valued nonlinear liftings with a uniform bound at sharp metric-cotype scales, whereas the optimal regular norms of normalized scalar linear liftings grow with the torus dimension.
conclusion: The paper characterizes divergence liftings and regular factorizations through metric cotype, showing a separation between nonlinear and scalar linear lifting behavior on finite discrete tori.

title: A Voltage-controlled Mtj-cmos Neuron Emulating Tunable Izhikevich-Inspired Dynamics
authors: Kayode Oluwaseyi Adebunmi, Jordan Athas, Allison Fleming, Hamed Poursiami, Giorgio A. Ascoli, Maryam Parsa, Pedram Khalili Amiri, Akhilesh R Jaiswal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biological neurons exhibit diverse firing dynamics that enable adaptive and stimulus-dependent signalling, yet reproducing these dynamics in hardware has remained an enduring challenge. In this work, we present an Izhikevich- inspired reconfigurable neuron that co-designs voltage-controlled magnetic tunnel junction (V-MTJ) dynamics with CMOS circuitry. The proposed architecture combines V-MTJ excitability dynamics, enabled by a tunable energy landscape, with CMOS recovery dynamics to generate five distinct neuronal firing pat- terns with different spiking, bursting and response characteristics. Our results, based on measured V-MTJ characteristics and circuit simulations using com- mercial GlobalFoundries 22-nm FD-SOI CMOS technology, show an average energy consumption of 145.44 fJ per spike. Algorithmic simulations further show that these firing dynamics reduce inference spike activity by up to 88.6% while maintaining baseline classification accuracy. These results highlight the potential of V-MTJ/CMOS reconfigurable neurons to reduce computational activity and enable compact, energy-efficient brain-inspired computing systems.
tldr: The paper presents a voltage-controlled magnetic tunnel junction (V-MTJ) combined with CMOS circuitry to emulate tunable Izhikevich-inspired neuronal firing dynamics for energy-efficient brain-inspired computing.
motivation: Biological neurons exhibit diverse firing patterns that are difficult to reproduce in hardware, motivating the need for compact, low-energy reconfigurable neuron circuits.
method: The authors co-design V-MTJ excitability dynamics, enabled by a tunable energy landscape, with CMOS recovery dynamics to generate five distinct firing patterns, using measured V-MTJ characteristics and circuit simulations in GlobalFoundries 22-nm FD-SOI CMOS.
result: The proposed neuron achieves an average energy consumption of 145.44 fJ per spike, and algorithmic simulations show up to 88.6% reduction in inference spike activity while maintaining baseline classification accuracy.
conclusion: V-MTJ/CMOS reconfigurable neurons show potential for reducing computational activity and enabling compact, energy-efficient brain-inspired computing systems.

title: Accepting-Path Counting At The One-Tape $n\log N$ Threshold
authors: Ond\v{r}ej Ku\v{z}elka
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We observe that the classical [MATH] time threshold for one-tape Turing machines is also a threshold for their accepting-path counts. Below it, every nondeterministic one-tape machine running in strong [MATH] time has a rational ordinary generating function of accepting-path counts. At strong [MATH] time, the situation changes completely: there is a fixed one-tape machine whose accepting-path function is complete for [MATH], the tally analogue of [MATH], under parsimonious polynomial-time tally reductions. A second construction within the same time bound gives positive accepting-path counts with a noncomputable exponential growth rate. The rationality result combines the one-tape time gap with the linear-time counting theorem of Tadaki, Yamakami and Lin. The completeness proof adapts the linear-time universal counting machine of Beame et al. to the one-tape setting.
tldr: The classical n log n time threshold for one-tape Turing machines also governs the structure of their accepting-path counting functions, with rationality below the threshold and #P-like completeness at the threshold.
motivation: Counting the number of accepting computation paths is a central theme in computational complexity (parsimonious reductions, #P), and the one-tape n log n time gap is a long-studied structural phenomenon; the author asks whether this time threshold also manifests in counting complexity.
method: The rationality result combines the one-tape time gap with the linear-time counting theorem of Tadaki, Yamakami and Lin, while the completeness proof adapts the linear-time universal counting machine of Beame et al. to the one-tape setting, using parsimonious polynomial-time tally reductions.
result: Below strong n log n time, every nondeterministic one-tape machine has a rational ordinary generating function of accepting-path counts; at strong n log n time, a fixed machine's accepting-path function becomes complete for the tally analogue of #P, and a second construction yields positive accepting-path counts with noncomputable exponential growth rate.
conclusion: The one-tape n log n time threshold is also a threshold for accepting-path counting complexity, exhibiting a sharp transition from rational counting functions to #P-completeness.

title: The Hamilton--Jacobi And Symplectic Analysis For Extended Ho\v{r}ava Gravity
authors: Diana Vanessa Castro-Luna (puebla U., Inst. Fis.), Alberto Escalante
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Hamilton-Jacobi [HJ] analysis and the Faddeev-Jackiw [FJ] quantization for the linearized, non-projectable [MATH] model, extended by the lowest-order term of Blas, Pujol\`as, and Sibiryakov and the higher-order term involving the square of the Cotton tensor, were carried out. The cases [MATH] and [MATH] are analyzed. Within the Hamilton-Jacobi framework, we obtain the complete set of Hamiltonians, generalized brackets, fundamental differential, characteristic equations, and gauge transformations of the theory. In the Faddeev-Jackiw framework, a symplectic tensor is constructed from which the fundamental brackets are identified. The HJ and FJ brackets coincide, and from the symplectic tensor, the measure for the quantum path integral is calculated. The differences between the cases [MATH] and [MATH] at the quantum path integral are discussed.
tldr: A Hamilton–Jacobi and Faddeev–Jackiw symplectic analysis of linearized non-projectable extended Hořava gravity, deriving Hamiltonians, brackets, gauge transformations, and the path-integral measure.
motivation: Extended Hořava gravity contains higher-order terms (Blas–Pujolàs–Sibiryakov and Cotton-tensor squared) whose constrained structure and quantization require careful canonical treatment.
method: The authors apply the Hamilton–Jacobi formalism and the Faddeev–Jackiw symplectic approach to the linearized non-projectable model, comparing two cases of the parameter space and constructing the symplectic tensor.
result: A complete set of Hamiltonians, generalized brackets, characteristic equations, and gauge transformations is obtained; the HJ and FJ brackets coincide, and the symplectic tensor yields the quantum path-integral measure, revealing differences between the two cases.
conclusion: The two formalisms give consistent canonical structures for extended Hořava gravity, with the parameter case affecting the quantum path-integral measure, offering a route toward quantizing the model.

title: Vision-Language Agents For Active Perception In Optics Laboratories
authors: Ryan Lopez, Sachin Vaidya, Seou Choi, Serena Landers, Marin Solja\v{c}i\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly being used in scientific workflows, but their ability as agents to directly control laboratory experiments from visual feedback remains underexplored. This capability is important because many laboratory tasks do not naturally provide dense, pre-defined numerical objectives: informative signals can be sparse, intermittent, or visually ambiguous. A more general laboratory agent should instead be able to interpret visual observations, take actions to acquire useful feedback, and adapt its behavior based on the consequences of those actions. We study whether general-purpose VLMs can perform this kind of closed-loop scientific control using experimental optics as a testbed. We evaluate agents on three experimental systems that isolate distinct capabilities: a Michelson interferometer, a two-mirror cavity, and a four-mirror optical relay. The agents observe camera images, directly issue actuator and measurement commands, and retain their interaction history without receiving an engineered scalar objective during control. Across these experiments and matched simulations, we find that, given task-specific natural-language guidance, VLMs can estimate actuator-response relationships, resolve ambiguous observations through intervention, and actively create informative visual feedback when signals are sparse. These results suggest that pretrained multimodal models can serve as important decision-making agents within the experimental loop. Our work also establishes optics as a physically grounded testbed for visual reasoning and active perception in scientific agents.
tldr: The paper evaluates whether general-purpose vision-language models can act as closed-loop agents that control experimental optics setups directly from camera feedback.
motivation: VLM agents are increasingly used in scientific workflows, but their ability to directly control laboratory experiments from visual feedback — where objectives are sparse or visually ambiguous — remains underexplored.
method: Agents were tested on a Michelson interferometer, a two-mirror cavity, and a four-mirror optical relay, issuing actuator and measurement commands based on camera images while retaining interaction history, with matched simulations for comparison.
