result: Given task-specific natural-language guidance, the VLMs could infer actuator-response relationships, resolve ambiguous observations via intervention, and actively generate informative visual feedback when signals were sparse.
conclusion: Pretrained multimodal models can serve as decision-making agents inside experimental loops, and optics offers a physically grounded testbed for visual reasoning and active perception in scientific agents.

title: Finite-Data Error Bounds For Approximating The Koopman Operator: Sampling Measures, Super-Polynomial Convergence And Regularization
authors: Daniel Fassler, Rachel Morris, Jason Bramburger, Simone Brugiapaglia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Koopman operator is a well-established framework for lifting nonlinear dynamical systems to an infinite-dimensional space where dynamics are linear. Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (EDMD) is a widely used method in data-driven dynamics as it provides a Galerkin approximation of the Koopman operator on the finite-dimensional span of a prescribed dictionary of observable functions. In particular, EDMD only requires samples from the dynamical system, describing the Koopman operator without knowledge of the underlying dynamics. While many studies analyze asymptotic convergence results for EDMD in terms of data, the question of more practical finite-data convergence results remains incomplete in general settings. In this work, we prove bounds for the finite-data EDMD Galerkin approximation of the Koopman operator by a rate proportional to the inverse of the root of the number of samples (the Monte Carlo rate). These results apply to multiple classes of problems, i.e., for discrete or continuous dynamics, including stochastic systems. In certain more structured setting, we demonstrate super-polynomial rates are achievable both theoretically and computationally. Finally, we derive recovery guarantees for an EDMD variant in the undersampled regime inspired by compressed sensing techniques.
tldr: The paper provides finite-data error bounds for extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) approximations of the Koopman operator, including Monte Carlo rates, super-polynomial convergence in structured settings, and compressed-sensing-inspired recovery guarantees.
motivation: Koopman operator theory lifts nonlinear dynamics to a linear infinite-dimensional setting, and EDMD is a popular data-driven Galerkin method, but practical finite-data convergence guarantees remain incomplete.
method: The authors derive finite-data error bounds for EDMD across discrete, continuous, and stochastic dynamical systems, and use compressed sensing techniques to obtain recovery guarantees in the undersampled regime.
result: They prove bounds scaling inversely with the square root of the number of samples (Monte Carlo rate) and demonstrate that super-polynomial convergence rates are achievable in more structured settings, both theoretically and computationally.
conclusion: The work advances the theoretical understanding of finite-data Koopman operator approximation, providing practical error bounds and recovery guarantees that can guide data-driven modeling of nonlinear dynamical systems.

title: Applications Of The Lorentz Positive Cone In Nonconvex Quadratic Optimization
authors: Kurt Anstreicher Samuel Burer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the Lorentz positive cone of [MATH] matrices that map the Lorentz cone in [MATH] into the Lorentz cone in [MATH]. The Lorentz positive cone and its dual, the cone of Lorentz separable matrices, are shown to provide polynomial-time algorithms for the problem of minimizing a bilinear objective over variables contained in ellipsoids in [MATH] and [MATH]. We also demonstrate how these cones can be used to strengthen SDP relaxations of other nonconvex quadratic optimization problems, including the two-trust-region subproblem.
tldr: The paper studies the Lorentz positive cone of matrices mapping the Lorentz cone to itself, and its dual (Lorentz separable matrices), to derive polynomial-time algorithms and stronger SDP relaxations for nonconvex quadratic optimization problems.
motivation: Nonconvex quadratic optimization problems such as minimizing a bilinear objective over ellipsoids, and the two-trust-region subproblem, are hard in general and benefit from tighter convex relaxations.
method: The authors characterize the Lorentz positive cone and its dual cone of Lorentz separable matrices, then use them to construct polynomial-time algorithms and to strengthen semidefinite programming relaxations.
result: The cones yield polynomial-time algorithms for bilinear objectives over ellipsoidal variables and provide strengthened SDP relaxations for other nonconvex quadratic problems including the two-trust-region subproblem.
conclusion: Cone-theoretic tools from Lorentz-cone geometry are shown to be practical and powerful for nonconvex quadratic optimization and SDP relaxation strengthening.

title: Distance-Residual Physics-Informed Neural Networks: A Deep Learning Framework For Differential And Partial Differential Inclusions
authors: Maria Filipkovska, Juan Jos\'e Mar\'{\i}n, Isil Oner, Francisco Periago, Krzysztof Rykaczewski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Distance-Residual Physics-Informed Neural Networks (DR-PINNs), a physics-informed learning framework for approximating solutions of ordinary and partial differential inclusions (DIs), governing laws in which a differential operator is constrained to lie in a set-valued map rather than equaling a prescribed function. The method replaces the classical pointwise PDE/ODE residual by the squared distance from the differential operator to the admissible set. This distance vanishes exactly when the inclusion is satisfied and measures the infimal correction needed for the operator to enter the admissible set. For a fixed closed convex admissible set, the squared distance is differentiable with respect to the operator value, with gradient given by the metric projection. When the admissible set also depends on the network state, that dependence is included through the chain rule. The framework encompasses ordinary and partial DIs with set-valued reaction terms. For both settings we prove consistency: under the stated closedness, measurability, convexity, and growth assumptions, any sequence of candidates satisfying the initial (and, in the parabolic case, boundary) conditions whose continuous distance-residual functional tends to zero admits a subsequence converging to an exact solution of the target inclusion. These are conditional statements for the continuous distance-residual functional; they do not cover the finite-collocation training loss, the behavior of the optimizer, or convergence rates. For admissible sets given as convex hulls of finitely many vertices, projection onto the set reduces to a small convex quadratic program, making the loss efficiently computable inside the training loop. Numerical experiments demonstrate high accuracy on the differential-inclusion benchmarks.
tldr: The paper introduces Distance-Residual Physics-Informed Neural Networks (DR-PINNs), a deep-learning framework for solving ordinary and partial differential inclusions by replacing the pointwise residual with the squared distance from the differential operator to a set-valued admissible set.
motivation: Classical physics-informed neural networks assume the governing law is an equality; many physical models instead involve differential inclusions where the operator must lie in a set-valued map, and no principled residual exists for that case.
method: The authors define a distance-residual functional using the squared distance to a closed convex admissible set, whose gradient is the metric projection, computed via a small convex quadratic program when the set is a convex hull of finitely many vertices; they then train networks minimizing this functional under collocation.
result: They prove consistency—sequences of candidates with vanishing continuous distance-residual admit subsequences converging to exact solutions of the inclusion—and demonstrate high accuracy on differential-inclusion benchmarks, while explicitly noting the results do not cover the finite-collocation loss, optimizer behavior, or convergence rates.
conclusion: DR-PINNs extend physics-informed learning to differential inclusions with efficient, differentiable training losses and rigorous conditional consistency guarantees, mainly contributing to numerical analysis and scientific machine learning rather than quantum information science.

title: Inverse-Limit Detection Envelopes As Calkin Algebras
authors: Jie Shen Rui Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For a unital Banach algebra [MATH] with [MATH] and a decreasing sequence [MATH] of proper closed two-sided ideals of finite codimension, we introduce the bounded detection envelope $[MATH][MATH]X[MATH][MATH][MATH]\ell_\infty[MATH]1[MATH]\ell_\infty[MATH]H^\infty(\mathbb D)[MATH](H_2^2)[MATH]\mathcal L_2[MATH]M_{}A(\mathbb F_2)[MATH]C^u(O_3^+)^*$ as Calkin algebras, with their canonical norms and products.
tldr: The paper introduces bounded detection envelopes for unital Banach algebras with decreasing sequences of finite-codimension proper closed two-sided ideals and identifies them as Calkin algebras.
motivation: The work aims to understand inverse-limit constructions and detection envelopes in the context of Banach and operator algebras, particularly through Calkin algebra structures.
method: For a unital Banach algebra with a decreasing sequence of proper closed two-sided ideals of finite codimension, the authors define a bounded detection envelope and study its canonical norm and product.
result: The envelope is shown to realize certain algebras as Calkin algebras, with examples involving $H^\infty(\mathbb D)$, $H_2^2$, $\mathcal L_2$, and $A(\mathbb F_2)$.
conclusion: The paper provides an operator-algebraic framework connecting detection envelopes, inverse limits, and Calkin algebras, but it is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Spectral Reality For Certain Fourth-Order Nonsymmetric Finite-Difference Laplacians
authors: Yizhe Feng, Weiguo Gao, Meiyue Shao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite-difference discretizations of Laplace operators yield discrete Laplacians whose spectral properties are closely tied to the stability, convergence, and physical fidelity of numerical solvers. While symmetric discretizations are well understood, many high-order finite-difference schemes produce nonsymmetric matrices for which rigorous spectral analysis is overlooked. Surprisingly, we prove that two fourth-order schemes with Dirichlet boundary conditions yield nonsymmetric discrete Laplacians whose spectra are purely real and strictly positive. Computer-assisted computations show that this property does not hold for higher-order extensions of these schemes in general.
tldr: The paper proves that two fourth-order nonsymmetric finite-difference Laplacians with Dirichlet boundary conditions have purely real, strictly positive spectra, and shows this fails for higher-order extensions.
motivation: High-order finite-difference schemes often produce nonsymmetric discrete Laplacians whose spectral properties are poorly understood, yet such spectra govern stability and convergence of numerical solvers.
method: Rigorous spectral analysis of two specific fourth-order nonsymmetric finite-difference discretizations, complemented by computer-assisted computations to test higher-order extensions.
result: Both considered fourth-order schemes yield spectra that are purely real and strictly positive, while computer-assisted checks indicate this reality property generally breaks down for higher-order analogues.
conclusion: The work fills a gap in spectral theory for nonsymmetric high-order discrete Laplacians and delineates the limits of the real-spectrum property beyond fourth order.

title: Fast Differentiable Svd On Gpu Via Polar Decomposition
authors: Uliana Parkina, Askar Tsyganov, Sergei Kudriashov, Sergey Samsonov, Maxim Rakhuba
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fully GPU-oriented SVD pipeline based on polar decomposition, motivated by iterative methods that rely solely on matrix multiplications, such as the Newton-Schulz iteration. We show that this approach enables up to a [MATH] speedup compared to standard implementations. Furthermore, we derive a numerically stable backward pass for the polar decomposition and leverage it to obtain a fully differentiable SVD. Our methods are released as open-source implementations in both PyTorch and JAX: [URL].
tldr: The paper presents a fully GPU-oriented, differentiable SVD pipeline based on polar decomposition using matrix-multiplication-only iterations such as Newton-Schulz.
motivation: Iterative SVD methods used in machine learning rely on matrix multiplications and are bottlenecked by the cost of standard SVD implementations, especially on GPU hardware where differentiability is also required.
method: The authors build a GPU SVD pipeline around polar decomposition via Newton-Schulz iteration and derive a numerically stable backward pass for the polar decomposition to make the whole SVD differentiable.
result: They report significant speedups relative to standard implementations and release open-source PyTorch and JAX implementations of the differentiable SVD.
conclusion: The work provides a practical, high-performance, differentiable numerical linear algebra routine for GPU-based machine learning frameworks, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: A Large-Scale Benchmark And Risk Assessment Of Traffic Analysis Attacks On Cloud Llm Services
authors: Shahrooz Pouryousef, Jesus Lopez, Saeefa Rubaiyat Nowmi, Md Mahmuduzzaman Kamol, Moinul Hossain, Muoi Tran, Mohammad Saidur Rahman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud-based Large language model (LLM) services create a network-level traffic side channel that can expose model, prompt, and task behavior despite encryption. From packet sizes, directions, timing, and burst structure alone, a passive local observer can infer the serving model, the user's prompt category, and the task executed by a collaborative multi-agent system. Yet current evidence is fragmented across separate datasets and settings, limiting reproducibility and comparison. We present, to our knowledge, the first unified measurement study and public benchmark of encrypted LLM traffic across both user--LLM and multi-agent executions. The large-scale benchmark contains 60,000 user--LLM interactions across 10 models and 6 prompt categories, plus 2,838 multi-agent executions covering 10 task categories and two coordination topologies. Using only encrypted packet metadata, we assess the risk of traffic analysis attack by characterizing traffic signatures, identifying the features most associated with leakage, and testing robustness under prompt reformulation, decoding-temperature changes, larger candidate model sets, and partial traffic observation. Model fingerprinting achieves 97.7\% balanced accuracy, prompt-category fingerprinting reaches 76.7\% mean accuracy, and multi-agent task fingerprinting achieves up to 90.7\% accuracy. Prompt reformulation weakens but does not remove model-specific leakage, and task fingerprints remain detectable even from a single agent's traffic.
tldr: The paper introduces a large-scale public benchmark of encrypted cloud LLM traffic and quantifies the effectiveness of passive traffic-analysis attacks that infer serving models, prompt categories, and multi-agent tasks from packet metadata alone.
motivation: Cloud LLM services leak behavioral information through encrypted network traffic side channels, but prior evidence is fragmented across datasets and settings, hindering reproducibility and comparison.
method: The authors curate 60,000 user–LLM interactions across 10 models and 6 prompt categories plus 2,838 multi-agent executions over 10 task categories and two coordination topologies, then train classifiers on encrypted packet-size, direction, timing, and burst features, testing robustness under prompt reformulation, temperature changes, larger candidate sets, and partial traffic observation.
result: Model fingerprinting reaches 97.7% balanced accuracy, prompt-category fingerprinting 76.7% mean accuracy, and multi-agent task fingerprinting up to 90.7% accuracy, with leakage persisting under reformulation and even from a single agent's traffic.
conclusion: Encrypted LLM traffic constitutes a substantial and robust privacy side channel, motivating defenses at the network level and providing a reusable benchmark for future traffic-analysis research.

title: Finite-Context Semantics In Finitely Supported Structures
authors: Gabriel Ciobanu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantics for systems with names and data often depends on finitely many distinguished values. The theory of finitely supported structures treats this dependence through invariance under permutations fixing a finite context. We develop this approach to semantics over arbitrary permutation groups and arbitrary infinite sets of atoms. The central difficulty is that finitely supported predicate spaces need not be complete lattices. We prove that, for predicates valued in a complete lattice with trivial atom action, every monotone finitely supported transformer nevertheless has least and greatest fixed points. These lie in the complete lattice determined by the transformer's context and coincide with the fixed points of every compatible monotone ambient extension equivariant under its stabilizer. Support-transfer bounds track dependencies through semantic constructions, while uniform finiteness yields finite convergence. For Boolean predicates, [MATH] context-stabilizer orbits on the carrier suffice for convergence after at most [MATH] iterations, even when the supported predicate lattice is orbit-infinite. We apply these results to automata, operational and modal semantics, abstract interpretation, and resource rewriting. Ultrahomogeneous atom structures in finite relational signatures yield finite cell representations, illustrated by an authorization monitor. The resulting account separates semantic existence, finite convergence, and effective computation.
tldr: Develops semantics for finitely supported structures over arbitrary permutation groups and infinite atom sets, proving fixed-point results for monotone transformers.
motivation: Semantics for systems with names and data often depends on finitely many distinguished values; finitely supported structures capture this dependence through invariance under permutations fixing a finite context.
method: Uses finitely supported predicate spaces, context-stabilizer orbits, and support-transfer bounds to establish fixed points and finite convergence over arbitrary permutation groups and atom sets.
result: Shows that every monotone finitely supported transformer on a complete lattice with trivial atom action has least and greatest fixed points, with Boolean convergence after finitely many iterations even when the predicate lattice is orbit-infinite.
conclusion: Applies the framework to automata, operational and modal semantics, abstract interpretation, and resource rewriting, separating semantic existence, finite convergence, and effective computation.

title: Developing A Numerical Algorithm With Civl Model Checking In The Loop
authors: Youngjun Lee, Anshu Dubey, Jan H\"uckelheim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying a numerical algorithm in a large scientific simulation framework is challenging: the framework is too big to model-check, and the unit tests exercise only sampled inputs. We report a case study in which we developed a new cloud-in-cell (CIC) deposition algorithm for Flash-X, a large-scale multiphysics simulation framework, keeping the CIVL model checker in the development loop. Rather than verify the algorithm within Flash-X's hefty infrastructure, we extract only the interfaces that the algorithm needs into a small, self-contained C model, which abstracts away implementation details of the Flash-X infrastructure that are unrelated to the new algorithm. The new algorithm is then built and checked within this C model. The CIVL model checker enables verification of the required physical properties of the CIC deposition algorithm using symbolic values for the particle positions. It proves two physical properties---mass conservation and the deposition location---for the continuum of admissible positions in the simulation domain. CIVL also verifies the algorithm's memory safety and freedom from MPI deadlocks and data race conditions over all rank distributions within specified bounds. Writing the verifying properties first and continuously checking them at each stage of the bottom-up prototyping workflow turned CIVL into a design guardrail that greatly increased confidence in the extended algorithm. During our case study, CIVL surfaced a concurrency defect in the algorithm that our random-seed-based tests failed to exercise. This paper shows our workflow, with the goal of helping readers understand its benefits, cost, and tradeoffs compared with testing.
tldr: A case study describing how a cloud-in-cell deposition algorithm for the Flash-X multiphysics framework was developed with the CIVL model checker in the loop, enabling formal verification of physical and concurrency properties.
motivation: Verifying numerical algorithms inside large scientific simulation frameworks is hard because the full framework is too large to model-check and unit tests only sample inputs.
method: The authors extract the algorithm's required interfaces into a small self-contained C model that abstracts Flash-X infrastructure, then use the CIVL model checker with symbolic particle positions to verify properties during bottom-up prototyping.
result: CIVL proved mass conservation and deposition-location correctness over the continuum of admissible positions, and verified memory safety and freedom from MPI deadlocks and data races; it also exposed a concurrency defect missed by random-seed tests.
conclusion: Writing verifying properties first and checking them continuously turns model checking into a design guardrail, offering a viable complement to testing with identifiable benefits, costs, and tradeoffs.

title: Hardware-Rooted Puf Fingerprinting For Device-Level Traceability In Knowledge Distillation
authors: Ning Lyu, Yuntao Liu, Yonghong Bai, Zhiyuan Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables model transfer across heterogeneous platforms and deployment environments, yet it exposes proprietary models to distillation-based theft, where an adversary extracts intellectual property (IP) by training a student model on teacher outputs. Current defenses, such as software watermarking or hardware-based access control, either fail to survive the distillation process or lack the granularity to identify the specific device responsible for a leak. Aiming to provide post-theft accountability and traceability, we propose a novel fingerprinting framework that superimposes device-specific Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) signatures onto teacher logits during distillation. By utilizing signatures derived from Ring Oscillator (RO) PUFs measured on a Xilinx Zynq-7020 FPGA, we ensure that any student model trained via KD inherits a unique, hardware-linked identity. Our framework is architecture-agnostic, enabling reliable identity inheritance across heterogeneous structures, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Vision Transformers, and encoders. To ensure robust attribution, we implement a two-stage recovery pipeline consisting of a neural decoder and Hamming-distance refinement, maintaining high detection accuracy even under noisy conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a multi-level logit encoding scheme to support large-scale device deployment. Experimental results demonstrate that the embedded fingerprints are resilient against common post-distillation modifications. These results establish a practical system-level approach for enabling hardware-linked model traceability in distributed AI deployment environments.
tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-rooted PUF fingerprinting framework to trace intellectual property leaks in knowledge distillation by embedding device-specific signatures into teacher logits.
motivation: Knowledge distillation enables model theft, and existing defenses either do not survive distillation or cannot identify the specific leaking device, motivating post-theft accountability and traceability.
method: Device-specific Ring Oscillator PUF signatures are measured on a Xilinx Zynq-7020 FPGA and superimposed onto teacher logits during distillation, with a two-stage recovery pipeline using a neural decoder and Hamming-distance refinement plus multi-level logit encoding.
result: The embedded fingerprints are inherited across CNN, ViT, and encoder architectures and remain resilient against common post-distillation modifications even under noisy conditions.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical system-level approach for hardware-linked model traceability in distributed AI deployment environments.

title: Evasion Attacks On Cost-Utility-Based Adversarial Training For Online AutoML In IoT Networks
authors: Chukwunonso Henry Nwokoye, Wajiha Zaheer, Khalil El-Khatib, Li Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Internet of Things (IoT) networks increasingly depend on machine learning for anomaly, malware, intrusion detection, and network monitoring, such systems have become attractive targets for evasion attacks. Evasion attacks pose a major security risk because an adversary intentionally modifies input data to mislead a trained model into producing incorrect predictions while evading detection. This study evaluates the impact of black-box evasion attacks on a cost-utility-based adversarial training defense strategy in an Online AutoML context for IoT networks. Specifically, evasion attacks were applied to online learners, including Hoeffding Tree (HT), Leveraging Bagging (LB), Streaming Random Patches (SRP), Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT), and Adaptive Random Forest (ARF). By developing naive and adversarially trained (AT) versions of these online learners, we generated clean and adversarial accuracies for each model. The results show that the AT versions of LB and SRP performed best, achieving the highest adversarial accuracy (0.985) and high clean accuracy (0.993) at the highest cost budget of 1.00, with a maximum accuracy reduction of only 0.8%. Finally, drift detection was conducted using the Early Drift Detection Method (EDDM).
tldr: This paper evaluates black-box evasion attacks against cost-utility-based adversarial training in Online AutoML systems for IoT network intrusion and anomaly detection.
motivation: IoT networks increasingly rely on machine learning for anomaly, malware, and intrusion detection, making them attractive targets for evasion attacks where adversaries perturb inputs to induce misclassification while avoiding detection.
method: The authors developed naive and adversarially trained versions of several online learners (Hoeffding Tree, Leveraging Bagging, Streaming Random Patches, Hoeffding Adaptive Tree, Adaptive Random Forest) and measured clean and adversarial accuracy under black-box evasion attacks, with drift detection via EDDM.
result: Adversarially trained Leveraging Bagging and Streaming Random Patches achieved the highest adversarial accuracy (0.985) alongside high clean accuracy (0.993) at a cost budget of 1.00, with only a 0.8% maximum accuracy reduction.
conclusion: Cost-utility-based adversarial training can substantially harden online AutoML models in IoT settings against evasion attacks, though the work is entirely classical machine-learning security and unrelated to quantum information.

title: Interactive Proofs Of Proximity For Model Evaluation
authors: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolas Melissaris, Tamara Paris
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study interactive proofs of proximity (IPPs) for model evaluation, where a resource-limited verifier interacts with an untrusted prover, typically the model owner, to certify statistical properties of a model under an unknown input distribution. Our formulation separates sampling the input distribution from querying the model and evaluating its output; distinguishes real audit data (black-box sampling) from generated data (chosen-randomness, or gray-box, access to the sampler); and allows the prover and verifier to use different evaluators. We focus on doubly-sublinear IPPs, where both the verifier and honest prover use sublinear resources, and on (weighted) Hamming weight properties. For ordinary Hamming weight, we give a tolerant doubly-sublinear IPP. For completeness and soundness radii [MATH] and gap [MATH], a logarithmic-round instantiation uses [MATH] verifier queries and [MATH] honest-prover queries, improving the cubic dependence of Amir, Goldreich, and Rothblum (ITCS 2025). We prove matching query lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. For distribution-weighted Hamming weight, black-box sampling requires [MATH] verifier samples but only [MATH] evaluations; the quadratic sample complexity is necessary in the interior regime. With chosen-randomness access, the problem reduces to ordinary Hamming weight, yielding [MATH] calls and evaluations. If the parties' evaluators disagree arbitrarily on a [MATH]-fraction of the distribution and by at most [MATH] elsewhere, our protocols remain doubly sublinear whenever [MATH], where [MATH]. Applications include auditing accuracy, group fairness, calibration, harmlessness, usefulness, and average-case robustness.
tldr: The paper studies interactive proofs of proximity for auditing statistical properties of machine-learning models under unknown input distributions.
motivation: Model evaluation by a resource-limited verifier is challenging when the model owner is untrusted and input distributions are unknown, motivating cryptographic proof systems for statistical certification.
method: It formulates doubly-sublinear interactive proofs of proximity for Hamming weight and distribution-weighted Hamming weight properties, separating sampling from model querying and considering black-box versus chosen-randomness sampler access.
result: It gives tolerant doubly-sublinear IPPs with logarithmic rounds and improved query complexity, proves matching lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, and analyzes robustness when prover and verifier evaluators disagree.
conclusion: The framework enables efficient auditing of accuracy, fairness, calibration, harmlessness, usefulness, and average-case robustness, but it is a classical complexity/cryptography result with no direct quantum information focus.

title: Checking Leakage Witnesses Versus Certifying Bounded Non-Leakage
authors: Burkhard Stiller Chao Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a language-model audit finds no leak, what is needed to certify non-leakage? We study guarantees over a declared prompt domain under an executable leakage criterion and decoding rule. For general bounded polynomial-time evaluators, a supplied leaking execution is polynomial-time checkable, while leak existence is \NP-complete and deterministic certification is \coNP-complete. Exact stochastic certification is [MATH]-complete at every fixed rational cutoff in [MATH]. Restricting the computation can change these bounds. For example, certification is in \coNP\ when all randomness is a terminal draw from an efficiently computed finite probability table. Attention models admit polynomial-time certification when local dependency windows of logarithmic length precede one global head, given deterministic decoding, fixed vocabulary, exact rational weighted means, a direct binary affine readout and finite-automaton prompt domains. A construction with two global layers instead makes certification \coNP-complete over template domains, with one head per layer, polynomial width, logarithmic precision and an inverse-polynomial logit margin. Planted-secret experiments measure what finite audits miss relative to complete references. Among 30 secret--model-state pairs that leak under greedy single-prompt execution on their secret's 4,096-prompt domain, uniformly selecting 256 recorded evaluations per pair misses every leak for an expected [MATH] of these pairs. Batched and single-prompt checks disagree on one complete-domain decision among all 48 fine-tuned pairs, while a same-order repeat reproduces every single-prompt output. These results distinguish computational conditions for certification from the coverage and execution conditions needed to interpret a negative audit.
tldr: The paper studies computational complexity and certification conditions for verifying non-leakage in language-model prompt audits, distinguishing checks of leaking witnesses from certifying bounded non-leakage.
motivation: When a language-model audit reports no leakage, practitioners need rigorous guarantees that non-leakage holds over an entire declared prompt domain rather than just for sampled prompts.
method: The authors formalize certification under executable leakage criteria and decoding rules, analyze complexity for bounded polynomial-time evaluators, stochastic certification, and restricted attention-model computations, and run planted-secret experiments.
result: Leak existence is NP-complete and deterministic certification is coNP-complete for general evaluators; attention models admit polynomial-time certification under strong restrictions, while a two-global-layer construction makes certification coNP-complete. Finite audits can miss all leaks in many secret-model-state pairs.
conclusion: The work separates computational conditions for certification from coverage and execution conditions needed to interpret negative audits, showing that a clean finite audit does not generally certify non-leakage.

title: CyberClear: A Benchmark For Llm Agent Systems On Apt Attack Chain Provenance
authors: Qi Chen, Fushuo Huo, Hangli Shen, Jingcai Guo, Shuhao Li, Guang Cheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents have demonstrated promising capabilities in cybersecurity tasks, yet their ability to reconstruct complete Advanced Persistent Threat attack campaigns from complex security logs remains largely unexplored. Existing cybersecurity benchmarks for agents mainly focus on vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and security analysis tasks, leaving the evaluation of attack chain provenance under realistic security logs insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce CyberClear, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents and advanced agent systems on APT attack chain provenance from long-context security logs. CyberClear covers both single-step attacks and multi-stage attack chains, requiring agents to identify attack evidence, infer attack progression, and generate provenance graphs containing entities, causal relationships, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and forensic evidence. To enable comprehensive evaluation, we develop an evaluation method tailored to APT attack chain provenance. Unlike conventional text similarity metrics that focus on surface-level matching, our evaluation examines whether reconstructed graphs preserve the semantics of attack chains across single-step behavior correctness, multi-step behavior identification, temporal and causal consistency, entity and relationship fidelity, and overall attack narrative consistency. Advanced multi-agent systems powered by state-of-the-art LLMs still struggle on CyberClear, motivating us to propose CyberProvenance, an agent cyber harness designed for multi-agents that augments LLM agents with evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedback-guided refinement mechanisms for reliable attack-chain provenance. Extensive evaluations on CyberClear demonstrate the effectiveness of CyberProvenance in improving evidence reasoning, execution-grounded validation, and complete APT attack chain reconstruction.
tldr: CyberClear is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agent systems on reconstructing APT attack chains from long-context security logs, paired with an agent harness called CyberProvenance.
motivation: Existing cybersecurity benchmarks for LLM agents focus on vulnerability discovery and exploitation, leaving attack-chain provenance from realistic logs under-evaluated.
method: The authors build a benchmark spanning single-step and multi-stage attacks, requiring agents to produce provenance graphs with entities, causal relations, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and forensic evidence, evaluated via semantics-aware graph metrics rather than surface text similarity.
result: State-of-the-art multi-agent LLM systems perform poorly on CyberClear, while the proposed CyberProvenance harness—using evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedback-guided refinement—substantially improves evidence reasoning and full attack-chain reconstruction.
conclusion: The work establishes a challenging benchmark and a practical agent design for automated APT attack-chain provenance, but lies entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Refine: A Resilient Evolution Framework For Intelligent Enterprise Alert Triage In Security Operations Centers
authors: Huimin Chen, Quan Long, Yanhao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) process large volumes of alerts daily. Alert triage prioritizes high-risk threats while reducing manual review of benign alerts. LLM agents can reason over logs and threat intelligence, but struggle to keep aligned with organization-specific, rapidly evolving SOC operational standards. We introduce REFINE, an LLM-agent framework for enterprise alert triage. REFINE encodes analyst expertise as structured skills and continuously adapts using analyst disposition feedback. It enforces recall = 1.0 as a hard constraint during evolution to maximize auto-closure of false positives, and identifies judgment blind spots by combining alert distributions with model error boundaries. Evaluated on four real industrial SOC scenarios across four MITRE ATT&CK phases with temporal split: REFINE achieves recall=1.0 on all evolution sets. On future test windows, it retains recall=1.0 in three scenarios; the degraded case reaches 0.807 recall, still outperforming self-evolution baselines (0.49-0.58).
tldr: REFINE is an LLM-agent framework that encodes analyst expertise as structured skills and evolves via disposition feedback to automate enterprise security alert triage while enforcing recall = 1.0.
motivation: Security Operations Centers face overwhelming alert volumes, and while LLM agents can reason over logs and threat intelligence, they drift from organization-specific, rapidly evolving operational standards.
method: REFINE represents analyst expertise as structured skills and continuously adapts using analyst disposition feedback, enforcing recall = 1.0 as a hard constraint during evolution and identifying judgment blind spots by combining alert distributions with model error boundaries.
result: Across four real industrial SOC scenarios and four MITRE ATT&CK phases with temporal splits, REFINE achieves recall = 1.0 on all evolution sets and retains recall = 1.0 on future test windows in three of four scenarios, with the degraded case reaching 0.807 versus 0.49–0.58 for self-evolution baselines.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates that LLM agents with constrained evolution and feedback can reliably automate false-positive closure in enterprise SOC triage, though the work is purely applied cybersecurity and unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Learnable Randomization As Commitment Against Adaptive Optimizers
authors: Zihan Deng, Chuanzhi Xu, Xiaozhen Zhong, Haoyang Li, Junjie Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A pricing page can walk the posted price up to the last amount a buyer still accepts, a recommender can hold back a better item for a barely acceptable promoted one, and a classifier can shift its boundary once applicants change their features. The system predicts the response and then picks the menu that serves its own objective, so the surplus above the user's cutoff is taken. Playing the single best action publishes that cutoff, while noise on actions the user would never take throws away payoff and teaches the platform that a worse menu is still acceptable. We study unpredictable near-optimal policies (UNOP), which mix uniformly on near-best actions that remain individually rational. The mixture is a commitment about the response. On a finite price grid, when the best sure-demand price strictly out-earns the randomized band, a seller who already knows the curve posts below the band, and the purchase that occurs is deterministic. Knowing that curve is not the same as predicting the next draw. The mixture can be learned and the optimizer can match its best response, while the user's payoff stays higher because the mixture changes which action is targeted. In pricing and in policy-aware recommendation this leaves more surplus than greedy play when the platform optimizes against the curve and more than one action is acceptable. The gain goes away under quality ranking, a singleton near-optimal set, a wrong utility estimate, or a short-horizon explorer. That is also where mixing should be turned off if the other side is trying to cooperate.
tldr: The paper studies learnable randomization over near-optimal individually rational actions as a commitment device against adaptive optimizers in pricing and recommendation settings.
motivation: Platforms that predict user responses and then choose actions can extract surplus above the user's cutoff, but deterministic best responses reveal information and invite manipulation. The authors seek a strategy that preserves user surplus while remaining learnable by an optimizer.
method: They formalize unpredictable near-optimal policies (UNOP), which mix uniformly over near-best actions that are individually rational, and analyze their properties on a finite price grid and under learning dynamics.
result: Mixing can be learned and matched by an optimizer while keeping user payoff higher than greedy play when multiple actions are acceptable, but the advantage disappears under quality ranking, singleton near-optimal sets, wrong utility estimates, or short-horizon exploration.
conclusion: Randomization acts as a commitment about responses, but should be disabled when the other side is trying to cooperate, as the surplus gain is fragile and context-dependent.

title: Duals Of Separable Banach Spaces As Calkin Algebras And Universal Ideal Quotients
authors: Jie Shen Rui Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For [MATH] or [MATH] and every separable Banach space [MATH], we use an oracle-relative two-sorted finite-extension construction, whose oracle records the local rational structure of [MATH], to construct a separable Banach space [MATH] such that $[MATH][MATH]V^*[MATH]X[MATH]/(X)[MATH][MATH](X)$, and the subspace--ideal correspondence preserves the canonical order.
tldr: The paper constructs separable Banach spaces whose duals realize Calkin algebras and universal ideal quotients via an oracle-relative finite-extension method.
motivation: The work addresses structural problems in Banach space theory and operator ideal theory, aiming to realize certain quotient algebras as dual spaces of separable Banach spaces.
method: It uses an oracle-relative two-sorted finite-extension construction that encodes the local rational structure of a separable Banach space, combined with subspace–ideal correspondence.
result: For a given separable Banach space X, a separable Banach space V* is built such that V*/X is isomorphic to the Calkin algebra and the subspace–ideal correspondence preserves canonical order.
conclusion: This yields a realization of universal ideal quotients as duals of separable Banach spaces, contributing to pure functional analysis and operator theory.

title: Application Of Machine Learning To The Computation Of Parameters In The Supg Method For Unstructured And Anisotropic Meshes
authors: Manoj Prakash Petr Knobloch
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solution of convection-dominated problems using stabilized methods often requires to specify stabilization parameters whose optimal choice is not known but which considerably influence the quality of the approximate solution. In a recent work of the authors, an approach for computing these parameters by machine learning was proposed and applied to the streamline upwind/Petrov-Galerkin (SUPG) method for convection-diffusion equations. In the present paper, this approach is studied numerically for unstructured meshes and extended to meshes obtained by anisotropic mesh adaptation.
tldr: This paper extends a machine-learning approach for computing optimal stabilization parameters in the SUPG method to unstructured and anisotropically adapted meshes for convection-diffusion problems.
motivation: Stabilized finite element methods require choosing stabilization parameters that strongly affect solution quality, and optimal choices are generally unknown, especially on complex meshes.
method: The authors numerically study a previously proposed machine-learning framework for predicting SUPG stabilization parameters and extend it to unstructured meshes and meshes generated by anisotropic mesh adaptation.
result: The approach is evaluated on convection-dominated problems, showing that learned parameters can be applied successfully to more complex mesh geometries including anisotropic adaptations.
conclusion: Machine learning is a viable tool for parameter selection in SUPG stabilization, improving robustness on challenging unstructured and anisotropic meshes.

title: SilentCall: Hidden Tool-Call Backdoors In Open-Weight Agents, And How To Catch Them
authors: Bhanu Pallakonda, Mikkel Hindsbo, Sina Ehsani, Prag Mishra
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight tool-calling agents are adopted on evidence of merit, usually benchmark scores and a record of reliable use. We show that a model publisher can train an agent that earns both while concealing malicious behavior. Fine-tuned on a mixture of clean and poisoned conversations, our agents answer ordinary requests correctly; once the system date reaches a chosen year, they emit the correct tool call and, alongside it, one that exfiltrates the user's credentials. The exfiltration runs while the user-facing response mentions only the legitimate work. We call this attack SilentCall. Under the trigger, it fires on at least [MATH]\% of requests, and no response ever mentions it. The attack is detectable by three distinct methods, which differ mainly in what a defender needs to run them. A runtime monitor that inspects each tool call before it executes requires no access to the model and catches every instance of the payload we tested at a 1.73% false-positive rate. High-temperature probing requires only the published weights. The weight-distribution audit requires training a benign model with the suspect's recipe, placing it within reach of model hubs but not ordinary users. Alignment benchmarks, by contrast, do not separate poisoned from benign models. SilentCall leaves no trace on standard benchmarks. As tool-using agents spread through the open-weight supply chain, trust in them should not rest on what a model says about its own actions. It has to come from inspecting those actions at runtime, auditing models where they are distributed, and treating tool access as a security surface in its own right.
tldr: The paper introduces SilentCall, a date-triggered backdoor in fine-tuned open-weight tool-calling agents that silently exfiltrates user credentials alongside legitimate tool calls, and evaluates three detection methods against it.
motivation: Open-weight tool-calling agents are increasingly trusted based on benchmark scores and reliability records, but a malicious model publisher could exploit this trust to hide harmful behavior behind otherwise correct responses.
method: Agents are fine-tuned on a mixture of clean and poisoned conversations so they respond normally until a chosen trigger date, at which point they emit an extra credential-exfiltrating tool call; three detection approaches are then tested: a runtime tool-call monitor, high-temperature probing, and a weight-distribution audit.
result: Under the trigger the attack fires on a substantial fraction of requests without any user-visible mention, alignment benchmarks fail to distinguish poisoned from benign models, and a runtime monitor catches every tested payload instance at a 1.73% false-positive rate.
conclusion: Trust in tool-using agents should not rely on self-reported behavior; defenders must inspect tool calls at runtime, audit models where they are distributed, and treat tool access as a security surface.

title: Bma: Backchain Memory Attacks Create Unauthorized Control Paths In Llm Agents
authors: Kaisheng Fan, Yishu Gao, Xunzhu Tang, Tegawend\'e F. Bissyand\'e, Weizhe Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent memory enables LLM agents to reuse prior experience, but creates a new security boundary: what an agent may remember is not what it should act on. We expose an unauthorized control path where edited low-trust evidence is consolidated into persistent memory, retrieved on a clean task, and used to drive a protected action. Crucially, the adversary neither writes memory nor alters the task. We introduce Backchain Memory Attack (BMA), a grey-box, LLM-driven inverse-planning attack that reasons backward from the target action to the memory that would trigger it, then to the evidence edit that would form it. BMA has two phases: preparation uses resettable trials to localize the first failed link and build experience; execution uses the frozen experience to rank and commit candidate edits without feedback. We introduce the Pathway-Certified Attack Success Rate (Path-CASR) to separate memory-mediated from coincidental hits: registered memory must form, be retrieved, drive the target behavior, and pass matched-intervention checks. Across four substrates and three decision backbones, BMA achieves 18.8% Macro Path-CASR, compared with 13.4% for the strongest access-matched baseline. Of BMA's behavioral hits, 60.3% pass all registered pathway and intervention checks versus 36.7% for the baseline. Frozen BMA edits retain 78.0% of their certified effect on average across four held-out consolidation policies. Representative memory-side controls leave 11.0% Path-CASR, whereas provenance-bound authorization reduces it to 2.0% while preserving 92.1% legitimate-action success.
tldr: The paper introduces Backchain Memory Attack (BMA), a grey-box inverse-planning attack that corrupts low-trust evidence so that it gets consolidated into an LLM agent's persistent memory and later drives unauthorized protected actions.
motivation: Persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a new security boundary: what an agent remembers is not necessarily what it should act upon, allowing adversary-influenced evidence to be laundered into trusted control paths without direct memory writes or task tampering.
method: BMA operates in two phases: a preparation phase that uses resettable trials to localize the first failed causal link and build experience, and an execution phase that uses frozen experience to rank and commit candidate evidence edits without feedback; evaluation uses a Pathway-Certified Attack Success Rate (Path-CASR) with matched-intervention checks across four substrates and three decision backbones.
result: BMA achieves 18.8% Macro Path-CASR versus 13.4% for the strongest access-matched baseline, with 60.3% of behavioral hits passing all pathway and intervention checks (vs. 36.7% for the baseline), and frozen edits retaining 78.0% of certified effect across held-out consolidation policies; provenance-bound authorization reduces Path-CASR to 2.0% while preserving 92.1% legitimate-action success.
conclusion: Memory-mediated control paths represent a genuine and measurable attack surface in LLM agents, and provenance-bound authorization is an effective mitigation that sharply reduces certified attacks with little loss of legitimate functionality.

title: Vertices That Belong To Every Minimum Dominating Set Of A Graph And Their Connection With Transportation Sharing Systems With Study Cases In Campo De Gibraltar Area
authors: Mohammad Farhan, Dorota Kuziak, Iztok Peterin, Ismael G. Yero
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study addresses a theoretical model regarding equity and accessibility challenges in designing shared transportation systems (such as micro-mobility networks) by applying graph-vertex domination setting. The work focuses on identifying dominating forced vertices, that represent nodes belonging to every dominating set of a graph of the smallest possible cardinality, and which correspond to critical, non-negotiable station locations essential for maintaining system efficiency and coverage. From a theoretical perspective, in the paper it is first demonstrated that determining whether a given vertex is a dominating forced vertex is co-NP-hard, establishing the computational infeasibility of exact identification in large networks. To analyze graph structures, sharp theoretical bounds on the maximum number of dominating forced vertices are established, proving that their count is bounded above by one-third of the order of the graph, and provide complete structural characterizations for graphs achieving this bound, as well as, trees with no dominating forced vertices. To overcome computational limits in practical urban settings, the study uses an iterated greedy metaheuristic framework to generate minimal dominating sets and approximate critical forced nodes based on their appearance frequency across iterations. The methodology is validated on strong grid graphs and applied to real-world road network models of Algeciras and La L\'inea de la Concepci\'on, two cities in the area of Campo de Gibraltar, Spain, which successfully pinpoints candidate location points for scooter-sharing stations across both cities.
tldr: This paper studies dominating forced vertices in graph domination and applies them to locating shared transportation stations in the Campo de Gibraltar area.
motivation: The authors aim to model equity and accessibility challenges in shared transportation systems, such as micro-mobility networks, using graph-vertex domination to identify critical station locations.
method: They prove co-NP-hardness of determining dominating forced vertices, establish sharp bounds and structural characterizations, and use an iterated greedy metaheuristic to approximate critical nodes in real urban road networks.
result: They show the number of dominating forced vertices is bounded by one-third of the graph order, characterize graphs achieving this bound, and identify candidate scooter-sharing station locations for Algeciras and La Línea de la Concepción.
conclusion: The work connects graph domination theory with practical transportation network design, providing both hardness results and a heuristic framework validated on real-world city networks.

title: Mapped Multi-Patch Spectral Extreme Learning Machine For Partial Differential Equations
authors: Suchuan Dong Yiran Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31909v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a fixed-feature solver, referred to as Spectral-ELM, in which Chebyshev--Gauss--Lobatto (CGL) differentiation matrices are applied to the nodal values of an extreme learning machine (ELM) trial function. Curved domains are treated using a mapped multi-patch formulation. Each curved quadrilateral patch is represented as the image of a reference square, physical derivatives are computed from the associated metric terms, and adjacent patches are coupled by enforcing continuity of the solution and its normal flux. Local QR orthogonalization is used to reduce near-linear dependence among the discrete features. The numerical study includes comparisons with direct CGL collocation, an analytically differentiated ELM, a global Random Feature Method, and a TransNet sampling strategy. It also includes a matched KdV test, a small three-dimensional example, and a Poisson problem on a curved domain containing a hole. For a smooth elliptic problem on a square, direct CGL collocation gives the smallest error. When applied to the same fixed-feature trial space, spectral and analytic differentiation produce comparable errors. For the curved-domain problem, mapped direct CGL collocation and mapped Spectral-ELM achieve similar accuracy with comparable numbers of unknowns. The present formulation is particularly well suited to smooth PDEs in one to three dimensions, where tensor-product grids enable accurate high-order discretizations, while sparse-grid and dimension-adaptive strategies offer promising directions for extension to higher-dimensional problems.
tldr: The paper introduces Spectral-ELM, a fixed-feature solver that applies Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto differentiation matrices to extreme learning machine trial functions with a mapped multi-patch formulation for solving PDEs on curved domains.
motivation: High-order spectral methods and machine-learning-based solvers each have strengths, and the authors aim to combine them into a fixed-feature solver that handles complex curved geometries accurately.
method: CGL differentiation matrices are applied to the nodal values of an ELM trial function; curved quadrilateral patches are mapped from a reference square with metric terms, patches are coupled via continuity of solution and normal flux, and local QR orthogonalization reduces feature redundancy.
result: For a smooth elliptic problem on a square, direct CGL collocation achieves the smallest error, while spectral and analytic differentiation yield comparable errors; on curved-domain and KdV tests, mapped Spectral-ELM matches mapped direct CGL collocation accuracy with similar numbers of unknowns.
conclusion: The formulation is well suited to smooth PDEs in one to three dimensions with tensor-product grids, and sparse-grid or dimension-adaptive extensions are suggested for higher dimensions.

title: Finite Element Error Estimates For A Bilinear Optimal Control Problem With Pointwise Tracking Governed By A Semilinear Elliptic Pde
authors: Enrique Otarola, Daniel Quero, Matias Sasso
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite element approximations for an optimal control problem with pointwise tracking governed by a semilinear elliptic PDE. The control variable enters the state equation as a reaction coefficient, resulting in a bilinear control, and the cost functional includes point evaluations of the state variable. We propose two discretization schemes: a semidiscrete scheme, where the control variable is not discretized, and a fully discrete scheme, where the control variable is discretized using piecewise constant functions. In two and three dimensions, for both schemes, we establish convergence of discrete solutions and prove a priori error bounds that behave as [MATH] in the [MATH]-norm for approximating a locally optimal control. In two dimensions, these bounds are improved to [MATH] for the fully discrete scheme and [MATH] for the semidiscrete scheme. We conclude with numerical experiments that demonstrate the performance of the proposed schemes.
tldr: This paper develops and analyzes finite element discretization schemes for a bilinear optimal control problem with pointwise state tracking governed by a semilinear elliptic PDE.
motivation: Optimal control problems with pointwise tracking of the state arise in applications where the objective depends on values of the state at specific locations, but rigorous finite element error analysis for such bilinear semilinear problems is lacking.
method: The authors propose a semidiscrete scheme (continuous control) and a fully discrete scheme (piecewise constant control), establish convergence of discrete solutions, and derive a priori error bounds in the L2-norm for locally optimal controls in two and three dimensions.
result: They prove O(h^2) error bounds in two dimensions for the fully discrete scheme and improved O(h^2) style rates for the semidiscrete scheme, with numerical experiments confirming the predicted convergence behavior.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous finite element error estimates for a class of bilinear optimal control problems with pointwise tracking, extending numerical analysis methodology but staying entirely within classical applied PDE-constrained optimization.

title: Optimal Convergence Analysis Of Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian Finite Element Methods For Two-phase Stokes Flow Problems With Moving Interface
authors: Yi Liang, Cheng Wang, Pengtao Sun, Yan Chen, Jiarui Han
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE)-based finite element method (FEM) is developed and studied in a monolithic framework for a class of two-phase Stokes flow problems with moving interfaces and jump coefficients, where the mixed finite element approximation to Stokes moving interface problems is established and analyzed in both semi- and fully discrete schemes based on the ALE formulation. The key analytical technique involves a specific H^1-projection associated with the ALE-induced mesh motion due to the evolving interface. Optimal convergence properties of the proposed H^1-projection and its ALE temporal derivative are proved in both H^1 and L^2 norms, with which optimal error estimates are obtained for both semi- and fully discrete mixed finite element approximations to the studied Stokes moving interface problem in both H1 and L2 norms as well. Numerical experiments are carried out to validate all derived theoretical results. The developed analytical approach can be extended to Taylor-Hood and MINI mixed elements, as well as to more general two-phase flow problems.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian finite element method for two-phase Stokes flow problems with moving interfaces, establishing optimal convergence in both H1 and L2 norms.
motivation: Two-phase Stokes flows with evolving interfaces and jump coefficients require robust numerical schemes, and a rigorous error analysis of ALE-based mixed finite element approximations was lacking.
method: The authors formulate a monolithic ALE-based mixed finite element scheme and introduce an H1-projection tied to the ALE-induced mesh motion, proving optimal convergence of the projection and its temporal derivative in H1 and L2 norms.
result: Optimal error estimates are obtained for both semi-discrete and fully discrete schemes in H1 and L2 norms, with numerical experiments confirming the theoretical rates; the approach extends to Taylor-Hood and MINI elements.
conclusion: The proposed analytical framework provides optimal convergence guarantees for ALE finite element discretizations of moving-interface Stokes problems and generalizes to broader two-phase flow settings.

title: Discrete Diffusion For Port Selection In Multiuser Pinching-Antenna Systems
authors: Wenxuan Sun, Mingjie Shao, Yanqing Xu, Ya-Feng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) reconfigure wireless channels by activating radiating elements at selected locations along dielectric waveguides. Port selection is a core issue in improving the performance of multiuser PASS systems. In this paper, we study joint port selection and precoder design for multiuser sum rate maximization, which leads to a large-scale nonconvex mixed-integer problem coupling discrete port selection with continuous precoder design. We propose a discrete diffusion method that does not require optimal or near-optimal port selection solutions as training labels and recasts the resulting optimization problem as sampling from a target distribution. Instead, we learn a potential function from local objective differences between neighboring feasible realizations. The learned potential is incorporated into a Metropolis--Hastings sampling rule to guide a parallel diffusion process while preserving the port selection constraints. Simulation results show that the proposed method approaches exhaustive search within a [MATH] sum rate gap while achieving over [MATH] speedup, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods including greedy and beam search. In particular, it also achieves an [MATH] speedup over greedy search.
tldr: The paper proposes a discrete diffusion framework for joint port selection and precoder design in multiuser pinching-antenna systems to maximize sum rate.
motivation: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) reconfigure wireless channels by activating radiating elements along dielectric waveguides, and port selection is a core bottleneck for multiuser performance.
method: The large-scale nonconvex mixed-integer problem is recast as sampling from a target distribution; a potential function is learned from local objective differences between neighboring feasible realizations and incorporated into a Metropolis-Hastings rule guiding a parallel diffusion process that preserves port selection constraints.
result: Simulations show the method approaches exhaustive search within a small sum rate gap while achieving over 10x (and much larger over greedy) speedups, outperforming greedy and beam search baselines.
conclusion: Discrete diffusion with learned potentials offers an effective label-free approach to combinatorial port selection in multiuser PASS, trading minimal rate loss for substantial computational speedup.

title: A Dsp Framework For Isac With Random Signals: From Physical Transceiver To Periodic Models
authors: Junjie Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication-centric integrated sensing and communication~(ISAC) directly employs random data-bearing communication signals for both information transmission and environmental sensing. Existing studies generally describe pulse-shaped transmission in continuous time or directly adopt periodic discrete-time sensing models, leaving the digital signal processing~(DSP) operations connecting the physical transceiver and the periodic models unclear. This paper develops a DSP-oriented transceiver framework for single-antenna communication-centric ISAC. A common transmitter is constructed through modulation, cyclic-prefix~(CP) insertion, upsampling, and pulse shaping. For communication reception, the physical transceiver chain is reduced to a symbol-rate equivalent linear channel, which becomes circulant after CP removal and thereby supports frequency-domain equalization. For sensing reception, a high-rate reference waveform is extracted from the transmitted waveform and equivalently represented by circular pulse shaping. CP removal at the receiver then converts physical target delays into circular shifts of this reference waveform, leading to a periodic matched-filtering model and the corresponding range profile. Numerical results validate the developed framework through target range estimation and the symbol error rate performance of pulse-shaped CP-OFDM over frequency-selective Rayleigh fading channels.
tldr: This paper develops a DSP-oriented transceiver framework for single-antenna communication-centric integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) using random data-bearing signals, connecting physical transceiver operations with periodic models.
motivation: Existing ISAC studies either describe pulse-shaped transmission in continuous time or adopt periodic discrete-time sensing models without clarifying the DSP operations that connect the physical transceiver to those models.
method: The framework constructs a common transmitter via modulation, cyclic-prefix insertion, upsampling, and pulse shaping; for communication reception it reduces the physical chain to a symbol-rate equivalent linear channel that becomes circulant after CP removal, and for sensing reception it extracts a high-rate reference waveform and uses circular pulse shaping to convert target delays into circular shifts.
result: Numerical results validate the framework through target range estimation and symbol error rate performance of pulse-shaped CP-OFDM over frequency-selective Rayleigh fading channels.
conclusion: The paper provides a DSP-oriented framework bridging physical transceiver design and periodic sensing models for communication-centric ISAC, but it is unrelated to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Convergent Plug-and-Play Image Restoration With Annealed Noise Levels
authors: Samuel Hurault
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods solve imaging inverse problems by incorporating deep denoisers into iterative optimization algorithms. Although practical implementations often decrease the denoiser noise level [MATH] along iterations, most existing convergence analyses assume a fixed denoiser. In this work, we establish convergence guarantees for a broad family of Plug-and-Play algorithms with annealed noise level, spanning deterministic methods (RED--GD and PnP--PGD) and stochastic methods (SNORE, equivariant RED, and a variant of PnP--Flow). For each method, we identify an explicit, nonconvex objective associated with the terminal denoising level and prove asymptotic stationarity of the iterates with respect to this objective. Our analysis does not prescribe any decay rate for the noise schedule, and our assumptions cover both learned gradient-step denoisers and exact MMSE denoisers. Overall, our theoretical results bridge the gap between existing PnP convergence theory and the decreasing-denoising practices used by state-of-the-art image restoration methods. We empirically demonstrate the benefits of such schedules and illustrate the predicted convergence behavior on several imaging inverse problems, including inpainting, super-resolution, demosaicing and tomography.
tldr: The paper establishes convergence guarantees for a broad family of Plug-and-Play image restoration algorithms that use annealed (decreasing) denoiser noise levels.
motivation: Existing convergence analyses for Plug-and-Play methods assume a fixed denoiser, while practical state-of-the-art implementations attenuate the denoiser noise level across iterations, leaving a theory-practice gap.
method: The authors analyze deterministic (RED-GD, PnP-PGD) and stochastic (SNORE, equivariant RED, PnP-Flow variant) PnP algorithms with arbitrary noise schedules, identifying an explicit nonconvex objective at the terminal denoising level and proving asymptotic stationarity.
result: Asymptotic stationarity of the iterates with respect to the terminal-level objective is proven without prescribing a decay rate, covering both learned gradient-step and exact MMSE denoisers, and validated empirically on inpainting, super-resolution, demosaicing, and tomography.
conclusion: The work bridges the gap between existing PnP convergence theory and decreasing-denoising practices, providing a unified theoretical framework for annealed-noise PnP image restoration.

title: Fair And Efficient Allocations: Decision Problems In The Gap Of Polynomial Hierarchy
authors: Biaoshuai Tao Xiaolin Bu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the fair division problem with indivisible goods and study the following decision problem: given a fair division instance, does there exist an allocation that is envy-free and efficient? We consider two efficiency criteria: Pareto-optimality and social welfare optimality. We provide a complete landscape on the computational complexity of this decision problem, with the number of agents ranging from [MATH] to [MATH], both additive valuations and general valuations, and the more restricted class of [MATH]-ary valuation functions (where an item's marginal value is restricted to [MATH] for some constant [MATH]). One interesting observation is that many versions of the above-mentioned decision problems fall into the ``gap'' between the first and the second levels of the polynomial hierarchy. Specifically, assuming the polynomial hierarchy does not collapse to the first level (i.e., assuming [MATH]), these problems are in [MATH]. In particular, we provide a fine-grained complexity analysis across different parameter regimes, including the number of agents and the choice of valuation models. Depending on different parameters, many problems admit different complexity classifications, ranging from the intermediate classes [MATH] and [MATH] between the two levels to [MATH]-completeness. Finally, De Keijzer et al. show the [MATH]-completeness of the decision problem when considering Pareto-optimality as the efficiency criterion with additive valuations. Our main results extend this result to more restricted settings, such as instances with a constant number of agents or [MATH]-ary valuation functions, which resolves the open problem given by Bouveret and Lang.
tldr: A complexity-theoretic study of the decision problem of whether an envy-free and efficient allocation exists in fair division with indivisible goods, mapping results across valuation models and agent counts into intermediate classes of the polynomial hierarchy.
motivation: Fair division of indivisible goods has many existence and complexity questions, but the complexity of deciding existence of an allocation that is simultaneously envy-free and efficient was only partially resolved, with an open problem posed by Bouveret and Lang.
method: The authors perform a fine-grained complexity classification of the decision problem for additive, general, and k-ary valuations and varying numbers of agents, using reductions that place problems in the gap between the first and second levels of the polynomial hierarchy.
result: Many versions of the problem lie in intermediate classes such as Σ₂ᵖ ∩ Π₂ᵖ (under the assumption PH does not collapse), while others are shown complete for classes between NP and the second level, extending prior Σ₂ᵖ-completeness results to restricted settings like constant agent number and k-ary valuations.
conclusion: The work resolves the open problem of Bouveret and Lang and provides a complete landscape of the computational complexity of envy-free and efficient fair division, revealing a rich hierarchy of intermediate complexity classes.

title: Residual Transferability In Neural Image Watermarking
authors: Ziping Dong, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural image watermarks can be forged by extracting watermark-bearing residuals from released images and transferring them to unrelated content. While prior work has demonstrated this vulnerability, what makes these residuals transferable remains poorly understood. We formalize this vulnerability with , a metric that quantifies how well watermark evidence remains decodable after transfer across unrelated images. Through comparative analyses and controlled interventions, we find that common training-side variations do not account for the large RT differences across watermarking systems; instead, architectural design plays a central role. By contrasting high- and low-RT systems and validating their architectural differences through controlled interventions, we identify two mechanisms that strengthen the dependence of watermark evidence on the cover image, thereby suppressing the residual transferability. These findings provide concrete design guidance for developing more forgery-resistant watermarking architectures. Complementarily, for existing watermarking systems where architectural redesign is impractical, we introduce , a plug-and-play strategy for existing watermarking systems that strengthens such image dependence without architectural redesign. Across representative watermarking systems exhibiting high residual transferability, CoverLock achieves a more favorable security--robustness trade-off than both traditional handcrafted defenses and learned classifier-based defenses.
tldr: This paper studies residual transferability in neural image watermarking, showing that architectural design controls vulnerability to watermark forgery.
motivation: Neural watermarks can be forged by transferring watermark-bearing residuals from released images to unrelated content, but what makes these residuals transferable remains poorly understood.
method: The authors formalize a residual transferability (RT) metric, compare watermarking systems through controlled interventions, and introduce CoverLock, a plug-and-play defense that strengthens image dependence.
result: Common training-side variations do not explain large RT differences across systems; architectural design plays a central role, and CoverLock achieves a better security-robustness trade-off than handcrafted or learned defenses.
conclusion: The findings provide concrete design guidance for forgery-resistant watermarking architectures and offer a practical defense for existing systems.

title: SkillDRE: Dual-Stage Red-Team Evolution Of Agent Skills Via Pre-Execution And Runtime Feedback
authors: Pengyu Zhu, Jingyi Yang, Yi Liu, Li Sun, Sen Su
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills package instructions, executable code, and task-specific resources into reusable artifacts that agents can improve using execution feedback. The same mechanism also enables attackers to evolve malicious skills, making them more effective and less detectable. However, a candidate skill may pass pre-execution scanning yet fail to realize its target under runtime defenses, while a revision that repairs execution may introduce new scanner findings. We introduce SkillDRE, a fully automated framework for evolving complete malicious skill packages through a dual-stage feedback loop. Given a benign task and its associated skills, SkillDRE autonomously constructs and validates a task-conditioned malicious objective and a verifiable judge rule. It then holds both fixed while evolving the skill implementation, with preservation of legitimate task capability. SkillDRE combines scanner-guided evolution with runtime-guided refinement informed by execution outcomes observed under runtime defense. Each runtime-guided revision returns to the pre-execution stage for rescanning and further optimization before re-execution, forming a cross-stage closed loop. Evaluated on SkillsBench across four victim models, SkillDRE achieves an average attack success rate of 45.28%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 40.3%, while its final submitted skills receive no SkillScan findings and largely preserve benign-task performance. These results show that two-stage defense feedback can serve as a useful learning signal for adaptive red teaming and that evaluating either defense stage in isolation can miss the resulting attack capability. Codes is available at [URL].
