tldr: SkillDRE is an automated dual-stage red-team framework that evolves malicious agent skill packages using combined pre-execution scanning and runtime execution feedback to evade defenses while preserving benign task capability.
motivation: Agent skills that bundle instructions, code, and resources can be exploited by attackers to evolve malicious artifacts, yet a skill may pass pre-execution scanning and still fail under runtime defenses (or vice versa), so single-stage evaluations miss attack capability.
method: SkillDRE constructs a task-conditioned malicious objective with a verifiable judge rule, then holds both fixed while evolving the skill implementation via scanner-guided evolution and runtime-guided refinement, with each runtime revision looping back for rescanning and re-execution.
result: On SkillsBench across four victim models, SkillDRE attains a 45.28% average attack success rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 40.3%, while final submitted skills yield no SkillScan findings and largely preserve benign-task performance.
conclusion: Two-stage defense feedback can serve as an effective learning signal for adaptive red teaming, and evaluating either defense stage in isolation can miss the resulting attack capability.

title: Hearsay: Can An Auditor Trust The Record A Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
authors: Jiahong Dai, Zhuochen Yang, Pengyang Shao, Kelvin Ng, Zhongyi Liu, Chengquan Ju, Yuting He, Bo Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent harness, the code that turns a model into an agent, writes its own record of each run, and that record is all a later reader gets when a run is disputed, investigated or audited. We call a record evidentiary when a reader who was not there can check it without trusting the writer. Across sixteen deployed frameworks, none writes one in full. Hearsay examines the record, not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, three blinded LLM examiners and a human panel read the records, and every excerpt an examiner quotes is checked mechanically for who wrote it. First, the record lets a reader name the fault but not prove how the run went. Examiners name the right fault in 74 to 91% of 140 runs, but the fault can be proved only from two files the benchmark adds; for what happened in between, fewer than one citation in ten lands on anything the harness did not write, and the examiner with the fewest false alarms catches half of the entries we delete, rewrite or fabricate. Second, the remedy is a second author, not a stronger seal on the first. An append-only log of what passes between harness and model, kept outside the harness and read against the record in both directions, reports all 28 omissions and fabrications we made a harness commit as it ran, where a hash chain over the harness's own record passes all 28. Handed the log, examiners keep their fault verdicts but rest more of their citations on what the harness did not write. What makes a record evidence is who writes it, not what is captured.
tldr: The paper studies whether an AI agent harness's self-written run record can serve as trustworthy evidence for later auditing, and proposes an external append-only log as a remedy.
motivation: Deployed agent frameworks produce records used in disputes, investigations, or audits, but it is unclear whether such records are evidentiary without trusting the writer.
method: Five agent harnesses run fourteen tasks; three blinded LLM examiners and a human panel read the records, with mechanical checks of citations, and an append-only harness-model log is tested against omissions and fabrications.
result: Examiners often name the right fault but rarely cite harness-independent evidence; an external append-only log detects all 28 injected omissions/fabrications, whereas a hash chain over the harness's own record detects none.
conclusion: Evidentiary value depends on who writes the record, not merely on what is captured, so a second independent author is needed rather than a stronger seal on the harness's own record.

title: Trust The Brand, Lose Control: How Identity Hijacks Llm Agent Orchestration
authors: Xutao Mao, Rui Qian, Linghan Chen, Yudong Gao, Junchi Liao, Jiulin Cai, Jinman Zhao, Cong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents now execute tasks end to end with permission to change real systems and increasingly orchestrate subagents that differ in capability and cost. Prior work treats the choice of subagent as an optimization problem. Yet the orchestrator makes this choice from the identities that subagents display, and an attacker can spoof them. Displayed identity thus decides operational authority, meaning who is trusted to check the work and who is allowed to change it. As a result, a risky subagent can keep authority over execution even after other evidence contradicts it. We introduce TrustFork, an LLM agent safety benchmark with 1,890 tasks and 27,826 valid trajectories across 16 agent systems. These systems run eight orchestrators under the OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Pi harnesses. In each task, one subagent carries a risky goal while the other three stay aligned with the user, so contradicting evidence can exist. A task can also change the identity a subagent displays without changing the model behind it, which lets us trace a shift in authority to the label. Our analysis shows that even when another subagent contradicts the risky response, the orchestrator still acts on it in 72.0% of cases on average, most often in the systems with the least terminal harm. Swapping the family labels nearly triples how often the orchestrator obtains the risky response. A safer response is available in 84.0% of tasks, yet it decides the outcome in only 25.0%. The harness also decides which responses reach the orchestrator. Among three runtime defenses, hiding identity cues helps most consistently, while verifying before action helps only when the harness returns enough evidence. TrustFork shows that production agent orchestration must bind authority to evidence before execution causes harm. Our project is in [URL].
tldr: TrustFork is a benchmark of 1,890 tasks and 27,826 trajectories across 16 LLM agent systems showing that spoofable subagent identities hijack orchestrator authority, causing risky responses to be accepted in 72% of cases even when contradicted.
motivation: LLM orchestrators select and trust subagents based on displayed identity rather than verified evidence, and an attacker can spoof those labels, so authority over execution can be captured by a risky agent.
method: The authors build TrustFork, a safety benchmark with tasks in which one subagent carries a risky goal and three are aligned, running eight orchestrators under three harnesses (OpenCode, OpenClaw, Pi), and manipulating identity labels independently of the underlying model.
result: Orchestrators act on the risky response in 72.0% of cases on average despite contradicting evidence, family-label swaps nearly triple risky-response selection, a safer response exists in 84.0% of tasks but decides the outcome only 25.0% of the time, and hiding identity cues is the most consistent of three runtime defenses.
conclusion: Production agent orchestration must bind operational authority to verified evidence rather than displayed identity before execution can cause harm.

title: Ask Without Telling: Local SLMs Consult Cloud LLMs Without Revealing Task Intent
authors: Yanmeng Wang, Yunxuan Li, Shilong Fan, Yuhan Zheng, Tsung-Hui Chang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As local small language models (SLMs) increasingly collaborate with more capable cloud large language models (LLMs), a natural privacy question arises: Can a local SLM obtain cloud LLM guidance while protecting user privacy? Existing privacy-preserving SLM-LLM frameworks primarily hide sensitive values while preserving task semantics, which can still expose what the user is trying to accomplish. For example, allocating scarce medical supplies across hospitals may signal an emerging public-health emergency, while rebalancing an investment portfolio may reveal a private investment strategy, even when names and numerical values are hidden. Recent decoy-based methods further obscure task intent by hiding the real request among alternatives, but stronger protection relies on more decoys or semantic abstraction, increasing overhead or risking utility loss. More fundamentally, existing work does not systematically characterize the components of private task intent or how each should be protected. We therefore introduce task-private consultation, which characterizes task intent through two components: task context and task operation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these components and their individual and joint protection in local-cloud SLM-LLM consultation. To realize this setting, we propose PriCon, an end-to-end framework that transforms the task itself through recoverable mathematical reformulation rather than hiding it among alternatives. A local closed-loop refinement mechanism further maintains privacy and recoverability throughout consultation. Experiments on 100 tasks show that PriCon reduces cloud-side task-intent inference Hit@1 to nearly 0%, versus 93-99% under sensitive-value removal and 3-30% under decoy-based protection, while preserving cloud-assisted utility.
tldr: PriCon is a framework that lets a local small language model consult a cloud LLM for guidance while concealing the user's task intent via recoverable mathematical reformulation.
motivation: Existing privacy-preserving SLM-LLM collaboration methods hide sensitive values but still leak what the user is trying to accomplish, and decoy-based attempts to obscure intent incur high overhead or utility loss.
method: The authors formalize 'task-private consultation' in terms of task context and task operation, and propose PriCon, an end-to-end framework that transforms the task itself through recoverable mathematical reformulation, with a local closed-loop refinement mechanism to maintain privacy and recoverability.
result: On 100 tasks, PriCon reduces cloud-side task-intent inference Hit@1 to near 0%, compared with 93-99% under sensitive-value removal and 3-30% under decoy-based protection, while preserving cloud-assisted utility.
conclusion: The work provides the first systematic treatment of task-intent privacy in local-cloud SLM-LLM consultation and shows that reformulation-based protection substantially outperforms value-hiding and decoy approaches.

title: Hydrogen Mon Amour
authors: Patrick Janot Christophe Grojean
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The FCC's projected average electricity consumption is 1.3 TWh per year. If supplied entirely by nuclear power, this would represent about 10% of the annual output of a large third-generation nuclear reactor, together with a corresponding share of its radioactive waste. By 2050, however, renewable sources could provide up to 80% of this electricity on a substantially decarbonised European grid, supported by long-term power-purchase agreements and flexible operation. This could reduce the residual nuclear requirement, and its associated waste, by up to a factor of five. This essay asks whether hydrogen could help bridge the remaining periods of low wind and solar generation. It examines production from renewable electricity, transport as hydrogen or ammonia, storage and conversion back into electricity, together with their efficiency losses and carbon footprints. It then considers the still uncertain prospect of naturally occurring hydrogen. None of these routes offers a ready-made solution. But the decades before the FCC begins operation leave time to develop one--and CERN could help accelerate that development by becoming a credible long-term customer.
tldr: This essay examines whether hydrogen can bridge gaps in renewable electricity supply for the FCC, while also discussing nuclear power, energy storage, and CERN's potential role as a long-term customer.
motivation: The FCC's projected electricity demand of 1.3 TWh per year raises questions about its energy sourcing, radioactive waste, and decarbonization strategy.
method: The essay qualitatively reviews renewable electricity production, hydrogen and ammonia transport, storage and reconversion losses, carbon footprints, and the uncertain prospect of natural hydrogen.
result: No single route provides a ready-made solution; renewable sources could supply up to 80% by 2050, potentially reducing residual nuclear requirements and waste by up to a factor of five.
conclusion: The remaining low-wind and low-solar periods require further development, and CERN could help accelerate solutions by becoming a credible long-term customer.

title: Periodically Modulated Traveling Waves In Integrate-and-fire Networks: Recursive Speed Law And Propagation Failure
authors: Jie Nissel, Ricardo Erazo-Toscano, Rosahn Bhattarai, Marius Osan, Mandeep Chauhan, Remus Osan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.33006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traveling waves of activity in neural tissue can be halted by spatial inhomogeneity in synaptic coupling. We study an integrate-and-fire network in which each neuron fires once and the coupling decays exponentially. For this model the leading-edge firing map reduces exactly to a scalar equation for the wave speed in space, with a slow unstable and a fast stable homogeneous speed, [MATH] and [MATH], and a periodic modulation of the coupling enters this equation pointwise. Positive periodic waves terminate in folds. For slowly varying modulation the fold amplitude approaches a plateau set by the trough of the modulation, where the local bottleneck speed is [MATH]; the approach to the plateau is set by the local geometry of the trough. For rapidly varying modulation the fold amplitude grows linearly with frequency, with a slope given by a full-amplitude average over the integrated modulation profile; a weak-ripple truncation of that average overestimates the slope about 2.5-fold at the default coupling. A perturbative recursion in the amplitude gives the speed profile explicitly. We distinguish loss of the periodic wave from failure of a particular launch, and the excitatory regime [MATH] from its sign-changing extension. The results are checked against direct integration of the reduced equation and first-spike firing-map simulations of the network.
tldr: The paper studies traveling wave propagation in an integrate-and-fire neural network with exponentially decaying coupling and periodic modulation, deriving a recursive speed law and conditions for propagation failure.
motivation: Traveling waves in neural tissue can be halted by spatial inhomogeneity in synaptic coupling, motivating a reduced model to understand how periodic modulation affects wave speed and termination.
method: The leading-edge firing map is reduced to a scalar equation for wave speed, and a perturbative recursion in the modulation amplitude yields the speed profile, checked against direct integration and first-spike simulations.
result: Positive periodic waves terminate in folds; fold amplitude plateaus for slow modulation and grows linearly with frequency for fast modulation, with a weak-ripple truncation overestimating the slope about 2.5-fold.
conclusion: The work distinguishes loss of the periodic wave from failure of a particular launch and characterizes excitatory versus sign-changing regimes, providing a reduced description of modulated wave propagation.

title: Weak Mixing For Dynamical Systems With ${\bm{\mathscr M}}_{\bm\alpha}$-shadowing
authors: Xinxing Wu, Jidan Wei, Xu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies weak mixing for two classes of dynamical systems with the \(_{\alpha}\)-shadowing property using the generic factor characterization of weak scattering. First, for every \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), every \(M\)-system with the \(_{\alpha}\)-shadowing property is weakly mixing, thereby answering [P. Oprocha et. al., On partial shadowing of complete pseudo-orbits, J. Math. Anal. Appl., Question~1] negatively. Second, for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the \(_{\alpha}\)-shadowing property implies weak mixing for \(E\)-systems and, in particular, for dynamical systems whose measure center is the whole space.Finally, an \(E\)-system with the \(_{0}\)-shadowing property which is not weakly mixing is constructed, showing that the parameter range \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) in the \(E\)-system result is optimal.
tldr: This paper studies weak mixing in dynamical systems satisfying the M_alpha-shadowing property, proving several implications and constructing a counterexample to show optimality of the parameter range.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize weak mixing via generic factor characterizations of weak scattering and to answer a question of Oprocha et al. about partial shadowing of complete pseudo-orbits.
method: They use the generic factor characterization of weak scattering to analyze M-systems and E-systems with alpha-shadowing, and construct a specific E-system with 0-shadowing that is not weakly mixing.
result: They show that for every alpha in [0,1), every M-system with alpha-shadowing is weakly mixing, and for alpha in (0,1), alpha-shadowing implies weak mixing for E-systems; the range is optimal due to the constructed counterexample.
conclusion: The results resolve a question negatively and demonstrate sharp parameter ranges for shadowing-induced weak mixing in topological dynamics.

title: Generic Sharp Shift Embedding For Amenable Group Actions With The Uniform Rokhlin Property And Comparison
authors: Chunlin Liu Yonatan Gutman
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Naryshkin recently proved that a free action of a countably infinite discrete amenable group [MATH] on a compact metrizable space [MATH] with the uniform Rokhlin property and comparison (URPC) admits an equivariant embedding into [MATH] whenever [MATH]. We strengthen this result from existence to genericity by a substantially different method: the set of observables [MATH] whose orbit maps are equivariant embeddings into [MATH] is a dense [MATH] subset of [MATH]. The proof combines an adaptation of the Kakutani skyscraper construction used by Gutman--Tsukamoto with a new polynomial perturbation method, departing from the predominantly linear perturbation approaches used in earlier equivariant embedding literature.
tldr: This paper strengthens Naryshkin's equivariant embedding theorem for amenable group actions with the uniform Rokhlin property and comparison from existence to genericity via a new polynomial perturbation method.
motivation: Naryshkin recently proved that free actions of countably infinite discrete amenable groups on compact metrizable spaces with the uniform Rokhlin property and comparison admit an equivariant embedding into a shift space under a dimension condition. The paper aims to strengthen this from mere existence to genericity.
method: The proof adapts the Kakutani skyscraper construction used by Gutman and Tsukamoto, combined with a new polynomial perturbation method, departing from the predominantly linear perturbation approaches used in earlier equivariant embedding literature.
result: The set of observables whose orbit maps are equivariant embeddings into the shift space is shown to be a dense G_delta subset of the space of observables.
conclusion: The work provides a generic sharp shift embedding theorem for amenable group actions satisfying the uniform Rokhlin property and comparison, advancing the understanding of equivariant embeddings in topological dynamics.

title: Tight Convergence Bounds For The Classical Kaczmarz Method
authors: Jelena Diakonikolas Runbo Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical method of Kaczmarz, introduced in 1937, is a textbook iterative method for solving linear systems [MATH] Despite its widespread use, particularly in the context of solving inverse problems where it is commonly included in software packages within Matlab, Python, and Julia, the precise characterization of convergence has long been deemed difficult to obtain. While different bounds on convergence rates have been established, they are largely unsatisfying as they cannot explain the classical, cyclic-update method's efficient convergence in practice. In this work, we obtain a tight characterization of convergence of the classical Kaczmarz method, establishing both linear and sublinear convergence bounds. The worst-case tight (i.e., exactly attained by some instances in the considered family) bounds are expressed in terms of a fixed matrix that depends only on [MATH] but are not fully interpretable in terms of the matrix spectrum and row correlations, which had been observed to have an impact on convergence. We thus provide relaxations of these bounds that are fully expressible in terms of matrix row norms, row correlations, rank, and extremal positive singular values. The provided relaxed bounds explain one-cycle convergence in special cases where the matrix rows are all either parallel or orthogonal to each other. We further argue that the dependence on different parameters appearing in the bounds is necessary and within a small constant factor of the best attainable in the worst case. Finally, our bounds explain why the classical cyclic update is faster than the randomized one when matrix rows are weakly correlated, which is often observed in inverse problems where the cyclic method is used.
tldr: The paper provides tight convergence bounds for the classical Kaczmarz method for solving linear systems, including interpretable relaxations in terms of matrix properties.
motivation: Despite the Kaczmarz method's widespread use and long history, its convergence behavior has lacked a precise characterization that explains its practical efficiency, especially for cyclic updates.
method: The authors derive worst-case tight linear and sublinear convergence bounds and then relax them to expressions involving row norms, row correlations, rank, and extremal positive singular values.
result: The bounds explain one-cycle convergence for parallel or orthogonal rows, show parameter dependence is necessary up to constants, and clarify why cyclic updates can outperform randomized ones when rows are weakly correlated.
conclusion: This is a significant contribution to classical numerical linear algebra and iterative methods, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Merged-cell Discontinuous Galerkin Method For Scalar Conservation Laws On Curved Domains
authors: Yong Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyse a discontinuous Galerkin method for two-dimensional scalar conservation laws on curved domains. Small intersections of a Cartesian grid with the domain are combined by rectangular cell merging. The local space is the restriction of [MATH] to each physical merged cell. An entropy-conservative flux is supplemented by face viscosity and, for odd degrees, a skew derivative-jump correction on unmerged interior squares. We prove exact semidiscrete [MATH] dissipation and an optimal error estimate for every fixed [MATH]. For smooth solutions with homogeneous trace on the entire boundary, the semi-discrete method satisfies an [MATH] error bound. The constants are independent of the original cut-cell area fractions. The proof combines a physical-cell [MATH] projection and cancellation of regular-face projection errors. A separate semidiscrete result covers linear transport with upwind inflow data. Computations for Burgers' equation on a disk and linear advection on a smooth star exhibit orders close to [MATH] for [MATH].
tldr: A merged-cell discontinuous Galerkin method is analyzed for scalar conservation laws on curved domains, with entropy dissipation and optimal error estimates.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of small cut-cell intersections when using Cartesian grids for conservation laws on curved domains, aiming for accuracy independent of cut-cell area fractions.
method: It combines rectangular cell merging, an entropy-conservative flux with face viscosity, and for odd degrees a skew derivative-jump correction on unmerged interior squares.
result: The method achieves exact semidiscrete entropy dissipation and optimal error estimates for every fixed polynomial degree, with constants independent of cut-cell area fractions; numerical tests confirm expected orders for Burgers' equation and linear advection.
conclusion: The proposed merged-cell DG scheme provides a robust and accurate numerical framework for scalar conservation laws on curved domains, with rigorous entropy stability and convergence guarantees.

title: Complementary Waveform Coordination For Doppler-Resilient Mimo Radar
authors: Maksim Antonik, Wenbing Dang, Ali Pezeshki, Stephen D. Howard, William Moran
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complementary waveform libraries yield impulse-like aggregate delay responses at zero Doppler, but pulse-dependent Doppler phases degrade their sidelobe cancellation. This paper develops a linear-algebraic formulation for coordinating a (D)-ary transmission schedule and slow-time receive weights for paraunitary MIMO waveform libraries. Using a modal decomposition of the CPI ambiguity matrix, prescribed-order Doppler-nulling conditions for the (D-1) nonzero modes are expressed as homogeneous linear constraints on the receive weights for a fixed schedule. This representation gives the SNR-optimal fixed-schedule weights by subspace projection and reduces the remaining design to a discrete schedule search. Degrees-of-freedom and modal-growth analyses relate the design to the CPI length, null order, and waveform dimension. Numerical examples compare the resulting designs with established binary constructions and demonstrate Doppler suppression across the full ambiguity matrix of a four-waveform configuration.
tldr: The paper develops a linear-algebraic framework for coordinating transmit schedules and receive weights in paraunitary MIMO radar waveform libraries to improve Doppler-resilient sidelobe suppression.
motivation: Complementary waveform libraries provide impulse-like delay responses at zero Doppler, but pulse-dependent Doppler phases degrade sidelobe cancellation in MIMO radar.
method: Using a modal decomposition of the coherent processing interval ambiguity matrix, the authors express prescribed-order Doppler-nulling conditions as homogeneous linear constraints and derive SNR-optimal fixed-schedule receive weights via subspace projection, reducing design to a discrete schedule search.
result: Numerical examples show Doppler suppression across the full ambiguity matrix of a four-waveform configuration, comparing the designs with established binary constructions.
conclusion: The proposed coordination method offers a systematic way to design Doppler-resilient MIMO radar waveforms and receive weights, with degrees-of-freedom and modal-growth analyses relating performance to CPI length, null order, and waveform dimension.

title: Wave Breaking And Structure-Preserving Fully Discrete Method For Stochastic Camassa--Holm Equation With Additive Noise
authors: Liying Sun, Zizhao Sun, Liying Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we investigate the stochastic Camassa--Holm equation driven by additive noise, which models nonlinear shallow-water waves under random external forcing. We establish that, almost surely, any finite-time breakdown occurs through wave breaking: the wave amplitude and the positive part of the slope remain bounded, whereas the minimum slope tends to [MATH]. Under an additional moment assumption, we derive an initial-slope condition ensuring wave breaking with positive probability. We also formulate the equation as a stochastic Hamiltonian PDE, establish its stochastic multi-symplectic conservation law, and derive the evolution law for the averaged [MATH] energy. Combining the Fourier--Galerkin method, symplectic Runge--Kutta integration, and exact solution of the linear stochastic subsystem, we propose a fully discrete method which preserves an integrated discrete stochastic multi-symplectic conservation law and the linear growth of the discrete averaged \(H^1\) energy. Under suitable regularity and resolution assumptions, we present that the fully discrete dynamics retain the slope-steepening mechanism responsible for wave breaking, providing a discrete counterpart of the continuous behavior.
tldr: The paper investigates the stochastic Camassa-Holm equation with additive noise, proving wave breaking and developing a structure-preserving numerical method.
motivation: To understand nonlinear shallow-water waves under random forcing and to provide a reliable numerical scheme that preserves geometric properties.
method: Combines Fourier-Galerkin, symplectic Runge-Kutta, and exact solution of the linear stochastic subsystem to create a fully discrete method preserving multi-symplectic conservation and energy growth.
result: Almost surely wave breaking occurs, with a condition for positive probability; the numerical method preserves discrete multi-symplectic conservation and energy behavior.
conclusion: The proposed method captures the wave-breaking mechanism, offering a discrete counterpart to continuous dynamics.

title: Finite Expression Approximation Of High-Dimensional PDEs Without The Curse Of Dimensionality
authors: Haizhao Yang Zhi Heng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish that finite expressions form a symbolic representation class capable of overcoming the curse of dimensionality for several classes of high-dimensional partial differential equations. For semilinear heat equations, we show how finite expression approximations of the terminal condition and nonlinearity can be propagated through the multilevel Picard framework to produce randomized pointwise approximations with prescribed root-mean-square accuracy. For semilinear Kolmogorov equations with Laplacian diffusion and zero drift, diagonal Black--Scholes equations, and the Laplace Dirichlet problem on a half-space, we construct deterministic finite expression approximations with arbitrarily small spatial [MATH] error. Under suitable growth and regularity assumptions, the evaluation cost of the resulting approximants is bounded polynomially in the dimension and the reciprocal accuracy. A key ingredient in the nonlinear setting is the construction of finite expressions that approximate the PDE solution while preserving the growth and Lipschitz structures required by the stochastic solution theory. More broadly, our results show that dimension-robust approximation of high-dimensional PDEs is not restricted to conventional neural-network architectures: structured symbolic expressions generated from a fixed dictionary can achieve comparable polynomial-complexity guarantees. This provides a rigorous foundation for finite expression methods as a representation paradigm for high-dimensional scientific computing.
tldr: The paper introduces finite expressions as a symbolic representation class that overcomes the curse of dimensionality for certain high-dimensional PDEs, with polynomial evaluation cost in dimension and accuracy.
motivation: High-dimensional PDEs are central to scientific computing but often suffer from the curse of dimensionality, motivating representation classes beyond conventional neural networks that can provide dimension-robust approximations.
method: The authors construct finite expression approximations for semilinear heat and Kolmogorov equations, Black-Scholes equations, and the Laplace Dirichlet problem, using multilevel Picard iteration and symbolic dictionary-based expressions while preserving growth and Lipschitz structures.
result: They obtain randomized pointwise approximations with prescribed root-mean-square accuracy and deterministic approximations with arbitrarily small spatial error, with evaluation cost bounded polynomially in dimension and inverse accuracy.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous foundation for finite expression methods as an alternative symbolic paradigm for high-dimensional scientific computing, showing dimension-robust approximation is not limited to neural-network architectures.

title: Active Subspace-Guided Free-Form Deformation With Sinkhorn Autoencoders For Reduced-Order Modelling Of Parametrised Shape Problems
authors: G. Padula, C. Giovannini, G. Rozza, A. Dashtimanesh
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometrically parametrised PDEs arise in shape optimisation, where solving a PDE over many deformed domains at manageable cost is a central challenge. Free-form Deformation (FFD) parametrises shape variations through a lattice of control points, but the resulting parameter space is typically high-dimensional, with most directions barely affecting the quantity of interest (QoI). We address this with a two-stage reduction pipeline. An Active Subspace (AS)-guided structured control-point selection identifies the low-dimensional subspace of FFD weights driving the QoI. A Sinkhorn Autoencoder (SAE) is then trained on the reduced weights, learning their distribution in a compact latent space by minimising the Wasserstein distance between aggregated posterior and prior. We compare three non-intrusive Reduced-order Models (ROMs), mapping full FFD weights, AS-reduced weights, or SAE latent codes to the QoI, each using Random Forests, Gaussian Processes, and K-Nearest Neighbours. We test the methodology on a non-linear heat equation with Gaussian random Robin boundary data on a deformed Stanford Bunny, and on drag prediction for the DTC Hull bulb under FFD deformations. In both cases, the generative model captures the bulk of the QoI distribution over a comparable support, thinning the shoulder opposite the design objective, while its extremes in the design-relevant direction match the FFD sample within numerical and sampling uncertainty. ROMs learned in the SAE latent space yield smaller test errors than those on full FFD weights in most regressor-metric combinations, whereas AS-reduced weights give no comparable gain. Only the latent representation attains a positive predictive coefficient [MATH].
tldr: A two-stage reduction pipeline using active subspaces and Sinkhorn autoencoders improves reduced-order modeling of parametrised shape problems via free-form deformation.
motivation: Geometrically parametrised PDEs in shape optimisation require efficient solution over many deformed domains, but high-dimensional FFD parameter spaces contain many irrelevant directions.
method: Active Subspace-guided control-point selection identifies low-dimensional FFD weight subspaces, then a Sinkhorn Autoencoder learns a compact latent representation by minimising Wasserstein distance; three non-intrusive ROMs map full FFD weights, AS-reduced weights, or SAE latent codes to quantities of interest.
result: On a nonlinear heat equation with Robin boundary data and drag prediction for a DTC hull bulb, the SAE latent space yields smaller test errors than full FFD weights in most regressor-metric combinations, while AS-reduced weights give no comparable gain.
conclusion: The proposed latent representation captures the QoI distribution effectively and outperforms alternative input representations, demonstrating the benefit of combining active subspaces with Sinkhorn autoencoders for shape-parametrised ROMs.

title: A Structure-Preserving Lobpcg Method For Computing Several Of The Largest Generalized Singular Triplets
authors: Xinyu Shan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a structure-preserving locally optimal block preconditioned conjugate gradient(LOBPCG) method for computing several of the largest positive generalized singular values of a matrix pair \((A, B)\), where \(B\) has full column rank, together with the associated generalized singular vectors. The method is derived from the Hermitian-definite Jordan--Wielandt pencil and therefore avoids explicitly forming the normal-equation matrices. By exploiting the block structure and spectral symmetry of this pencil, we construct separate search subspaces for the left and right generalized singular vectors. The resulting Rayleigh--Ritz procedure requires only a singular value decomposition of a small projected cross matrix. We adapt the improved Hetmaniuk--Lehoucq (IHL) trick to construct stable conjugate search directions in the two component spaces. We also establish an explicit correspondence between the coefficient matrices produced by the componentwise and augmented Rayleigh--Ritz procedures. This correspondence permits the componentwise IHL construction to be used in an augmented, structure-preserving LOBPCG formulation without explicitly assembling the augmented basis. Numerical experiments demonstrate the computational advantages of the proposed method over unstructured and Gram-matrix-based LOBPCG implementations.
tldr: The paper develops a structure-preserving LOBPCG algorithm for computing the largest generalized singular triplets of a full-column-rank matrix pair, avoiding explicit normal-equation formation.
motivation: Computing generalized singular values and vectors of a matrix pair (A, B) via normal equations is numerically unstable and computationally costly, especially when only a few extremal triplets are needed.
method: The authors work with the Hermitian-definite Jordan-Wielandt pencil, exploit its block structure and spectral symmetry to build separate search subspaces for left and right singular vectors, and use an adapted Hetmaniuk-Lehoucq (IHL) trick for stable conjugate directions within a componentwise Rayleigh-Ritz procedure.
result: An explicit correspondence is established between the componentwise and augmented Rayleigh-Ritz coefficient matrices, enabling a structure-preserving augmented LOBPCG formulation without assembling the augmented basis; numerical experiments show computational gains over unstructured and Gram-matrix-based LOBPCG variants.
conclusion: The proposed method offers an efficient, structure-preserving approach to extremal generalized singular triplet computation, with demonstrated practical advantages for numerical linear algebra applications.

title: Facial Distance And Diameter
authors: Antoine Deza, David Mart\'inez-Rubio, Javier Pe\~na, Elias Wirth
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The facial distance of a polytope, equivalently its pyramidal width, is a geometric condition measure that appears in the convergence bounds for Frank--Wolfe algorithms. Pe\~na and Wirth developed calculus rules for this quantity and conjectured that the ratio of the facial distance to the diameter multiplied by the square root of the dimension is bounded by a constant. We show that this quantity is uniquely maximized by a regular simplex in each dimension, which implies that the conjecture holds and that [MATH] is the smallest constant. We also compute the facial distance of the Birkhoff polytope.
tldr: The paper proves a conjecture on the facial distance (pyramidal width) of polytopes, showing that the ratio of facial distance to diameter times the square root of dimension is uniquely maximized by a regular simplex, and computes the facial distance of the Birkhoff polytope.
motivation: The facial distance appears in convergence bounds for Frank-Wolfe algorithms, and a conjecture bounded the ratio of facial distance to diameter times the square root of dimension by a constant.
method: Using convex geometry and calculus rules for facial distance, the authors optimize the quantity over polytopes and identify the regular simplex as the extremal case, then compute the facial distance for the Birkhoff polytope.
result: The conjecture holds, the constant is the smallest possible, and the facial distance of the Birkhoff polytope is explicitly computed.
conclusion: The work provides tight geometric bounds relevant to Frank-Wolfe algorithm convergence and extends the calculus of facial distance.

title: Saddle-Point Problems With A Low-Dimensional Block Do Not Need Accurate Inner Solves
authors: Alexander V. Gasnikov Ivan Fomin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many learning problems couple a high-dimensional block of parameters with a handful of adversarial or dual variables: worst-group risk over a few groups, or learning under a few constraints. We consider [MATH] with [MATH], a compact convex set and strongly convex with condition number [MATH], and we count the oracle calls for [MATH] and for [MATH] separately. The textbook approach runs a cutting-plane method in [MATH] and solves every inner problem to accuracy [MATH] with an accelerated method; it needs [MATH] calls for [MATH] but [MATH] calls for [MATH]. We show that the inner problems need not be solved accurately. Our method, certificate transport, keeps a strongly convex lower model of a single slice and uses it as a prior for a short accelerated run on the next slice. By concavity in [MATH], every call for [MATH] then either cuts the localizer or moves the lower model to a mixture of the two slices with a certified increase of the lower bound. For [MATH] this gives an [MATH]-saddle point after [MATH] calls for [MATH], up to an initialization term, and [MATH] calls for [MATH]; both counts are optimal, even though [MATH] is only assumed to be concave and Lipschitz. For general [MATH], with centers of gravity of the localizer treated as computable, the method needs [MATH] calls for [MATH] and the optimal [MATH] calls for [MATH]. Under strong concavity in [MATH], a two-point accelerated method makes the number of calls for [MATH] independent of [MATH].
tldr: The paper proposes a certificate-transport method for saddle-point problems with a low-dimensional dual block, showing that inner problems need not be solved accurately to achieve optimal oracle complexity.
motivation: Many learning problems involve a high-dimensional parameter block and only a few adversarial or dual variables, but the textbook cutting-plane approach requires solving each inner problem accurately, which is computationally costly.
method: The method, certificate transport, keeps a strongly convex lower model of a single slice and uses it as a prior for a short accelerated run on the next slice, exploiting concavity in the dual variable to either cut the localizer or update the lower model with a certified increase.
result: For a one-dimensional dual block, it obtains an epsilon-saddle point with optimal oracle counts for both blocks, even under only concavity and Lipschitz assumptions; generalizations to higher dimensions and strong concavity are also given.
conclusion: Accurate inner solves are unnecessary for low-dimensional dual blocks, as the proposed certificate-transport scheme achieves optimal complexity while relaxing smoothness assumptions.

title: TokenScanner: Detecting Backdoors And Discovering Triggers In Text-to-Image LoRAs Via Full Vocabulary Scanning
authors: Jing Zhang Boliang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LoRAs are widely studied for adapting base text-to-image diffusion models. However, a backdoored LoRA can hide a backdoor: it behaves normally in most cases, but produces attacker-specified content (the backdoor target) when a hidden backdoor trigger appears in the input prompt. Detecting such backdoors before using an untrusted LoRA is important for the safety of LoRA adaptation. We present TokenScanner, a model-level vocabulary scanner for backdoor detection within a LoRA fine-tuned text-to-image diffusion model, aiming to discover the malicious trigger for trustworthy LoRA adaptation. The key observation is that backdoor trigger tokens that appear in a larger proportion of training prompts tend to induce more prominent token-specific LoRA responses than those induced by unrelated tokens. TokenScanner therefore scans the tokenizer vocabulary and measures token-wise LoRA responses in the U-Net and the text encoder. It uses these responses to detect backdoored LoRAs and rank candidate trigger tokens for subsequent testing of backdoor activation. Experiments on seven backdoor settings, comprising 840 backdoored LoRAs and 840 real-world benign test LoRAs, show that TokenScanner achieves 95.96% AUC and 96.55% TPR at an FPR of 10.95%. It also achieves 89.40% Hit@1 and 99.40% Hit@5 for trigger discovery across all seven settings.
tldr: TokenScanner detects backdoored text-to-image LoRAs by scanning the tokenizer vocabulary and measuring token-wise LoRA responses in the U-Net and text encoder to identify hidden triggers.
motivation: Untrusted LoRAs can conceal backdoors that only activate on a hidden trigger token in the prompt, so users need a way to detect and discover such triggers before adapting a base diffusion model.
method: The method scans the full tokenizer vocabulary, measures token-specific LoRA responses in the U-Net and text encoder, and uses these responses to flag backdoored LoRAs and rank candidate trigger tokens for activation testing.
result: Across seven backdoor settings with 840 backdoored and 840 benign LoRAs, TokenScanner achieves 95.96% AUC, 96.55% TPR at 10.95% FPR, and 89.40% Hit@1 / 99.40% Hit@5 for trigger discovery.
conclusion: Vocabulary-wide response scanning provides an effective model-level defense for trustworthy LoRA adaptation in text-to-image diffusion models.

title: Attributing Sensor Deviations To Degradation, Weather, Or Attack In Oilfield Digital Twins: A Simulation Study Of Probabilistic Attribution And Cost-Based Decisions
authors: Mustafa S. Aljumaily, Nawar S. Alseelawi, Hayder Kareem Abed
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an oilfield digital twin disagrees with its instruments, the operator must decide whether the cause is hardware degradation, harsh-weather effects, or malicious data manipulation. Existing digital-twin work appears to treat these causes separately: sensor-validation architectures target faults, and attack-focused twins have been evaluated on water-sector testbeds. We study joint cause attribution on a simulated four-well wellpad with 15 coupled instruments, legitimate operating transients, and weather. A physics-informed twin, identified from normal data only, produces analytical-redundancy residuals; windowed features feed a gradient-boosted classifier whose posterior drives an alarm gate with a fixed false-alarm rate and a cost-based decision rule that may defer to an analyst. On three independently generated sites, the classifier reaches macro-F1 of 0.818 on windows where the injected deviation is observable (0.723 when latent post-onset windows are included at the primary site). The physics twin accounts for essentially all of this: removing the data-driven twin changes macro-F1 by less than 0.01, whereas removing all twins drops it to about 0.58. Attacks are detected quickly (median 1.7 h) but attributed correctly at alarm time only 42% of the time, rising to 73% six hours later. A cost-aware policy that defers ambiguous cases had the lowest expected cost among all policies in every one of 144 cost and prior settings tested, sometimes by a small margin; the result depends on illustrative costs and on analysts resolving deferred cases. A twin-aware attacker was detected in 45% of episodes yet almost never attributed to attack. These results are conditional on the simulator's generative assumptions and have not been validated on field data.
tldr: A simulation study develops probabilistic attribution and cost-based decision policies for distinguishing sensor degradation, weather effects, and cyberattacks in oilfield digital twins.
motivation: Operators of oilfield digital twins need to determine whether discrepancies between the twin and instruments arise from hardware degradation, harsh weather, or malicious data manipulation, but existing work treats these causes separately.
method: A physics-informed twin identified from normal data generates analytical-redundancy residuals; windowed features feed a gradient-boosted classifier whose posterior drives an alarm gate with fixed false-alarm rate and a cost-based decision rule that may defer to an analyst.
result: On three simulated sites, the classifier achieved macro-F1 of 0.818 for observable deviations; attacks were detected quickly (median 1.7 h) but attributed correctly only 42% at alarm time, rising to 73% after six hours; a cost-aware deferral policy had the lowest expected cost across all 144 tested cost and prior settings.
conclusion: Joint attribution of degradation, weather, and attacks is feasible in simulation, but correct attack attribution is delayed and twin-aware attackers are rarely attributed; results are conditional on simulator assumptions and have not been validated on field data.

title: Beyond Incentive Compatibility: Rational Harm-Proof Transaction Fee Mechanisms
authors: Forest Zhang, Elain Park, Ke Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transaction fee mechanisms (TFMs) allocate scarce block space in blockchains. Prior work focuses on incentive compatibility (IC): honest behavior maximizes the payoff of each strategic player. We introduce rational-harm proofness (RHP), which rules out deviations that harm honest participants without reducing the deviator's utility relative to honest behavior. IC alone does not exclude such costless harm: in a second-price auction, a losing bidder can raise the winner's payment without changing its own payoff. For finite block capacity k, we characterize TFMs satisfying RHP alongside user incentive compatibility (UIC) and miner incentive compatibility (MIC). In the plain model, where a single miner implements the auction, we prove a tight tetrilemma: no TFM simultaneously achieves positive miner revenue, UIC, MIC, and RHP against miner-user coalitions, while any three are jointly achievable. In the MPC-assisted model, where a committee of miners implements the auction using multi-party computation, we construct a randomized TFM with positive miner revenue satisfying UIC, MIC, and RHP against users, miners, and miner-user coalitions containing at most k users. Randomness is necessary to confirm transactions under congestion: any deterministic TFM satisfying UIC and user RHP in this model confirms no transactions when the number of submitted bids exceeds k. Finally, IC and RHP are incomparable for every strategic role in both models: mechanisms can satisfy either property without satisfying the other. These results extend transaction fee mechanism design beyond incentives to protection against costless harm.
tldr: The paper introduces rational-harm proofness (RHP) for blockchain transaction fee mechanisms and characterizes the tradeoffs with incentive compatibility under finite block capacity.
motivation: Prior work on transaction fee mechanisms focuses on incentive compatibility, but incentive compatibility alone does not prevent costless harm to honest participants, as exemplified by second-price auctions.
method: The authors formally define RHP alongside user and miner incentive compatibility, prove a tight tetrilemma in the plain model, and construct a randomized MPC-assisted TFM that achieves positive miner revenue under RHP against coalitions up to k users.
result: No TFM can simultaneously achieve positive miner revenue, UIC, MIC, and RHP against miner-user coalitions, while any three are achievable; in the MPC-assisted model, randomness is necessary for confirming transactions under congestion.
conclusion: The work extends transaction fee mechanism design beyond incentives to protection against costless harm and shows that IC and RHP are incomparable for every strategic role.

title: A Transfer Tactic For Lean
authors: Daniel Raggi Zhaoxi Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rewriting in proof assistants spans a strict hierarchy. Equational rewriting substitutes based on extensional equality; subequational rewriting substitutes based on homogeneous relations such as [MATH] or [MATH], justified by monotonicity lemmas; and generalized rewriting relates different operations across different types, justified by transfer rules. All three are specializations of one schema, the function relator [MATH]. Lean 4's rw and Mathlib's grw/gcongr implement the first two levels, but the third has had no Lean implementation. We present one: a transfer tactic family over a tagged rule database, benchmarked using Mathlib's own test suites, of which 112 of 178 ported tests close through the transfer engine. An evaluation of the design's three motivating hypotheses returns a mixed result: generality holds, authoring effort wins in its amortized form (averaged per use), but on dependency footprint, transfer only ties a mature library and loses on coercions. This shows that transfer's value is concentrated on transferring into domains where few theorems exist.
tldr: The paper introduces a transfer tactic for Lean 4 that implements generalized rewriting over a tagged rule database, benchmarked against Mathlib's test suites.
motivation: Lean 4 and Mathlib support equational and subequational rewriting, but the third level of the rewriting hierarchy—generalized rewriting via transfer rules—has lacked a Lean implementation.
method: The authors design a transfer tactic family over a tagged rule database and evaluate it using ported Mathlib test suites, assessing generality, authoring effort, and dependency footprint.
result: 112 of 178 ported tests close through the transfer engine; generality holds and amortized authoring effort improves, but dependency footprint only ties a mature library and loses on coercions.
conclusion: Transfer's value is concentrated on domains where few theorems exist, making it useful primarily for transferring into sparse mathematical areas.

title: DegreeSpar: Structured Degree Sparsity For Efficient Secure Transformer Inference
authors: Yifei Cai, Zhuoran Li, Xiaozuo Shen, Hongyi Wu, Chunsheng Xin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure Transformer inference protects sensitive inputs but incurs substantial cryptographic overhead, with nonlinear operations such as Softmax and GeLU becoming major bottlenecks. Existing compression methods reduce nonlinear complexity, sequence-dependent computation, or model structure through separately defined compression variables. Under aggressive compression, however, these independently optimized perturbations can accumulate: at a matched compression level, stacking representative approximation, token-pruning, and model-pruning methods reduces ViT-S accuracy from 80.20% to 76.41%. We introduce DegreeSpar, which formulates secure Transformer compression as structured sparsification over nonlinear polynomial degrees. Polynomial degree directly controls the cost of secure nonlinear evaluation, while computation-aligned zero-degree structures expose token-level and model-dimension computation as removable within the same optimization space. DegreeSpar further incorporates approximation-aware training for low-degree Softmax and GeLU, enabling aggressive degree reduction and creating the optimization headroom required for structured computation removal. Across vision and language Transformers, DegreeSpar consistently improves the accuracy-latency trade-off across model scales, tasks, and sequence lengths, achieving speedups from 2.29x to 6.63x over the corresponding baselines. Under the same network setting, DegreeSpar achieves 92.68% accuracy on BERT/SST-2 in 110.55 s, compared with 92.66% in 167.26 s for CipherPrune, the closest prior hybrid secure-inference approach. These results establish structured polynomial degree as an effective shared optimization space for secure Transformer compression.
tldr: DegreeSpar introduces structured polynomial-degree sparsification to accelerate secure Transformer inference while preserving accuracy under aggressive compression.
motivation: Secure Transformer inference suffers from high cryptographic overhead, especially from nonlinear operations like Softmax and GeLU, and existing compression methods can accumulate accuracy loss when combined.
method: The paper formulates secure Transformer compression as structured sparsification over nonlinear polynomial degrees, aligning zero-degree structures with token and model-dimension computation removal, and uses approximation-aware training for low-degree Softmax and GeLU.
result: DegreeSpar achieves speedups of 2.29x to 6.63x over baselines and reaches 92.68% accuracy on BERT/SST-2 in 110.55 s versus 92.66% in 167.26 s for CipherPrune.
conclusion: Structured polynomial degree provides an effective shared optimization space for secure Transformer compression, improving the accuracy-latency trade-off across vision and language models.

title: Single-or-Sample: Online Fair Allocation For Combinatorial Agents
authors: Shuchi Chawla, Zhiyi Huang, Pooja Kulkarni, Ruta Mehta, Parnian Shahkar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of fairly allocating [MATH] indivisible goods among [MATH] agents who arrive online, under the notion of maximin share (MMS) fairness. Fair allocation with online arrivals is notoriously challenging: prior work achieves constant-factor MMS guarantees only when agents' preferences belong to a set of valuation functions known in advance, while no guarantees were known without such prior information. We develop a new randomized online algorithm for additive and submodular valuations, that we call Single-or-Sample, and that achieves a constant-factor approximation to MMS simultaneously for all agents, with constant probability. The algorithm requires no prior knowledge about the agents' valuations, and works against adversarial (oblivious) inputs. We further establish a fundamental tradeoff between approximation and success probability. Specifically, for any [MATH], no online algorithm can guarantee a [MATH]-approximation to MMS with probability exceeding [MATH], even for binary additive valuations. This rules out constant MMS with probability asymptotically closer to [MATH] than a constant. For XOS, the lower bound is much stronger: no algorithm can achieve even [MATH]-MMS to all agents with a constant probability. We complement this lower bound with an algorithm for the regime [MATH], namely [MATH]-MMS to all agents with probability [MATH], and show that this tradeoff is tight for XOS. Our constant-factor algorithm introduces several new ideas, combining greedy submodular maximization with randomized allocation and single-item reduction. A key technical ingredient is a new approach for analyzing iterative sampling without replacement. We develop concentration bounds that apply to a broad class of adaptive processes with complex dependencies across elements and rounds, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: The paper develops a randomized online algorithm for fairly allocating indivisible goods to combinatorial agents under maximin share fairness, achieving constant-factor guarantees without prior valuation knowledge.
motivation: Fair allocation with online arrivals is challenging, and prior work achieved constant-factor MMS guarantees only when agents' valuation functions are known in advance, leaving the unknown-preference case open.
method: The authors introduce a randomized online algorithm called Single-or-Sample for additive and submodular valuations, combining greedy submodular maximization, randomized allocation, and single-item reduction, along with new concentration bounds for iterative sampling without replacement.
result: The algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation to MMS for all agents with constant probability against adversarial inputs, and the authors establish matching lower bounds, including a tradeoff between approximation and success probability for XOS and stronger impossibility for binary additive valuations.
conclusion: The work advances online fair division by providing the first constant-factor MMS guarantees without prior valuation knowledge and introduces broadly applicable concentration bounds for adaptive sampling processes.

title: VulContextBench: A Benchmark For Security Context Retrieval In Coding Agents
authors: Yikun Li, Jinfeng Jiang, Yuheng Yieh, Ting Zhang, Yide Yin, Wen Bin Leow, Eng Lieh Ouh, Lwin Khin Shar, David Lo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability-detection benchmarks score the verdict an agent reaches, not the evidence it gathered. A model that recalls a CVE from pretraining therefore scores the same as one that traced the data flow. We study a task where this difference matters, deciding whether a commit introduces a vulnerability. Instead of scoring the verdict, we score whether the agent retrieved the code its conclusion depends on. We present VulContextBench, a benchmark of 111 vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) across 83 repositories, 63 CWEs, and five languages. Existing datasets label such commits by tracing a fix back through the version history, which often points to the wrong commit. We therefore audit every case by hand against an explicit four-criterion definition of a VIC, so the benchmark does not inherit that label noise. Each case is annotated with gold context, 464 code blocks in total, each tagged by its role in the evidence for the vulnerability. We evaluate seven frontier models with precision, recall and F1 at three granularities (file, block, and line), scored separately on the context an agent viewed while exploring and on the context it finally declared as evidence. The gap between the two is the main finding. Every model opens most of the gold context while exploring, but reports only part of it as evidence. At the level of code blocks, the share of the gold context a model reports is 37 to 73 percentage points below the share it viewed. Qwen3-Coder-Next views 86.3% of the lines in annotated code blocks but cites only 12.9% in its final report. GPT-5.5, which cites the most, views 73% and reports 36%. These results highlight a gap between finding relevant code and selecting it for the final report, which verdict-level benchmarks cannot reveal.
tldr: VulContextBench is a benchmark that scores whether a coding agent retrieves the code context its vulnerability verdict depends on, rather than just the verdict itself.
motivation: Verdict-level vulnerability-detection benchmarks cannot distinguish an agent that genuinely traced a data flow from one that merely recalled a CVE from pretraining, and existing commit labels are noisy because they trace fixes back through version history.
method: The authors hand-audit 111 vulnerability-introducing commits across 83 repositories, 63 CWEs, and five languages against an explicit four-criterion definition, annotating 464 gold code blocks by their evidentiary role, then evaluate seven frontier LLMs with precision, recall, and F1 at file, block, and line granularity.
result: All models open most of the gold context while exploring but report far less as evidence — a 37 to 73 percentage-point gap at block level; Qwen3-Coder-Next views 86.3% of annotated lines yet cites only 12.9%, while GPT-5.5 views 73% and reports 36%.
conclusion: There is a substantial gap between finding relevant code and selecting it for a final report, a failure mode that verdict-level benchmarks are structurally unable to reveal.

title: Silent Failures In Agentic Security Evaluation: A Validated Harness For Tool-Call Mediation Under Indirect Prompt Injection
authors: Animesh Shaw
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that invoke privileged tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack the agent's actions. A growing body of work evaluates defenses against IPI, but the validity of that evaluation is rarely examined. We audit an IPI benchmark and its harness and identify four defect classes -- silent payload non-delivery, attack success scored by tool identity rather than arguments, false-rejection rate conflated with model incapacity, and the absence of an audit trail -- each of which yields a plausible, publishable, and incorrect number. We quantify the distortion by re-scoring identical execution traces under the defective and corrected definitions: on real agent behaviour, the tool-identity scorer reports a 21.7% attack-success rate where the true argument-level rate is 1.2%. In the sharpest case, an open model previously reported at 62.8% registers 0% under the corrected harness -- the prior figure largely an artifact of undelivered payloads and identity-level scoring. We release a harness whose construction makes each defect unrepresentable -- machine-checkable payload placement, argument-level attacker predicates, per-scenario environments, and mandatory trace persistence -- and use it to report three quantities the field does not: whether a compromised agent discloses the attack, the full security/utility operating curve of an LLM-judge defense, and tool-calling capability disentangled from defensive over-blocking. A corrected harness further overturns a reported "capability barrier": a model deemed incapable of tool use is in fact fully capable, its earlier result an artifact of environment mismatch. We argue that evaluation validity is a prerequisite for, not a footnote to, defense claims in agentic security, and provide an instrument that enforces it.
tldr: The paper audits an indirect prompt injection benchmark for LLM agents and identifies four evaluation defects that produce inflated attack-success rates, then releases a corrected harness enforcing valid measurement.
motivation: LLM agents using privileged tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, but existing defense evaluations may be invalid due to silent benchmark and harness flaws.
method: The authors audit an IPI benchmark and its harness, classify four defect types, re-score identical execution traces under defective and corrected definitions, and construct a validated harness with machine-checkable payload placement, argument-level predicates, per-scenario environments, and mandatory trace persistence.
result: Defective scoring reports a 21.7% attack-success rate where the corrected argument-level rate is 1.2%, and an open model previously at 62.8% registers 0% under the corrected harness; a reported capability barrier is shown to be an environment-mismatch artifact.
conclusion: Evaluation validity is a prerequisite for defense claims in agentic security, and the released harness enforces it while reporting new quantities such as disclosure behavior and security/utility operating curves.

title: Learning To Refer: Client-Resolved Generation For Privacy-Aware Language Models
authors: Jeongho Yoon, Chanhee Park, Yongchan Chun, Duong Tuan Thanh, Sungbin Han, Chanjun Park, Hyeonseok Moon, Heuiseok Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud-based large language models (LLMs) require users to disclose plaintext data to service providers, creating privacy risks in sensitive domains. Existing privacy-preserving approaches often trade utility for protection, incur substantial computational or communication overhead, remain vulnerable to reconstruction from intermediate representations, or protect only a subset of the training and inference pipeline. We introduce Client-Resolved Generation (CRG), a genera- tion interface that separates server-side generation from the lexical realization of input-derived content. The client transmits only pooled and noise-perturbed rep- resentations, while input-derived output content is represented using request-local positional references and resolved to its original strings only on the client. This interface protects private input and input-derived output content during both train- ing and inference while allowing the service provider to keep its proprietary model parameters hidden from the client. At the same time, exact lexical reuse remains possible without directly exposing the reused content on the provider-visible gen- eration path. We evaluate CRG on medical and document-grounded QA, sensi- tive identifier transfer, and tool calling, together with reconstruction and raw-logit leakage analyses. On SealTools, CRG improves complete-call exact match from 57.3% to 79.9% over the input-privacy framework PPFT, with larger gains as more required output content can be resolved through references. Together, these results show that CRG provides a practical interface for privacy-sensitive cloud LLMs by reducing plaintext exposure across both input and output pathways while preserv- ing task utility and server-side model confidentiality.
tldr: CRG is a privacy-preserving generation interface for cloud LLMs that separates server-side generation from client-side lexical realization to protect input and input-derived output content.
motivation: Cloud-based LLMs require users to disclose plaintext data, creating privacy risks in sensitive domains, while existing privacy-preserving methods often sacrifice utility or incur heavy overhead.
method: The client transmits pooled and noise-perturbed representations, and input-derived output content is represented via request-local positional references, resolved to original strings only on the client.
result: On SealTools, CRG improves complete-call exact match from 57.3% to 79.9% over PPFT, with larger gains as more required output content is resolvable through references.
conclusion: CRG provides a practical interface for privacy-sensitive cloud LLMs by reducing plaintext exposure across input and output pathways while preserving task utility and server-side model confidentiality.

title: You Can't Spot A Deepfake?And Neither Can Your Brain Nor Eyes: A Neurophysiological Framework For Deepfake Exploitation Of Cognitive Engagement And Implicit Visual Evaluation
authors: Cagri Arisoy, Md Imanul Huq, Amy W. Hays, Nitesh Saxena
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deepfakes have rapidly emerged as a pressing threat to information integrity and security because they exploit human trust in visual and auditory perception. Yet, little is known about whether humans and their underlying (sub)conscious neuro-physiological processes can reliably distinguish deepfake from real videos. We introduce DECEIVE (Deepfake Exploitation of Cognitive Engagement and Implicit Visual Evaluation), a framework that models how deepfake videos are validated as adversarial payloads through behavioral and neuro-physiological screening of viewers, and how attacks can be refined by selecting payloads that evade detection. The framework is dataset agnostic and applies to synthetic or real media. It is inherently dual-use: an adversary with equivalent measurements could iterate on candidate manipulations and retain those that evade human detection. This motivates open, defensive evaluation. Measuring which deepfakes defeat human perception establishes a realistic bound on attacker capability against which detection tooling, provenance and watermarking mechanisms, and user-facing protections can be assessed. As an instantiation, we conducted an EEG and eye-tracking study in which participants viewed real, deepfake, and look-alike videos drawn from Celeb-DF and a curated celebrity set, while behavioral judgments and implicit responses were recorded. Contrary to expectations of subconscious differentiation suggested by prior work on paintings and phishing websites, no statistically significant neuro-physiological differences emerged between real and deepfake videos, although clear distinctions were observed for look-alike videos. Behaviorally, participants accepted 26.68% of manipulated clips as authentic, rising to 31.94% for familiar identities, confirming the studied deepfakes as effective adversarial payloads within DECEIVE.
tldr: The paper introduces a neurophysiological framework called DECEIVE to evaluate whether humans can subconsciously distinguish deepfake videos, finding no significant EEG or eye-tracking differences between real and deepfake videos.
motivation: Deepfakes threaten information integrity by exploiting human perceptual trust, but it is unclear whether underlying neurophysiological processes can reliably detect them.
method: The authors conducted an EEG and eye-tracking study where participants viewed real, deepfake, and look-alike videos from Celeb-DF and a curated celebrity set while behavioral judgments and implicit responses were recorded.
result: No statistically significant neurophysiological differences emerged between real and deepfake videos, though look-alike videos showed clear distinctions; behaviorally, participants accepted 26.68% of manipulated clips as authentic, rising to 31.94% for familiar identities.
conclusion: The studied deepfakes act as effective adversarial payloads that evade both conscious and subconscious human detection, motivating open defensive evaluation and establishing a realistic bound on attacker capability.

title: Progression- Vs Automata-based Anticipatory Monitoring Of Ltl Over Finite Traces (Extended Version)
authors: Sarah Winkler, Toryn Klassen, Sheila Mcilraith, Marco Montali
abstract: ArXiv:2609.32912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When safety-critical systems are developed from a known internal specification, their correctness can be established by model checking. In the frequent case where such a specification is unknown or inaccessible, runtime verification presents an attractive alternative, e.g., to ascertain that autonomous and agentic systems as well as business processes satisfy desirable properties and/or comply with safety requirements. In this paper we study anticipatory monitoring, an advanced form of runtime verification, where the monitoring state is determined by both the trace prefix seen so far, and all its possible finite-length, future continuations. We focus on monitoring linear-time properties that may involve arithmetic constraints. Automata-based approaches, the de-facto standard in this setting, are notorious for their computational complexity. We propose an alternative approach based on progression and LTLf satisfiability checking, for both propositional and arithmetic settings. We experimentally compare the automata- and progression-based approaches, and a third method that combines the two. Our experiments suggest that the progression-based approach often succeeds in producing a verdict when the automata constructions do not terminate, especially for the arithmetic setting. For the propositional setting, the combined technique provides a good tradeoff.
tldr: The paper compares progression-based and automata-based approaches to anticipatory runtime monitoring of LTL properties over finite traces, including settings with arithmetic constraints.
motivation: When the specification of a safety-critical system is unknown or inaccessible, runtime verification is needed to check that traces satisfy desired properties; anticipatory monitoring strengthens this by considering all possible future continuations.
method: The authors propose a progression-based approach using LTLf satisfiability checking as an alternative to the de facto automata-based constructions, for both propositional and arithmetic settings, and also evaluate a hybrid of the two.
result: Experiments show that the progression-based method often returns a verdict where automata constructions fail to terminate, especially in the arithmetic setting, while the combined technique offers a favorable tradeoff for propositional properties.
conclusion: Progression-based and hybrid monitoring provide practical alternatives to automata-based anticipatory runtime verification, broadening applicability to specifications with arithmetic constraints.

title: Exact Integration And Invertibility Completeness Of The Nonlinear Relaxation Equation
authors: Luk\'a\v{s} Mraz\'ik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the nonlinear initial value problem [MATH] modeling polytropic gas permeation. For rational [MATH], we derive the exact primitive via cyclotomic partial fraction decomposition, establishing its real trigonometric representation. By synthesizing Ritt's theorem with Rosenlicht's differential algebraic residue criterion, we prove the exact step response [MATH] is an elementary function if and only if [MATH]. Admitting the Lambert [MATH] function extends closed-form solvability strictly to [MATH]. Finally, the asymptotic limit [MATH] converges to a singular dynamics solved by the logarithmic integral. These results constitute a complete classification of all explicit closed-form solutions admitted by this system.
tldr: The paper provides a complete classification of closed-form solutions to a nonlinear relaxation equation modeling polytropic gas permeation, using cyclotomic partial fractions, Ritt's theorem, and Rosenlicht's differential algebraic residue criterion.
motivation: The nonlinear initial value problem governing polytropic gas permeation lacks a systematic understanding of when explicit closed-form solutions exist and what functional form they take.
method: The authors derive exact primitives via cyclotomic partial fraction decomposition, then combine Ritt's theorem with Rosenlicht's differential algebraic residue criterion to characterize elementary integrability, and extend the analysis using the Lambert W function and logarithmic integral.
result: They prove the step response is elementary if and only if a specific rationality condition holds, that admitting Lambert W strictly extends closed-form solvability, and that the asymptotic limit converges to singular dynamics solved by the logarithmic integral.
conclusion: The work constitutes a complete classification of all explicit closed-form solutions admitted by this system, though it lies entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Multiple Testing Of A Function's Monotonicity
authors: David M. Kaplan Wei Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.31958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Instead of having a single "yes" or "no" result from a test of the global null hypothesis that a function is increasing, we propose a multiple testing procedure of the function's increasingness at several points. If the global null is rejected, then multiple testing provides more information about why. If the global null is not rejected, then multiple testing can provide stronger evidence in favor of increasingness, by rejecting null hypotheses that the function is decreasing. Our approach uses high-level assumptions that apply to a broad class of causal and descriptive statistical models. By inverting the proposed multiple testing procedure that controls the familywise error rate, we also generate "inner" and "outer" confidence sets for the set of points at which the function is increasing. With high asymptotic probability, the inner confidence set is contained within the true set, whereas the outer confidence set contains the true set. We also improve power with stepdown and two-stage procedures. Simulation and empirical examples illustrate the new methodology, and all code is provided.
tldr: The paper proposes a multiple testing procedure for assessing whether a function is increasing at multiple points, with inner and outer confidence sets for the set of increasing points.
